rationale: This trial tests ivonescimab (a PD-1/VEGF bispecific) plus ligufalimab (a CD47 antibody) against pembrolizumab, with overall survival as the primary endpoint. Phase 2 data in first-line HNSCC showed high response rates, and ivonescimab beat pembrolizumab on progression-free survival in China (HARMONi-2); Akeso's China-only phase 3 trials have generally succeeded. Against that, OS against an active PD-1 comparator is a hard bar, VEGF blockade in HNSCC (E1305) did not significantly improve OS, and CD47 agents have repeatedly failed elsewhere. I am not aware of any topline result, so I land near a coin flip, slightly below.

This is a small (about 45 patients), open-label, Lilly-sponsored pediatric phase 2 trial, likely run to meet pediatric regulatory obligations, testing a CDK4/6 inhibitor added to temozolomide in newly diagnosed non-pontine pediatric high-grade glioma. CDK4/6 inhibitors have shown little efficacy in adult or pediatric gliomas, and pediatric HGG adjuvant trials have almost uniformly failed to improve survival endpoints. With this sample size, power to show a two-sided p<0.05 benefit in event-free survival is low, even if the protocol uses a lenient one-sided alpha. Success is therefore unlikely.

Levulan Kerastick (ALA 20%) with blue-light PDT is an approved AK therapy, and prior vehicle-controlled trials showed large effects: complete clearance of roughly 50-70% versus 5-30% for vehicle, including short-incubation (1-3 h) field-directed face/scalp studies. With about 40 patients per arm, 4-8 mild to moderate lesions per patient, and two possible PDT sessions, the trial is well powered even if a reformulation or shorter incubation trims the effect somewhat. The main risks are an unusually high vehicle-plus-light response or underpowered per-incubation-time comparisons, but one arm succeeding is very likely. The trial is still recruiting, so no result is public.

Placebo-controlled phase 3 LGS trials using percent change in drop seizures have historically succeeded fairly often (rufinamide, clobazam, cannabidiol, fenfluramine), though soticlestat narrowly failed. Carisbamate has mixed prior efficacy: inconsistent phase 3 results in focal epilepsy, and only small open-label phase 2 signals in LGS. Having two dose arms gives two chances to hit, and ~84 patients per arm is reasonably powered for typical LGS effect sizes. The trial is still recruiting with primary completion in 2027, so no result is public.

This is essentially a Chinese replication of NETTER-1, which compared 177Lu-DOTATATE with high-dose octreotide LAR in SSTR-positive, SSA-progressed G1/G2 GEP-NETs and showed a very large PFS benefit (HR ~0.21, with 20-month PFS of about 65% vs 11%). With 184 patients randomized 1:1 and an 18-month PFS rate endpoint, the trial is well powered for even a much smaller effect than NETTER-1 found. Remaining risks include the quality of the domestic radiopharmaceutical, execution at a single site, an open-label design, and the trial still recruiting near its planned completion date. I am not aware of any public topline result.

vYF is Sanofi's Vero-cell, serum-free version of the same 17D-204 live-attenuated strain used in Stamaril and YF-VAX. Phase II and adult Phase III data have generally shown seroconversion rates similar to the licensed vaccines. Seroconversion after yellow fever vaccination is very high, about 90% or more even in young children, and with about 600 vYF recipients per age stratum, a non-inferiority margin on the first-listed comparison against Stamaril should be met. The residual risk is lower immunogenicity from the new manufacturing process in infants, or a tight margin across multiple comparisons.

LBL-024 is Leads Biolabs' PD-L1/4-1BB bispecific, which has shown encouraging activity in extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma. This NSCLC substudy has only experimental arms; the one randomization in Cohort 1A compares LBL-024+docetaxel with or without bevacizumab, so the ORR primary endpoint is likely descriptive, with no powered comparison against a true control. A sponsor would probably call reported ORRs positive, but a formal significant between-arm difference is unlikely, so resolution is ambiguous. I have no knowledge of results, and primary completion is not until late 2026.

The FGF21 class is well validated in MASH: efruxifermin (an Fc-fusion like AP025), pegozafermin and efimosfermin all hit biopsy endpoints in phase 2 with large effects on NASH resolution and fibrosis. The primary endpoint here is a lenient composite (NASH resolution OR fibrosis improvement), which helps, but with about 40 patients per arm, variable placebo rates in Chinese biopsy trials, and unknown potency for this specific molecule, the trial could be underpowered. The record still shows recruiting and no results appear to be public, so I estimate a moderate-to-favorable chance of success.

NoNO-42 is a next-generation PSD-95-targeting neuroprotectant, likely engineered to resist the alteplase/plasmin cleavage that undermined nerinetide. Nerinetide itself failed in ESCAPE-NA1 overall and in ESCAPE-NEXT, and acute stroke neuroprotection has a long history of near-universal phase 2/3 failure. A 600-patient open-label, blinded-endpoint trial with an mRS shift primary endpoint has only modest power for the small effects plausible in a thrombolysed population. The trial is still recruiting at only 9 Canadian sites, so no result is public, and the base rate points to a low probability of success.

UBT251 is a GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist licensed from United Laboratories, and early Chinese studies reportedly showed substantial weight loss. Incretin-class agonists almost always beat placebo on percent body-weight change over 28 weeks, so Part B's efficacy comparison is very likely to be significant. The first-listed primary outcome (Part A TEAEs) is descriptive safety with no hypothesis test, which makes it unclear how the trial will be scored. The main uncertainty is therefore resolution ambiguity rather than drug efficacy, and I know of no public topline result for this trial.

REGN7508 (cenvacibart) is a factor XI catalytic-domain antibody. As I recall, Regeneron's Phase 2 ROXI-VTE TKA studies showed markedly lower VTE rates than enoxaparin and numerically lower rates than apixaban. Across the class (abelacimab, osocimab, FXI-ASO, milvexian), FXI inhibition has consistently beaten enoxaparin in knee arthroplasty on venographic VTE endpoints. The primary comparison is probably non-inferiority or superiority versus enoxaparin and/or apixaban, and with about 2000 patients and high event rates the trial is well powered, though superiority over apixaban would be the harder bar. Primary completion is not expected until February 2027, so no results are public.

Phase III trials of intra-articular MSC products for knee OA have mixed results: Korea's JointStem reported positive WOMAC results, but many MSC trials show large placebo responses and modest separation, and this trial uses an active hyaluronate comparator, which raises the bar. CBMG/Wuxi Cellular's earlier ReJoin and AlloJoin studies reported favorable WOMAC trends versus HA, and Chinese industry-sponsored trials tend to report positively. The 520-patient sample gives reasonable power for a moderate effect. Still, a 48-week WOMAC difference against an active comparator is uncertain, and results are not yet public (primary completion is planned for December 2026 and enrollment was still ongoing).

The first-listed primary outcome is phase Ib safety, and the efficacy primary is ORR in a small, open-label randomized phase II of roughly 25–35 patients per arm against gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel, whose ORR is typically about 25–35%. Early Akeso data for ivonescimab plus cadonilimab plus chemotherapy in PDAC reportedly showed high response rates, and a sponsor-run open-label trial with an ORR endpoint favors a positive-looking readout. However, the design looks descriptive rather than powered for a formal comparison, and with small arms even a 20-point ORR gain may not reach p<0.05. PD-1/VEGF and CTLA-4 strategies also have a poor record in pancreatic cancer.

ZEN-3694 plus enzalutamide showed encouraging but uncontrolled rPFS (about 9 months) in the post-abiraterone phase 1b/2a study, and enzalutamide after abiraterone is a weak control, especially in poor abiraterone responders. Against that, BET inhibitors have a poor track record, dose-limiting toxicities such as thrombocytopenia may limit exposure, and the Cohort A comparison is modestly sized. Enrollment by a small sponsor appears slow, with the trial still recruiting close to its planned primary completion. Base rates for randomized phase 2 oncology combinations of a novel mechanism suggest roughly a one-in-three chance of a significant rPFS benefit.

This is a randomized, double-blind equivalence trial comparing Qilu's denosumab biosimilar QL1206 with Prolia on percent change in lumbar-spine BMD at 12 months, a sensitive, low-variability endpoint. Comparative trials of denosumab biosimilars against Prolia have almost uniformly met their equivalence margins, and QL1206 is already approved in China against Xgeva, which supports analytical and PK similarity. The main risk is the modest sample size of 278, which leaves less room if the margin is tight or variability is higher than expected. Primary completion is planned for January 2027, so no result is public yet.

Randomized trials of new immunotherapies and vaccines in newly diagnosed glioblastoma have almost uniformly failed (e.g., rindopepimut, nivolumab in CheckMate-498/548, DCVax controversies), so the base rate is very low. IGV-001's evidence comes from a small single-arm Phase 1 at Thomas Jefferson with encouraging PFS in a higher-dose subgroup, which is weak evidence prone to selection bias. This Phase 2b is small (n=99), so it can only detect a large PFS effect, though centrally reviewed PFS is a somewhat more attainable endpoint than OS and a Phase 2b may use a relaxed alpha. I know of no public topline result, and primary completion is planned for 2027-01.

IBAT inhibition is a validated mechanism for cholestatic pruritus in PBC: GSK's linerixibat met its Phase 3 GLISTEN itch endpoint. Mirum's VANTAGE Part 1 interim data showed meaningful itch reductions on volixibat, which supported advancing the 20 mg dose. The main risks are the high placebo response typical of PBC itch trials (linerixibat's Phase 2b missed partly for this reason) and diarrhea-related unblinding or dropout. Powering looks adequate with about 333 patients, and primary completion is listed for 2027-01, so the topline result does not appear to be public.

This is a small open-label phase 2 trial (n≈100, 3 sites) from a micro-cap sponsor, testing an autologous irradiated whole-tumor-cell vaccine with BCG as adjuvant therapy after prostatectomy. Earlier cell-based prostate cancer vaccines, such as GVAX, failed in randomized trials, and autologous tumor-cell vaccines have rarely shown significant DFS benefits. With about 22 months of follow-up and a modest event count, the study has little power unless the effect is very large, and enrollment and completion risk is also substantial. An open-label design measuring PSA recurrence could introduce some bias, but a statistically significant DFS win still looks unlikely.

Telitacicept (TACI-Fc) produced a large MG-ADL benefit over placebo in RemeGen's Chinese Phase 3 in generalized MG and is approved in China, so the mechanism has supporting evidence and the sponsor-run Chinese trials have tended to succeed. Ocular MG is harder to win in: it has lower antibody positivity, its primary endpoint is patient-reported (MGII PRO ocular) and prone to placebo response, the sample is modest (120 patients), and there are no validated precedents for drug success in this population. Balancing the strong prior efficacy signal against these design and disease uncertainties gives a probability modestly above even.

The primary endpoint is safety and tolerability (AE, SAE, DLT and AESI rates) in a small Phase 1/2 multiple-ascending-dose study, with no formal efficacy comparison against placebo. XTMAB-16 is an anti-TNFα monoclonal antibody, a well-characterized mechanism with a known safety profile, so serious unexpected toxicity at these doses seems unlikely. Sponsors usually describe such trials as having met the primary endpoint when the drug is generally well tolerated. The main risks are the ambiguity of scoring a non-comparative safety endpoint, plus possible infection signals or slow enrollment at a small sponsor.

Adding a BCL-2 inhibitor to a BTK inhibitor is biologically well validated: ibrutinib plus venetoclax deepened responses and improved PFS over ibrutinib alone in FLAIR, and lisaftoclax has shown activity and gained approval in China. The main risks are a low PFS event rate in patients already controlled on BTKi for at least 12 months, an open-label design, and a still-recruiting trial that may need long follow-up to collect enough events. The sponsor is small, but the combination-versus-backbone design generally favors success, so I place the probability moderately above the phase 3 oncology base rate.

Empagliflozin is a proven SGLT2 inhibitor that reliably lowers HbA1c by about 0.6–0.8% versus placebo when added to metformin plus a DPP-4 inhibitor, as seen in prior Korean triple-therapy trials. This is a regulatory-style Korean Phase 3 by Celltrion, supporting a fixed-dose combination, with about 57 patients per arm. That gives very high power for a placebo-adjusted effect of roughly 0.5% or more. The main risks are operational (enrollment, a high placebo response) rather than pharmacological, and no results are public yet.

The first-listed primary outcome is safety (TEAE and SAE incidence), not an efficacy comparison, so a sponsor topline would most likely describe it as met if claseprubart is well tolerated. That seems likely, given clean safety in prior claseprubart studies and in other complement C1s antibodies. The mechanism is also supported in this disease: argenx's empasiprubart (anti-C2) Phase 2 ARDA trial in MMN reduced the need for Ig retreatment, so the time-to-Ig-retreatment secondary endpoint could plausibly favor drug even with only 46 patients. The main risks are how a safety-only endpoint gets adjudicated and a small chance of an imbalance in adverse events or infections.

NMD670 is a first-in-class ClC-1 chloride channel inhibitor; its single-dose Phase 1/2a study showed numerical QMG improvements, which gives proof of mechanism but no robust multi-dose efficacy data. This Phase 2b trial is small (about 21 per arm) and short (21 days), with placebo-controlled QMG change on top of background therapy. A symptomatic agent may give only modest effects of 1–3 points against placebo responses of a similar size, so power is marginal. Having three dose arms helps, but multiplicity adjustments and the historical failure rate of first-in-class Phase 2 trials in neuromuscular disease keep the probability below even.

HDM1005 is a GLP-1/GIP dual agonist tested head-to-head against tirzepatide, an approved drug with the same mechanism, in an open-label phase 2 trial with about 93 patients per arm. The record does not say whether the comparison is for superiority or non-inferiority. If superiority is required, beating tirzepatide by a significant margin is unlikely given similar mechanisms and doses. Non-inferiority or just a numerically similar result is more plausible, but whether that would count as success is unclear, so the probability stays modest.

Zasocitinib is a selective TYK2 inhibitor, which acts mainly through IL-23/IL-12 and type I IFN signalling. IL-23 blockade (guselkumab, risankizumab) has failed in HS, whereas broader JAK1 or TYK2/JAK1 inhibitors (upadacitinib, povorcitinib, brepocitinib) have shown activity, so the mechanistic rationale for a pure TYK2 agent is uncertain. The primary endpoint, HiSCR75, is stringent, and HS placebo responses are noisy. With only about 91 patients, the trial needs a large effect to reach significance, so I assign a below-base-rate probability for this first test of a new mechanism in a hard disease.

In REMIX-1/2, remibrutinib separated from placebo on UAS7 as early as Week 1, with roughly a 7–9 point placebo-adjusted change by Week 2–4. In CUPID, dupilumab's benefit built slowly and was only modestly above placebo at early timepoints. Novartis chose the Week 4 endpoint to exploit that onset-speed difference, and with ~400 patients randomized 1:1 a plausible 4–6 point advantage (SD ~11–12) gives very high power. The main risks are a faster-than-expected dupilumab response with the 600 mg loading dose, high US placebo-like improvement in both arms shrinking the gap, and the inherent unpredictability of head-to-head trials.

The primary outcomes are safety measures (number and severity of adverse events) with no prespecified efficacy comparison, so 'success' likely amounts to acceptable tolerability. Edgewise has publicly reported that sevasemten was generally well tolerated in LYNX and related Duchenne and Becker studies, with CK and fsTnI reductions during the 12-week placebo-controlled part. The main risk is scoring ambiguity, since a safety-only endpoint has no clean statistical win, plus some chance of emerging long-term safety signals before the 2027 primary completion.

Zongertinib is a potent, HER2-selective, EGFR-sparing TKI. In the Beamion LUNG-1 treatment-naive cohort it produced an objective response rate around 75% with durable responses, which led to accelerated approval. Pembrolizumab plus platinum-pemetrexed works relatively poorly in HER2-mutant NSCLC, with median PFS of roughly 6–8 months, and first-line targeted agents in oncogene-driven NSCLC have usually beaten chemotherapy-based controls on PFS. Remaining risks are an open-label design, possible crossover or durability surprises, and a large sample, but a central-review PFS benefit appears likely and no topline result is public yet.

This is a non-inferiority comparability trial of the same MVA-BN virus, given in the same infectious-unit dose range, with only the production cell substrate changed from CEF to the CCX.E10 quail line. The sponsor is very experienced, with prior lot-consistency and freeze-dried versus liquid comparability trials of MVA-BN that met their margins. With about 485 per arm, the study is well powered for a GMT-ratio margin, assuming the usual 0.67 or 0.5. The main risk is that a substrate change alters immunogenicity per infectious unit, causing a GMT shortfall, but that seems unlikely given the sponsor's process development.

This is a PK equivalence trial of a biosimilar (ABP 234) against Keytruda, run by Amgen, which has a strong biosimilar track record; the success bar is AUC ratio 90% CIs falling within standard bioequivalence margins (typically 80–125%). Biosimilar PK similarity studies almost always succeed when the analytical similarity work was solid, though variability in a patient population (n=163) and the co-primary steady-state AUC requirement add some risk. Other pembrolizumab biosimilars (e.g., Samsung Bioepis, Sandoz, Amgen's own) have generally shown PK equivalence. I am not aware of any public topline result for this trial, and primary completion is planned for December 2026.

HDM1002 is Huadong's oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist. In this Chinese metformin add-on trial its HbA1c change is compared with dapagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor that typically lowers HbA1c only about 0.8–1.0%. Oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonists such as orforglipron have beaten dapagliflozin on HbA1c (ACHIEVE-2), and earlier-phase HDM1002 data reportedly showed meaningful glucose lowering, so 200 patients per arm gives ample power for one of three doses to succeed. The main risks are an unexpected safety problem (e.g., liver signals seen in the class), high dropout from GI tolerability, or a weaker-than-expected effect, so I discount from near-certainty.

Oral L-fucose has a clear mechanistic rationale in LAD II (SLC35C1-CDG). Case reports show restored sialyl-Lewis X expression on neutrophils in responders, and this trial excludes known non-responders, so the biomarker effect is likely large and consistent. However, with only about 4 patients in a crossover, formal significance is fragile: nonparametric tests cannot reach p<0.05 at n=4, and results may be reported descriptively. The trial has also been recruiting since 2022 at a single site under a small sponsor, so it may not complete with an interpretable topline.

SPH4336 appears to be a CDK4/6 inhibitor from Shanghai Pharmaceuticals. It is being tested here as CDK4/6 rechallenge plus endocrine therapy after progression on a prior CDK4/6 inhibitor, a setting with mixed precedent: postMONARCH and MAINTAIN were positive on PFS, while PACE and PALMIRA were negative. The first-listed primary endpoint is objective response rate, which in this setting differed only modestly and non-significantly even in positive trials (e.g., 17% vs 13% in postMONARCH), so a significant ORR difference at about 254 patients is hard to achieve. The trial is still recruiting, has no public results, and the sponsor has limited global track record, so I put the probability modestly below the base rate.

Cariprazine is a proven antipsychotic in adult schizophrenia, and most atypicals (aripiprazole, risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, lurasidone) succeeded in adolescent placebo-controlled trials. However, several adolescent trials failed or were mixed (asenapine, ziprasidone, paliperidone at some doses, brexpiprazole not reaching significance) because of high placebo response and heterogeneous enrollment. This trial has two doses, which raises the chance that at least one arm succeeds. It has also enrolled very slowly over about seven years, partly at Eastern European sites disrupted by the war, which adds noise and dropout risk, so I put it modestly above even odds.

This is a small (n=100), descriptive Phase 3 safety and immunogenicity study of Sanofi/SK bioscience's PCV21 against Prevnar 20 in children with sickle cell disease, and none of the primary outcomes appears to carry a formal superiority or non-inferiority hypothesis. Earlier PCV21 (SP0202) data showed robust immunogenicity and acceptable reactogenicity, and special-population studies like this one are usually reported as favorable or supportive. The main uncertainty is how a descriptive outcome will be scored, plus a small chance of a safety or immunogenicity signal in this population. I estimate a moderately high probability that the result will be read as meeting its primary objectives.

Ritlecitinib is an approved oral JAK3/TEC-family inhibitor, and its TEC-family coverage includes BTK. BTK inhibition is clinically validated in CSU, with remibrutinib positive in phase 3 and rilzabrutinib positive in phase 2, so the mechanistic rationale is strong and Pfizer likely moved forward on supportive signals. With about 65 patients per arm, two doses and a continuous UAS7 change endpoint at week 12, the trial has reasonable power to detect the typical 5–10 point separation from placebo. Remaining risks are a high placebo response, and that ritlecitinib's BTK occupancy in mast cells may be weaker than that of dedicated BTK inhibitors.

Pharmacotherapy for sepsis-associated ARDS has an extremely poor track record: statins, beta-agonists, keratinocyte growth factor, interferon-beta, sivelestat and many others have failed to improve ventilator-free days or mortality in randomized trials. YD0743 is a novel continuous-infusion agent from a small Chinese sponsor, and there is no public phase 1b or efficacy data. Its bleeding-related exclusions hint at an anticoagulant or anti-protease mechanism, a class with a history of failure in sepsis. With about 100 patients per arm, a noisy ventilator-free-days endpoint and two doses offering slight multiplicity, the chance of a significant result is low but not negligible, given possible single-site or homogeneous-population effects in China.

Remigromig (EYE103/Restoret, now Merck's MK-3000) is a multispecific antibody that activates the Wnt/Frizzled-4 pathway and also blocks VEGF. The first-listed primary endpoint appears to be non-inferiority in BCVA change at week 52 against monthly ranibizumab, with superiority listed as a secondary outcome. Because both arms are dosed monthly in year 1 and the drug carries its own anti-VEGF activity, matching ranibizumab within a typical ~4-letter margin is likely, and early-phase AMARONE data reportedly showed good visual gains. The main risks are an unexpected safety or immunogenicity problem, a dose-related shortfall, or tight margins in a large trial, though one of two doses succeeding is enough.

The registered primary outcomes are now only descriptive safety measures (DLT counts, any AE, discontinuations due to AE), with no prespecified comparison against belzutifan monotherapy. Such endpoints have no significance test, so 'success' depends on whether a tolerable recommended palbociclib dose is established. The record looks amended: only combination arms remain and enrollment is just 60, which suggests the randomized efficacy comparison was dropped or deprioritized, a weak signal for the program. Belzutifan plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor is likely tolerable at some dose, but because a descriptive-safety trial is ambiguous to score, I stay near even with a slight lean toward 'met'.

This Phase 3 catch-up study of Sanofi/SK bioscience's PCV21 (SP0202) against Prevnar 20 has descriptive primary endpoints: the first-listed outcome is immediate adverse events, followed by immunogenicity counts with no stated non-inferiority margin or hypothesis test. Catch-up studies like this usually just describe safety and immune responses, and an outcome would likely be judged successful if the vaccine's safety is comparable and immune responses are robust. Phase 2 infant data for SP0202 showed immunogenicity comparable to PCV13 and an acceptable safety profile, and catch-up regimens in older children are generally highly immunogenic. The main risk is ambiguity about how a descriptive result gets scored, plus a small chance of an unexpected safety signal.

IBR854 is an early-stage cell therapy from a small Chinese biotech, tested here in a tiny 30-patient, 2:1 randomized, open-label phase II against pazopanib, which has a median PFS of about 8–11 months in first-line ccRCC. With roughly 10 control patients and a planned primary completion of end-2026, there will be few PFS events, so the trial has very little power to show a statistically significant difference unless the effect is very large. The study looks exploratory and is unlikely to have been powered for formal significance, and no mechanistic precedent strongly supports large benefit, so success is improbable.

ZILRETTA, an extended-release intra-articular triamcinolone, beat saline on week-12 pain in its pivotal knee OA Phase 3, a difference of about 1 NRS point. Pacira reportedly moved to Phase 3 after supportive Phase 2 shoulder data, though I am not certain of those results. Shoulder OA trials tend to have high placebo responses, and this one is small (100 vs 50); with an NRS SD near 2.5, power is roughly 60–75% for a difference of 0.8–1.0. The placebo-response-reduction training and a proven mechanism help, but saline injections in a joint carry substantial placebo effects, so I am only moderately confident.

This is a small open-label phase 2 with no control arm, and its primary endpoints are safety and ELISpot immunogenicity, so there is no formal superiority test to pass or fail. The pNGVL3-hICD HER2 ICD plasmid vaccine with GM-CSF has repeatedly induced HER2-specific T-cell responses with good tolerability in earlier breast cancer studies. A sponsor-run proof-of-concept trial like this is likely to be reported as positive on immunogenicity and safety. The main risks are ambiguity in how 'success' is judged without a statistical comparison, and possibly weaker immune responses after gastrectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy.

The first-listed primary outcome is a safety measure: the proportion of participants with grade ≥3 adverse events versus placebo by day 90, in a small (n=36) phase 1/2 trial of what appears to be an allogeneic biologic or cell-derived product. Under a strict superiority reading, a statistically significant reduction in grade ≥3 adverse events versus placebo is nearly impossible at this size. However, a sponsor would likely announce the primary safety endpoint as 'met' if there is no excess toxicity, which seems plausible. Given that ambiguity in how the result will be scored, and the trial still recruiting with no public results, I put this near the middle, leaning below 50%.

ARTEMIS is the first outcomes test of IL-6 inhibition with ziltivekimab, given early after myocardial infarction. Genetic IL-6 receptor data and CANTOS (IL-1β inhibition, HR about 0.85, p of about 0.03 with roughly 1,400 events) support the inflammation hypothesis. However, CLEAR SYNERGY's neutral result with colchicine in a similar post-MI population shows how hard incremental MACE benefit is to demonstrate on top of modern standard of care. With 10,000 patients and only about 2 years of follow-up, the trial likely accrues fewer events than CANTOS, so a modest CANTOS-like effect could easily miss significance, and infection risk could offset some of the benefit.

This is an exploratory, open-label phase II study of Kelun's SKB518 ADC. The first-listed primary outcome is AE incidence, and the efficacy endpoints (ORR, PFS) are mostly single-arm, with no clear prespecified statistical comparison. Kelun's ADCs have generally shown good activity in lung cancer, and SCLC responds well to novel ADCs, so a positive-sounding readout is plausible. Still, the lack of a formal hypothesis test and the uncertainty about how success would be judged keep this forecast moderate.

This is a first-in-human Phase 1/2a SAD/MAD study whose primary endpoints are purely descriptive safety measures (TEAEs, labs, ECG, vital signs), with no formal efficacy comparison against placebo. Such trials are usually counted as meeting their primary endpoint when the drug proves acceptably safe and tolerable at the doses studied, which most oral small molecules do in short dosing. The main risks are unexpected toxicity, early termination, or a small sponsor losing funding. I have no knowledge of any public results.

This is a small (n=30, roughly 7 per arm) exploratory phase II trial of a first-in-class anti-IL-11 antibody in pathological scar, a new mechanism in an indication where systemic biologics are unproven. The trial is not powered for formal significance testing, and a 12-week window is short for measurable change on mVSS, so a statistically significant win over placebo is unlikely even if the drug has some activity. Three dose arms raise the chance that one arm reaches nominal significance somewhat, but sponsor-reported results will more likely describe numerical trends.

This is an investigator-driven trial from the Necker/Pasteur group, whose earlier open-label and retrospective series of ceftriaxone plus metronidazole followed by rifampicin, moxifloxacin and metronidazole reported high remission rates in Hurley 1–2 hidradenitis suppurativa. Lymecycline is a weak comparator, so IHS4-90 remission at week 12 in the control arm should be low, perhaps 10–15%. With 92 patients, a true difference of about 25–30 points would be well powered. Risks include effect shrinkage under double-blind conditions, the stringent IHS4-90 endpoint, and dropouts from poor tolerance of the intensive regimen.

This is a small randomized phase 2 (about 120 patients, 2:1) testing whether adding the CD70 antibody cusatuzumab to venetoclax/azacitidine prolongs overall survival in unfit AML. Overall survival on that backbone is a demanding endpoint, and a trial this size can only detect a large hazard ratio. Many add-on strategies to ven/aza or aza have failed on survival, including magrolimab, sabatolimab and pevonedistat. Cusatuzumab's earlier single-arm data with aza and with ven/aza were encouraging but not clearly better than historical controls, so a statistically significant OS benefit appears unlikely.

PHOENIX (ibrutinib + R-CHOP in non-GCB DLBCL) missed its primary endpoint. Its signal was limited to patients under 60, and R-CHOP intensity suffered from toxicity in older patients. ESCALADE uses the better-tolerated acalabrutinib, caps age at 75 and enrolls about 611 patients, which plausibly gives it a better chance than PHOENIX. Even so, frontline DLBCL add-on trials have a poor track record (POLARIX is the main exception), and the inclusion of IPI 1 and unclassified patients dilutes the ABC-specific effect, so modest odds seem right.

SHR0302 (ivarmacitinib) is a selective JAK1 inhibitor that has already succeeded in phase 3 trials in rheumatoid arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis. In psoriatic arthritis, the same mechanism has consistently beaten placebo on ACR20 (tofacitinib, upadacitinib, filgotinib). With about 140 patients per arm, a largely biologic-naive population, a placebo comparator and the sensitive ACR20 endpoint, the trial is well powered for the typical 20-30 point treatment difference. Primary completion is not until December 2026, so I am not aware of any public result.

This is an uncontrolled Phase Ib dose-escalation and expansion study whose primary outcomes are DLT incidence, safety and PK, so there is no superiority comparison; 'success' can only mean defining an MTD/RP2D and characterizing tolerability. Conference reports have described the ribociclib+letrozole doublet and the triple combination with alpelisib, with RP2Ds identified but notable hyperglycemia and other toxicity in the triplet. Ribociclib+letrozole later went on to approval, which suggests the doublet objectives were met. Because success is ambiguous for a safety-only primary endpoint and the final results are not formally posted, I put the probability moderately above even.

This is a tiny (n=36, single-site) phase 2a first-in-patient efficacy test of a novel antifungal, occidiofungin, at a low gel concentration, run by a small sponsor. The primary endpoint is strict: a VSS total score of 0 at Days 4, 8 and 25, so even an active drug may score low (a Day 4 complete cure is rare), although placebo rates should also be low. With roughly 18 per arm, power is limited, and the study may be largely descriptive with no formal hypothesis test. A real antifungal effect versus placebo is plausible, but a statistically significant win on this composite is uncertain.

This is an uncontrolled, randomized dose-optimization phase 2 with no comparator. The first primary endpoint is TEAE frequency, so there is no formal superiority test, and 'success' depends on the sponsor reporting acceptable safety and meaningful PSA50 activity. Prior TATCIST data for 225Ac-PSMA-I&T in post-177Lu-PSMA patients showed PSA50 rates of roughly 40-50% with manageable xerostomia and hematologic toxicity. AstraZeneca's acquisition of Fusion suggests continued development and a likely favorable framing, but the descriptive endpoint and the hard post-Lu population leave substantial uncertainty.

IBI363 is Innovent's PD-1/IL-2α-bias bispecific fusion protein, and here it is tested head-to-head against an active standard, pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, whose pCR rate in non-squamous NSCLC is roughly 18–25%. With about 85 patients per arm, a statistically significant pCR gain would need an absolute improvement near 15–20 points, a large effect that no next-generation IO agent has yet shown in the neoadjuvant setting. The trial is also a single-site, open-label phase 2 that may be primarily descriptive, and IBI363's strongest signals so far have come in IO-resistant squamous disease rather than non-squamous. Promising early data and the IL-2 mechanism leave some room for a large effect, but superiority over an active comparator is more likely to fail than succeed.

AK112 (ivonescimab, a PD-1/VEGF bispecific) has won Akeso-run Chinese phase 3 trials in NSCLC, including head-to-head studies, and early phase 2 data with FOLFOXIRI in first-line mCRC showed high response rates. However, the population is mostly MSS colorectal cancer, where adding PD-1 blockade to chemo plus bevacizumab has given inconsistent results: AtezoTRIBE showed a modest PFS gain, but CheckMate 9X8 failed. The trial must beat an active bevacizumab comparator on BICR-assessed PFS, which is a demanding bar, though Akeso's strong execution record and the 560-patient sample give it a reasonable chance.

AHB-137 is an antisense oligonucleotide. Phase 2 data in NA-suppressed, HBeAg-negative patients with low baseline HBsAg (≤3000 IU/mL) showed high on-treatment HBsAg loss and meaningful functional-cure rates off treatment. The placebo-plus-NA arm should give near-zero rates of HBsAg clearance sustained 24 weeks off all therapy, so the ~577-patient trial is powered to detect even a modest absolute difference. The same mechanism appears validated by bepirovirsen's positive phase 3 results; the main risks are durability off NA therapy and Phase 2 effects shrinking at scale.

This is a multi-cohort phase 2 trial whose primary efficacy endpoint is BICR-confirmed ORR, mostly in single-arm cohorts, so success likely means beating a historical response threshold rather than winning a head-to-head comparison. Disitamab vedotin has produced roughly 50% ORR in HER2-expressing urothelial cancer in Chinese trials, and early Cohort C data with pembrolizumab in first-line disease reportedly showed high response rates; Pfizer has advanced the combination to a phase 3 trial. Risks include weaker activity in HER2-low and post-enfortumab-vedotin cohorts, and ambiguity in how the randomized part of Cohort C would be judged.

Two PARP inhibitor-plus-ARPI combinations met rPFS in unselected first-line mCRPC: PROpel (olaparib + abiraterone, HR ~0.66) and TALAPRO-2 (talazoparib + enzalutamide). MAGNITUDE (niraparib + abiraterone) succeeded only in HRR-positive patients and was futile in the HRR-negative cohort. This trial, with about 496 patients, a BICR-assessed rPFS endpoint and DRD-positive patients enriching the all-comer cohort, should be adequately powered for an effect like PROpel's. The remaining risks are the MAGNITUDE-like negative signal in non-DRD patients, the dose limits of combining with fuzuloparib, and uncertainty in the global execution. I am not aware of a topline announcement.

FcRn inhibition is already validated in CIDP: efgartigimod's ADHERE trial used nearly the same responder-enriched randomized-withdrawal design and showed a strong reduction in relapse risk (HR ~0.39, p<0.0001). Nipocalimab produces deep IgG lowering and is approved in gMG, so the class effect should carry over. Withdrawal designs that enrich for open-label responders and use time to relapse as the endpoint tend to succeed when the drug works. Remaining risks are a fairly modest sample size, a slow trial still recruiting near its planned primary completion, and possible differences in dosing or relapse adjudication, so I place this somewhat below the near-certain level.

Solriamfetol is an established wake-promoting agent with large, consistent MWT effects in narcolepsy and OSA. In shift work disorder, modafinil and armodafinil both separated from placebo on nighttime MWT, so the mechanism and endpoint are validated. With about 170 patients per arm, two doses including 300 mg, and an objective MWT primary endpoint, the trial is well powered for a plausible effect size. Residual risk comes from the heterogeneity of shift-work populations and Axsome's mixed record in non-sleep indications, but this is the drug's core use.

Brivekimig is a bispecific nanobody against TNF and OX40L. TNF inhibition is a validated mechanism in Crohn's disease, and the drug showed positive phase 2 signals in hidradenitis suppurativa. Against that, the trial is small (about 33 per arm), enrolls many patients who have already failed advanced therapies (possibly including anti-TNFs), and uses centrally read endoscopic response at Week 16, so power for a 20–25 point placebo-adjusted difference is only moderate. Dose-ranging phase 2 studies also sometimes lack strict formal significance testing, so I put the chance of a statistically significant win for at least one dose slightly above even.

Dapagliflozin reliably lowers UACR by about 30% in CKD, and the CONFIDENCE trial showed an SGLT2 inhibitor added substantial further albuminuria reduction on top of mineralocorticoid-pathway blockade with finerenone. With about 111 patients per arm and typical log-UACR variability, a 25–30% between-arm difference would give high power, and the hemodynamic UACR effect appears within weeks, well inside the 12-week window. The main risks are that baxdrostat's mechanism overlaps with the SGLT2 inhibitor's, which could shrink the incremental effect, and the modest sample size, so I set the probability high but below certainty.

SL1002 appears to be a chemical neurolytic injection, likely phenol-based and aimed at the genicular nerves, given the diagnostic nerve block enrichment criterion. Saol reportedly saw encouraging Phase 2 signals, which supports a mechanism plausibly stronger than many intra-articular agents. Against that, knee OA pain trials with saline injection controls have high placebo responses, and 150 patients (about 75 per arm) is a small Phase 3 from a small sponsor. Those factors temper the estimate to roughly a coin flip, slightly favoring success.

Iltamiocel (autologous muscle-derived cells) has a weak track record. The earlier randomized fecal incontinence trial did not clearly separate from placebo overall, and the urinary incontinence trials (CELLEBRATE and its follow-up) missed or only marginally met their primary endpoints, with sponsors relying on subgroup findings. This Phase 3 enriches for women with obstetric sphincter injury on the strength of such a post-hoc subgroup signal, and fecal incontinence episode-frequency endpoints have large placebo responses that a vehicle-injection control will share. With about 200 participants and a modest plausible effect, success is possible but less likely than the Phase 3 base rate.

Phase 3 trials of topical agents for venous leg ulcer healing have a poor track record: growth factors, peptides and various gels have repeatedly failed to beat good compression-based standard of care on complete closure. TR987 has only limited phase 2 data, from a small sponsor, and those results did not clearly establish an effect. The add-on-to-standard-of-care design with a non-vehicle control could modestly help, and 312 patients gives reasonable power for a ~15-point difference. Still, high SOC healing rates at 16 weeks and the small sponsor and site count keep the probability low.

This is a descriptive, open-label ovulation-inhibition study of a norelgestromin patch, which may be progestin-only, with planned application errors. Success would likely mean showing low ovulation incidence, as judged by Hoogland-Skouby score and the Landgren criterion, rather than a formal significance test. Norelgestromin patches such as Evra have generally kept ovulation suppressed despite extended patch-free intervals, and the sponsor presumably moved this to error testing after a successful earlier study. Still, a possibly estrogen-free formulation, the deliberate stress-testing of errors, and the ambiguity of 'success' for a descriptive endpoint warrant moderate rather than high confidence.

BGM0504 is BrightGene's GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, and the injectable form has already produced substantial weight loss in Chinese phase 2 studies. The mechanism is well validated against placebo on body weight. The main risk is oral peptide bioavailability, but four dose arms of about 40 participants each over 20 weeks leave ample power if exposure is even modest, and only one dose needs to succeed. The primary result is not yet public, with primary completion planned for February 2027.

CT-P53 is a proposed ocrelizumab biosimilar compared against EU- and US-Ocrevus, and the first-listed primary endpoint is PK equivalence (AUC), which biosimilar programs from experienced developers like Celltrion almost always meet. The efficacy co-primary, new GdE lesions to Week 24, sits near a floor because ocrelizumab almost completely suppresses lesion activity, so equivalence there is also likely. The main residual risks are three-way PK equivalence failing on one comparison, manufacturing or analytical differences, and operational problems. Primary completion is not until 2027, and I am not aware of any public results.

This is a small (n=24), uncontrolled, three-dose Phase 2a study from a micro-cap sponsor, with a microbiological primary endpoint: the rate of ≥2-log CFU reduction per pathogen versus baseline. With no placebo arm and about 8 patients per arm, a formal statistically significant between-arm comparison is unlikely, so 'success' would rest mainly on the sponsor describing within-patient bacterial reductions as positive. Topical antimicrobials plus intensive debridement often reduce bacterial load substantially, and the earlier Nu-3 iDFU study reportedly showed microbial effects, which favours a positive-sounding readout. Against that, the absence of a formal hypothesis test, the risk of small or underpowered results, and enrollment or timing uncertainty keep the estimate below even.

SYT-510 is a first-in-class endocannabinoid reuptake inhibitor being tested in a small (n=24), single-dose, single-site experimental-medicine crossover. The first-listed primary endpoint is amygdala BOLD response to fearful faces, which is noisy at this sample size and after only one dose. Related endocannabinoid-enhancing drugs (FAAH inhibitors) have reduced amygdala reactivity in healthy volunteers, but only after repeated dosing and with mixed clinical translation. With many co-primary measures, a sponsor could claim a 'positive' signal on some of them, but a significant result on the first-listed fMRI outcome is less likely than not.

TQB3616 is a novel CDK4/6 inhibitor being tested as adjuvant therapy with endocrine treatment against placebo. The mechanism has a mixed adjuvant record: abemaciclib (monarchE) and ribociclib (NATALEE) succeeded, while palbociclib (PALLAS, PENELOPE-B) failed, so roughly half of these trials have worked. At about 1,946 patients this trial is much smaller than monarchE or NATALEE, so success likely depends on a high-risk population and enough IDFS events, neither of which is clear from the record. Chinese sponsor trials have a fairly good record of positive readouts, which roughly offsets the uncertainty, leaving an estimate near 50%.

The primary outcomes are safety, tolerability and PK, with no prespecified efficacy comparison, so 'meeting the primary endpoint' amounts to finding a tolerable dose and characterizing PK without prohibitive toxicity. Small first-in-human studies of this kind almost always report as successful, and Clearmind has a habit of announcing favorable interim safety updates. The main risks are unexpected toxicity from MEAI, a psychoactive aminoindane, or the study stalling or not completing, given a small sponsor and a planned completion of December 2026. I don't know of any topline result for the full study yet.

MT1013 is an IV peptide dual-target agonist that appears to act through the CaSR, like etelcalcetide, which was both non-inferior and superior to cinacalcet on PTH-reduction endpoints in its head-to-head trial. The design is double-dummy against cinacalcet, which tends to be under-dosed or poorly tolerated in Chinese dialysis patients, and the PTH-reduction endpoints are pharmacologically sensitive with 424 patients, so non-inferiority or even superiority is plausible. It is unclear whether the first-listed >50% endpoint is tested for superiority or non-inferiority, which adds risk, but sponsor Phase 3 trials of this mechanism usually succeed. No results are public yet; the record still shows recruiting, with primary completion planned for late November 2026.

Apraclonidine is a potent alpha-adrenergic vasoconstrictor, and low-dose alpha-2 agonists such as brimonidine 0.025% (Lumify) have reliably beaten vehicle on Ora Calibra redness scores. That makes the first-listed 15-minute endpoint close to certain to succeed. The 14-hour co-primary is a more demanding duration claim, but Alcon very likely chose it based on earlier-phase data. The vehicle-controlled design with about 115 subjects per arm gives ample power, so the main residual risk is the long-duration co-primary failing if both endpoints are required.

The prior Phase I/II Allocetra knee OA study appears to have shown benefit mainly in a subgroup of older patients with primary, age-related OA rather than in the overall population, as I recall. This Phase IIb enriches for that subgroup (age ≥64, primary OA), and trials built on post-hoc subgroups often fail to replicate. Intra-articular knee OA trials also face large placebo responses on WOMAC pain, and with about 91 patients per arm only a moderate effect would reach significance. The mechanism is novel and the sponsor small, so a probability somewhat below the Phase 2 base rate seems right.

This is an open-label, single-site, dose-ranging Phase 2 of an oral HIF-PHI with no control arm, so its 'primary endpoint' is a descriptive HI-E/transfusion-independence response rate with no stated threshold, which makes a topline 'success' a judgment call. HIF-PHIs have shown modest erythroid responses in lower-risk, low-transfusion-burden MDS: open-label roxadustat cohorts reported roughly 30–40% transfusion independence, which a sponsor would likely frame as positive. However, roxadustat's placebo-controlled MATTERHORN trial failed, and this small Chinese sponsor's trial is still recruiting, so results may be unimpressive or slow to appear. I land slightly above even odds.

Oregovomab monotherapy maintenance already failed in earlier phase 3 trials (IMPACT), and front-line ovarian cancer add-on immunotherapy has repeatedly failed, including checkpoint inhibitors. The randomized phase 2 chemo-combination signal (PFS ~42 vs ~12 months) came from a small, open-label study, and effects that large usually shrink in a confirmatory phase 3. The trial appears to have continued past an interim analysis without an early efficacy stop, and the sponsor is a small biotech, which slightly lowers confidence. I put the probability of a significant PFS benefit well below the phase 3 oncology base rate.

The first-listed primary endpoint is phase II ORR across three arms of roughly 30 patients each, likely an exploratory comparison rather than one formally powered for significance. Disitamab vedotin combined with a PD-1 inhibitor has shown ORRs of about 40% or higher in HER2-expressing gastric cancer, against roughly 15–20% for second-line paclitaxel. A gap that size could reach significance even with ~30 per arm. Against that, including HER2 IHC 1+ patients may dilute the effect, the small arms make the result noisy, and the sponsor may report ORR only descriptively, so I put the chance of a clearly significant win near a coin flip.

The primary outcome is a descriptive safety comparison (TEAEs and ECG intervals) of a prolonged-release reformulation against the same active drug, in a small open-label crossover of 24 patients at a single Belgian site. No efficacy hypothesis or prespecified test is stated, so a significant superiority result is very unlikely, but the sponsor would probably describe comparable safety as a success. How "meeting the endpoint" gets adjudicated is therefore ambiguous, which keeps this forecast near the middle. The trial is still recruiting, with primary completion planned for January 2027, and no results are public.

Licaminlimab (OCS-02), a topical anti-TNFα antibody fragment, appears to have shown only modest or mixed results in Oculis's earlier Phase 2b RELIEF trial, as best I recall. The TNFR1 genotype enrichment hypothesis seems to come from exploratory or post hoc analyses, which often fail to replicate prospectively. Dry eye symptom endpoints such as ocular discomfort score are notoriously noisy with large vehicle responses. A 160-patient trial, in which the genotype-positive primary population may be only a subset, gives limited power, though the targeted enrichment and the sponsor's belief in the signal give it some chance.

MARITIME-1 is a large Phase 3 trial of a GLP-1 agonist/GIPR antagonist antibody against placebo over 72 weeks. In Phase 2, MariTide produced roughly 16-20% mean weight loss at 52 weeks versus about 2.6% on placebo in people without diabetes. With nearly 4,000 participants and three dose arms, statistical superiority on percent weight change is nearly certain; the main uncertainties are tolerability-driven discontinuation and the size of the effect, neither of which threatens significance. Primary completion is January 2027, so results are not yet public.

608 is Sunshine Guojian's anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, a mechanism already validated in ankylosing spondylitis. Secukinumab and ixekizumab, and Chinese IL-17A agents such as xeligekimab and gumokimab, have consistently beaten placebo on ASAS40 at week 16, typically by 15–25 percentage points. With about 500 patients randomized against placebo, power to detect an effect of that size is very high, and 608 has already shown efficacy in psoriasis. Primary completion is planned for January 2027, so no result is public yet; the residual risk lies mainly in execution, a high placebo response, or the dose chosen.

This is an uncontrolled, multi-arm Phase II with ORR as the primary endpoint, so 'success' will likely be judged descriptively, by whether any arm shows clinically meaningful activity, rather than by a formal comparison. Interim data I recall from this program showed confirmed responses of roughly 45% for naporafenib (LXH254) plus trametinib in NRAS-mutant melanoma after checkpoint inhibitors. That signal was strong enough for Erasca to start the SEACRAFT-2 Phase 3, while the LTT462 and ribociclib combinations looked weaker. With no control arm and no formal hypothesis test, it is uncertain how a 'met primary endpoint' verdict will be scored, which keeps the probability moderate.

LAD328 is an undisclosed-mechanism IV biologic from Almirall in a small (n≈50), single-site Phase 2 proof-of-concept trial in moderate-to-severe HS, with IHS4-55 at week 12 as the primary endpoint. HS trials have substantial placebo response (about 25-35% on IHS4-55/HiSCR50), so with roughly 25 patients per arm a placebo-adjusted difference of about 35-40 points would be needed for p<0.05. Only the most potent mechanisms, such as IL-17 blockade, have achieved that. First-in-indication PoC studies in HS often show numerical trends without reaching significance, so I place the probability below the base rate for a Phase 2 dermatology trial.

DPP1 inhibition is validated in bronchiectasis: brensocatib's phase 3 ASPEN reduced the annualized exacerbation rate by about 20%, and BI 1291583 had a positive phase 2, as I recall HSK31858's own Chinese phase 2 did. This trial enrolls a high-risk population (at least 2 exacerbations in the prior year), and the endpoint is exacerbation frequency against placebo, which fits the mechanism. The main risk is power: about 335 patients per arm is modest against a roughly 20% rate reduction given how variable exacerbation counts are, though Chinese trials sometimes show larger effects. Its primary result has not been reported as of my knowledge.

SGLT2 inhibitors have improved KCCQ in symptomatic HFpEF (PRESERVED-HF about +5 points, CHIEF-HF about +4), which gives sotagliflozin a plausible mechanistic rationale in HCM with its shared diastolic dysfunction. However, HCM-specific evidence is limited to small or observational data. In nonobstructive HCM, even the potent cardiac myosin inhibitor mavacamten failed on KCCQ in ODYSSEY-HCM, and a likely 2-4 point effect against placebo in a mixed oHCM/nHCM population of about 500 leaves power marginal. Weighing the new-indication base rate and the modest expected effect against a validated but noisy endpoint, I estimate a below-even chance of success.

DENALI Part 2 is a single-arm, registration-intent ORR study of azenosertib in Cyclin E1-positive platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, so success means the confidence interval for ORR clears a prespecified null rate, likely around the 10-15% that standard chemotherapy achieves. Earlier pooled data at 400 mg 5:2 in Cyclin E1-positive PROC showed ORR around 30-35%, and a cohort of about 100 patients would likely give a lower bound above a modest null. Risks are dilution in more heavily pretreated patients (prior mirvetuximab, bevacizumab and PARP inhibitors), regression to the mean from small early cohorts, and a stricter-than-expected FDA-negotiated threshold. I am not aware of a public topline readout for Part 2.

WD-890 is an oral allosteric TYK2 inhibitor. That mechanism is well validated in plaque psoriasis: deucravacitinib and zasocitinib consistently beat placebo on sPGA 0/1 and PASI75 at week 16 by wide margins. With about 375 patients against placebo and a phase 2 program that presumably supported moving to phase 3, the trial is well powered for both co-primary endpoints. The main risks are lower potency than the class leaders or execution problems at a single site, but placebo-controlled phase 3 psoriasis trials of validated oral mechanisms rarely fail.

SHR-1819 is Hengrui's anti-IL-4Rα antibody, and a mechanistically similar drug (stapokibart/CM310) already met the identical endpoint, 2-week rTNSS change versus placebo, in a Chinese seasonal allergic rhinitis phase 3 with fewer patients. This trial has 220 patients, enrolls people with a poor response to intranasal steroids during an autumn pollen season, and runs at one experienced site, all of which favor a detectable effect. Residual risks are a high placebo response, variable pollen exposure, and the short 2-week primary window.

HRS-9563 appears to be Hengrui's injectable, likely siRNA-based, RAAS-targeting agent (probably angiotensinogen-directed, like zilebesiran), though this identification is not confirmed. That mechanism has already shown large placebo-adjusted reductions in 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure in KARDIA-1, so the proof of concept is strong. This trial compares four doses with placebo in about 238 untreated mild-to-moderate hypertensives, which gives ample power for ambulatory reductions on the order of 10 mmHg or more, and only one arm needs to succeed. The remaining risks are a weaker-than-expected candidate, durability at month 6, and single-site execution; I do not know of any public results.

This is a single-arm-style intraoperative imaging trial: the primary endpoint is the proportion of patients with a clinically significant event, almost certainly tested against a prespecified low threshold, as in pafolacianine's ELUCIDATE, which succeeded. Abenacianine's Phase 2 VISUALIZE trial reportedly found clinically significant events in roughly a third or more of patients, comfortably above typical thresholds of about 10%. With about 115 evaluable NIR patients, power should be ample, though the exact threshold, the interpretation of the open-label design, and the trial's dependence on how often standard of care misses lesions add some risk. Results do not appear to be public yet.

Bexicaserin is a selective 5-HT2C agonist, and in the Phase 1b/2a PACIFIC study in developmental and epileptic encephalopathies it produced roughly a 50%+ median reduction in countable motor seizures. Serotonergic therapy has strong validation in Dravet through fenfluramine, and Dravet Phase 3 trials of active drugs (fenfluramine, cannabidiol, stiripentol) have generally succeeded with modest placebo responses. However, the more selective 5-HT2C agonist lorcaserin reportedly missed its Phase 3 Dravet primary endpoint, and a roughly 108-patient trial leaves limited margin. This trial's results are not yet public, so I land somewhat above the Phase 3 base rate.

Randomized add-on trials to Stupp radiotherapy plus temozolomide in newly diagnosed GBM have an extremely poor track record, and a 100-patient trial powered on overall survival needs a large hazard-ratio improvement to reach p<0.05. The rationale is mechanistic (GBM is often ASS1-deficient) and a small phase 1b cohort reported an encouraging median OS of about 29 months, but single-arm GBM survival data are notoriously unreliable. ADI-PEG 20 has been mixed elsewhere, failing in phase 3 HCC and succeeding modestly in mesothelioma with chemotherapy. The primary outcome also leans on subgroup and biomarker exploration, suggesting limited confidence in an all-comers OS win, though a small chance of success remains.

This is PROTEUS, the phase 3 trial of neoadjuvant and adjuvant apalutamide plus ADT around prostatectomy; I do not recall its pCR or MFS readout being public. In phase 2 work (ARNEO, enzalutamide and abiraterone neoadjuvant studies), adding an AR inhibitor to ADT consistently deepened pathologic response, though true pCR stayed low (about 3-10% versus 0-3% with ADT alone). With about 2,500 patients, even a 2-3 percentage-point absolute pCR difference would likely be significant at a split alpha. The main risks are that pCR rates are extremely low in both arms or that a stringent alpha allocation is missed, so I place success somewhat above the oncology phase 3 base rate.

Ritlecitinib 30 mg beat placebo on HiSCR50 at week 16 in Pfizer's earlier phase 2a HS study (about 64% vs 42%), and other JAK inhibitors (povorcitinib, upadacitinib) have shown activity in HS. This trial uses a loading dose, which suggests a higher exposure that could enlarge the effect. However, HiSCR50 placebo responses are high and variable (roughly 30–45%), and with about 128 patients a 20-point difference gives only modest power, so a miss is quite possible. Primary completion is December 2026, so no result is public yet.

Ninerafaxstat, a cardiac metabolic modulator that partially inhibits fatty acid oxidation, was safe in the small Phase 2 IMPROVE-HCM trial in non-obstructive HCM. Its efficacy signals there were exploratory, notably better VE/VCO2 slope and KCCQ gains in more symptomatic patients, not a robust primary-endpoint win. Non-obstructive HCM has been a hard indication: mavacamten failed ODYSSEY-HCM on KCCQ-CSS, and KCCQ endpoints carry large placebo responses, which makes a 12-week trial of about 165 patients underpowered for modest effects. The Phase 2b base rate and a plausible but unproven mechanism support a below-even probability, and the trial is still recruiting, so no result is public.

rhPRG4 (lubricin) showed signal-level benefits in earlier small dry eye studies, and the endpoint of complete clearance of corneal staining from a mild baseline (Oxford 1–2) was likely chosen from prior data, which modestly helps. Still, this is a small trial (about 40 per arm) with a binary responder endpoint at only 28 days. A PBS vehicle often produces substantial staining improvement on its own, and dry eye trials frequently fail on sign endpoints. Given the low base rate for phase 2 dry eye trials and limited power, success is less likely than not.

ICP-332 (soficitinib) is an oral TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor. In its Phase 2 atopic dermatitis study it produced large, dose-dependent EASI-75 responses with placebo-adjusted gains well above what this trial needs. Oral JAK1-class drugs (upadacitinib, abrocitinib, ivarmacitinib) have consistently beaten placebo on EASI-75 and vIGA-AD at week 16 in Phase 3, and this trial has about 550 patients, ample power for a likely effect size of 30 percentage points or more. The main residual risks are execution issues or an unusually high placebo response, so I put success at about 95%.

RYZ101 (225Ac-DOTATATE) showed encouraging activity in the ACTION-1 Phase 1b part, with an objective response rate of roughly 29% in patients who had progressed after 177Lu-PRRT. Targeted alpha therapy (including 212Pb-DOTAMTATE) has repeatedly shown meaningful efficacy in this setting. The comparator, investigator's choice of everolimus, sunitinib or high-dose SSA, gives modest PFS in post-PRRT patients, and BICR-assessed PFS with 143 events gives reasonable power. Risks include patient selection (enrolment required at least 6 months of prior disease control on Lu-177), possible toxicity or dose-reduction effects, and the general phase 3 failure rate in oncology, so I settle around 0.68.

In the Phase 2 DAHLIAS trial, nipocalimab 15 mg/kg IV beat placebo on ClinESSDAI change, but the lower dose did not, and Sjögren's has a long record of Phase 3 failures with high placebo responses. Recent successes such as ianalumab's two NEPTUNUS trials on ESSDAI show the endpoint can be met, and 300 patients per study with a 48-week readout gives reasonable power. Risks include the switch to subcutaneous dosing, which may lower IgG less than the effective IV dose, and the modest, variable effect seen on ClinESSDAI. Balancing these, the chance of a positive primary result is a little above even.

This is a sponsor-run Phase 2 diagnostic trial whose primary endpoint is SUVmax, mainly descriptive, with Part 2 presumably testing whether uptake discriminates ISUP grades. Earlier investigator-led studies of 64Cu-DOTA-AE105 showed uPAR PET uptake correlating with Gleason/ISUP grade, and I believe Curasight reported Part 1 favourably and chose the 200 MBq dose. Descriptive or correlation-type imaging endpoints with an adequate sample (~141) are usually reported as met, but separating low grades (ISUP 1 vs 2–3) is genuinely harder than prior comparisons, so meaningful uncertainty remains. Part 2 topline results are not yet public.

This is a randomized phase 2 dose-optimization study of the c-Met ADC telisotuzumab adizutecan (ABBV-400) plus 5-FU/leucovorin/bevacizumab against FOLFIRI-bevacizumab in second-line mCRC, with ORR as the first primary endpoint. FOLFIRI-bevacizumab gives modest second-line response rates (about 5-20%), and a topoisomerase-I-payload ADC combined with FFB could plausibly reach 30-50%, which would be significant even with roughly 40 patients per arm. However, the stage 2 comparator cohort may be descriptive rather than powered for a formal test, and c-Met expression was not required for enrollment, which may dilute efficacy. Together these leave the outcome close to a coin flip.

This is an exploratory phase 2 platform with about 180 patients split across three placebo-controlled substudies, so roughly 60 per substudy, in a hard-to-treat bDMARD-inadequate-responder population, judged on the demanding ACR50 endpoint at week 12. IL-1 blockade (anakinra) has historically given only modest benefit in RA, and prior anti-CD40 antagonists such as BI 655064 failed to separate from placebo in RA. The combination arm and the three independent chances to win raise the odds of at least one significant result. Still, small arms, a stringent endpoint and weak mechanistic precedent keep the probability below even.

This registration largely copies the original SURMOUNT-1 design: tirzepatide 5, 10 and 15 mg against placebo, with percent weight change at 72 weeks as the primary endpoint. The original Lilly trial showed placebo-adjusted weight loss of roughly 13–18% with p<0.001, an effect that is very hard to miss. The odd features (an unfamiliar sponsor, a single site in China, a timeline inconsistent with a 72-week endpoint) raise some risk around trial conduct and reporting, but not the drug's efficacy against placebo. A placebo-controlled trial of a proven drug like this succeeds almost every time, so a high probability is warranted.

IRIS uses the intensified anifrolumab regimen that, in the Phase 2 TULIP-LN trial, showed a numerically higher complete renal response rate (about 45% vs 31%) even though that trial missed its proteinuria primary endpoint. Lupus nephritis add-on trials have a mixed record: belimumab, voclosporin and obinutuzumab succeeded, while rituximab, abatacept and ocrelizumab failed, and a TYK2/interferon-pathway drug (deucravacitinib) also failed in this disease. With about 180 patients per arm, a strict week-52 complete renal response endpoint and a Phase 2 signal of roughly 14 points, power is moderate, and Phase 2 effect estimates often shrink in Phase 3. Primary completion is February 2027, so no topline result is public yet.

BT-114143 appears to be a novel antifibrinolytic or hemostatic agent, tested in this phase 2 trial against an active tranexamic acid regimen (20 mg/kg pre-incision plus 1 g postoperatively), not placebo. Showing statistically significant superiority in Gross-formula total blood loss over well-dosed TXA with about 90 patients per arm is hard, because TXA already captures most of the achievable antifibrinolytic benefit in TKA. The record specifies neither a non-inferiority margin nor a formal hypothesis, so the trial may be largely dose-finding and estimation, which lowers the chance of a clear 'met primary endpoint' outcome. Some upside remains if the high dose is substantially more potent, or if the sponsor frames the result as a non-inferiority success.

AGA2118 is a bispecific antibody against sclerostin and DKK1, a validated anabolic pathway. Romosozumab's phase 2 showed lumbar spine BMD gains of about 11% versus placebo at 12 months, and early AGA2118 studies reported bone-formation marker increases and BMD gains. With about 54 women per arm, six dose arms and a sensitive BMD endpoint against placebo, at least one arm reaching significance is highly likely. The main residual risk is execution or safety problems; I am not aware of any public topline result for this trial.

The first-listed primary outcome is the number of treatment-emergent adverse events, a descriptive safety endpoint with no prespecified efficacy comparison. 'Success' therefore most likely means the sponsor declaring invobenitug safe and well tolerated, which is plausible given earlier experience with DPP3 antibodies. Against that, adverse events are near-universal in cardiogenic shock, so a significant difference favoring the drug is very unlikely. The trial is still recruiting, no results are public, and the scoring interpretation is ambiguous, so I place the forecast near 50%.

QLS1410 appears to be an aldosterone synthase inhibitor; the trial design (uncontrolled or resistant hypertension on a diuretic, potassium exclusions) closely mirrors baxdrostat's BrigHTN and lorundrostat's Target-HTN, both of which beat placebo on systolic BP in phase 2. Three doses with about 65 patients per arm give reasonable power for a 7–10 mmHg placebo-adjusted drop, and only one dose needs to succeed. Risks are a fast-follower compound with uncertain potency or selectivity (some earlier inhibitors had cortisol off-target problems), a possibly large placebo response, and a single-site Chinese trial.

IBI302 (efdamrofusp alfa), a VEGF/complement bispecific, is compared head-to-head with faricimab in a small Phase 2 DME study (~50 per arm), with BCVA change at week 16 as the primary endpoint. Beating an effective anti-VEGF/Ang-2 comparator on BCVA by a statistically significant margin at this sample size is unlikely, especially since faricimab gets four monthly loading doses against IBI302's three plus PRN. The trial looks exploratory or non-inferiority in spirit, so even a favorable 'comparable efficacy' readout would probably not count as significant superiority. I am not aware of any public topline result.

Icotrokinra is an oral IL-23 receptor antagonist peptide with strongly positive Phase 3 psoriasis results (ICONIC program), and IL-23 pathway blockade (guselkumab, risankizumab) has reliably beaten placebo on ACR20 in PsA, including in biologic-experienced patients. With about 270 patients per arm and ACR20 at Week 16 against placebo, the trial is well powered even for a modest effect. The main risks are that the oral peptide's exposure may be lower than injectable IL-23 blockers, that there was apparently no dedicated PsA Phase 2, and that placebo response could be high in a mixed population. Primary completion is not until 2027, so results are not yet public.

Tonlamarsen (ION904) is a GalNAc-conjugated antisense oligonucleotide against hepatic angiotensinogen, and earlier studies showed large, consistent plasma AGT reductions. The first listed primary outcome (Part A variability) is descriptive, so the meaningful test is Part B's placebo-controlled percent change in AGT at Week 4, a pharmacodynamic endpoint the mechanism almost always hits. The main risks are operational: Part B may be delayed or not run, or results may be reported only descriptively, rather than any doubt about efficacy.

Both arms receive the active HT-101 + HT-102 combination, which is likely a siRNA plus an antibody or immunomodulator. Cohort B differs only by an 8-week placebo lead-in followed by 16 weeks of treatment, so the primary comparison at W60 is effectively 24 versus 16 weeks of the same regimen. Functional cure rates in low-HBsAg (<3000 IU/mL), NA-suppressed patients can be meaningful with such combinations, but a statistically significant between-arm difference with about 30 patients per arm is unlikely. The design is exploratory, and no results are public.

Alirocumab is an approved PCSK9 antibody that reliably lowers LDL-C by about 45-60%, so weekly dosing of an adequate dose will almost certainly produce large LDL-C reductions from baseline. However, the control arm is itself alirocumab (likely the approved regimen), and the open-label dose-ranging design suggests the goal is dose selection or showing comparability, possibly for co-formulation with obesity drugs, rather than superiority. If success is judged as within-arm LDL-C reduction or comparable efficacy, it is near-certain. Formal superiority over an active alirocumab control is unlikely, so I discount for how the outcome will be adjudicated.

Colgate runs many single-site six-month gingivitis and plaque trials of 0.45% stannous fluoride against a regular fluoride negative control, and these almost always show significant reductions in MGI, bleeding and plaque. The first-listed primary endpoint (MGI) compared against the negative control is a near-certain win given this proven technology and the sponsor's track record. The main uncertainty is whether the prespecified comparison is instead against the 67% bicarbonate (Parodontax-type) positive control, which would be harder to beat, but one arm succeeding against its control is enough here. With roughly 40 subjects per arm, power is adequate for the expected effect against the negative control.

The primary outcomes are descriptive safety measures (incidence of TEAEs, SAEs and discontinuations) in a Phase 2a exposure-response study, so there is no prespecified efficacy comparison that could come out significant for the drug. Success therefore depends on how 'met' is judged: a sponsor might call acceptable tolerability a success, but a significant between-arm safety benefit is implausible. Cardiac myosin inhibition also carries an LVEF-lowering risk, and mavacamten failed in non-obstructive HCM (ODYSSEY-HCM), which adds uncertainty about whether BMS will describe the safety profile favorably in HFpEF. Given the ambiguity, a near-coin-flip estimate is appropriate.

The primary comparison is almost certainly a non-inferiority test of HPV16/18 GMTs one month after three doses of Cervavac versus Gardasil, the same mechanism and antigen types. Serum Institute's earlier Indian phase 2/3 trial showed Cervavac non-inferior to Gardasil, with numerically higher GMTs. Women in this trial have well-controlled HIV (CD4 above 350) and receive the same three-dose schedule as the comparator, so immune blunting should hit both arms equally. The main risks are the modest sample of 150 per arm, assay or site variability across three African countries, and some uncertainty about how success is defined, so I keep the forecast below 0.9.

This is SunRISe-2. As I recall, in 2024 Johnson & Johnson stopped the trial after a planned interim analysis, when the independent data monitoring committee concluded that TAR-200 plus cetrelimab was unlikely to beat concurrent chemoradiotherapy on bladder-intact event-free survival. Even without that, beating chemoradiotherapy, an established bladder-sparing standard, with an open-label superiority design would have been a hard bar. Because the futility stop appears to be public, the probability of meeting the primary endpoint is very low.

TAK-861 (oveporexton), an OX2R agonist, showed very large, highly significant ESS improvements over placebo in NT1 in the phase 2b trial and the phase 3 FirstLight and RadiantLight trials, and phase 2 data showed symptoms return soon after stopping the drug. This randomized withdrawal design enrolls open-label responders and switches half to placebo, so placebo patients should relapse quickly on ESS while those continuing the drug stay stable. That makes time-to-loss-of-response a sensitive endpoint even with roughly 70–90 randomized. The main risks are a small sample, the relapse definition, or the short 4-week window, but the effect size should easily overcome them.

PACIFIC-9 tests whether adding a CD73 antibody (oleclumab) or an NKG2A antibody (monalizumab) to consolidation durvalumab improves PFS, based on the small, open-label phase 2 COAST trial (PFS HRs about 0.4). Such phase 2 signals for IO add-ons to PD-(L)1 have repeatedly failed to hold up in phase 3: IDO, TIGIT in SKYSCRAPER, and monalizumab's own INTERLINK-1 failure in head and neck cancer. Oleclumab has also been deprioritized elsewhere. Having two arms gives two chances, and the control arm is well characterized, but the base rate for novel IO combinations beating active PD-L1 therapy in phase 3 is low.

Navtemadlin showed real spleen activity in the phase 1b/2 add-on cohort in ruxolitinib suboptimal responders. In BOREAS, as monotherapy in relapsed/refractory MF, it gave numerically about three times the SVR35 rate of best available therapy. Here the placebo-plus-ruxolitinib arm should have a low SVR35 rate because these patients have already responded suboptimally after run-in, and a 2:1 randomization of a few hundred patients gives reasonable power on the first-listed SVR35 endpoint. The main risks are MDM2-inhibitor GI and hematologic toxicity limiting exposure, the modest effect sizes seen earlier, and some ongoing placebo-arm response from continued ruxolitinib; I recall no topline results yet.

AZD0780 is an oral PCSK9 inhibitor that cut LDL-C by about 50% versus placebo on top of statins in the phase 2b PURSUIT trial. This is a large placebo-controlled phase III trial (about 3,100 participants) with a biomarker primary endpoint (percent change in LDL-C at 12 weeks), so statistical success is nearly certain if the drug is active. Merck's oral PCSK9 inhibitor enlicitide recently succeeded in similar phase III trials, which supports the mechanism. The remaining risk is mainly operational or safety-driven, and topline results are not yet public, with primary completion planned for January 2027.

This is a first-in-human Phase 1/2a SAD/MAD study whose primary endpoint is safety and tolerability (AE counts), with no prespecified efficacy comparison. In practice, sponsors of such trials almost always report a topline of "safe and well tolerated," which is how meeting the endpoint would be judged.
