IGT-303 appears to be Ingenia's Tie2-activating antibody, a mechanism without known major class-wide safety signals, so dose-limiting toxicity severe enough to stop development is uncommon. I see no public topline yet; the main risks are an unexpected safety signal or no clear public readout.

BPC 157's support comes almost entirely from rodent studies, and there is no rigorous human efficacy data, so this is effectively a first test of a new mechanism. In acute hamstring strains, biologic add-ons to standard rehabilitation (e.g., PRP) have generally failed to shorten return-to-play in blinded trials. The trial is modest in size (n=120) against what is likely a small effect, and its registration is of low quality (both arms list both interventions, and the placebo arm is labeled experimental). Single-site trials from small sponsors do report positive results somewhat more often, so I lift the estimate slightly above the low base rate for an unproven peptide.

ENV-294 is a first-in-class oral small molecule from Enveda with an undisclosed, non-JAK mechanism and no prior efficacy data in atopic dermatitis. Most novel oral non-JAK mechanisms tested in moderate-to-severe AD have failed or shown only modest effects. The primary endpoint, percent change in EASI against placebo, is continuous and fairly sensitive, but about 52 patients per arm can only detect roughly a 20-point difference given a 25-35% placebo response. Phase 2 base rates in dermatology and this unvalidated mechanism point to a below-even chance of success.

VVN461 is a topical JAK1/TYK2 inhibitor, and this Chinese pivotal trial (n=154) is very likely a non-inferiority comparison against Pred Forte on Day 14 change in anterior chamber cell grade. Earlier-phase data reportedly supported anti-inflammatory activity, and non-inferiority on a change-from-baseline endpoint within a modest margin is attainable. However, topical prednisolone is a highly potent comparator, topical JAK inhibition is unproven in uveitis, and the margin and sample size are uncertain. That leaves a moderately favorable but uncertain outlook.

This is an open-label, dose-randomized phase II study of three HLX43 doses with no comparator, so 'success' amounts to an encouraging ORR in heavily pretreated NPC. That outcome is fairly plausible: topoisomerase-I ADCs have shown 30–50% ORRs in later-line NPC, and HLX43 showed meaningful phase 1 activity in NSCLC. The main uncertainty is that, without a formal hypothesis test against a control, there is no clear pass/fail criterion. Its novel anti-PD-L1 ADC mechanism is also unproven in NPC, and no results appear to be public yet.

T89 (Dantonic, a Danshen/Sanqi botanical extract) showed only modest, inconsistent improvement in exercise duration in its US Phase 2 trial. The benefit was mainly at the high dose and was not robust across timepoints. Treadmill exercise-duration endpoints in chronic stable angina carry large placebo and training effects, so many antianginal agents fail them, and botanical drugs especially lack a strong track record in FDA-style Phase 3 trials. Recruitment has run since 2019 with no public results. Two doses give a modest boost to the chance of success, but the overall likelihood stays below even.

This is one of many near-identical registrations from a single sponsor-investigator. It compares two generic raloxifene products, and its primary outcome only measures and reports SNP genotypes, with no prespecified hypothesis test, superiority comparison, or non-inferiority margin. The design is internally incoherent (an off-label 120 mg dose called 'chemotherapy', 'measurable disease' in LCIS, one site, 600 patients), which makes it doubtful the trial will produce interpretable or publicly reported results. With no testable comparison and a low chance of credible results, a positive topline on the primary endpoint is unlikely, though a purely descriptive endpoint could be claimed as met.

In earlier randomized trials, tesamorelin reduced MRI-measured hepatic fat in people with HIV and NAFLD, with an absolute reduction of about 4 points versus placebo in the 2019 Lancet HIV trial, and growth hormone axis stimulation has reduced liver fat in obese non-HIV adults too, so the mechanism has proof of concept. With 120 participants randomized 1:1, baseline PDFF of at least 10%, 52 weeks of treatment and a placebo comparator, MRI-PDFF should have adequate power for a plausible effect. Risks include a weaker effect in general MASLD than in HIV-associated visceral adiposity, a placebo response from lifestyle counseling, dose reductions for high IGF-1, and an unusual single-site record from a small sponsor (only participants masked, both arms labeled experimental). The trial is still recruiting, with primary completion planned for February 2027, so no result is public.

Gardasil 9 and its quadrivalent predecessor are highly effective against persistent HPV infection at genital and anal sites in HPV-naive people, and observational data suggest vaccination cuts oral HPV prevalence by roughly 80-90%. The main risks are a low incidence of persistent oral infection, which could leave the trial with few events even with about 6,000 men and long follow-up, and possibly a prespecified success criterion requiring a vaccine-efficacy lower bound above some threshold. Oral rinse PCR may also pick up transient deposition rather than true infection. I do not recall the primary result being public; primary completion is planned for January 2027.

BFB759 is a first-in-class multi-cytokine-inhibiting mAb from a small biotech. A Phase 2 placebo-controlled AD trial with roughly 75 patients per arm and EASI percent change at week 16 is reasonably powered for a moderate effect, and placebo responses in AD are modest. However, many novel mechanisms in AD Phase 2 have failed or been marginal (IL-33, IL-18, TSLP, IL-22), and public data on this drug are limited. Two dose arms add some chance that one succeeds, so I put this close to a coin flip.

This is the ECHO trial (ACE-LY-308). AstraZeneca announced in 2024 that it met its primary endpoint of IRC-assessed PFS. The reported result was HR about 0.73, p≈0.016, with median PFS 66.4 vs 49.6 months; it was presented at EHA 2024 and led to FDA approval of acalabrutinib plus BR in untreated MCL in early 2025. The registry's later primary completion date likely reflects continued follow-up rather than a pending primary analysis.

NLS-133 appears to combine an alpha-1 blocker such as silodosin with a second approved agent. Silodosin and similar uroselective alpha-blockers are known to produce marked, often near-complete, loss of ejaculate volume within hours, so a large effect on semen volume versus placebo is pharmacologically very plausible. With only 10 men the study is small, but the within-subject crossover design, a large expected effect and uncorrected alpha make a significant reduction in semen volume at one or more timepoints likely. Remaining risks are the small sample, the nonparametric test across several arms and timepoints, and uncertainty about how the primary comparison will be defined and reported.

Budesonide orodispersible tablet 1 mg BID is well proven in EoE, with histological remission around 90% at 6 weeks in EOS-1 and higher in EOS-2, and this trial compares the same total daily dose given once daily. With roughly 150 patients per arm and high expected remission rates, the confidence interval should be narrow enough to meet a typical 10–15% non-inferiority margin, unless once-daily dosing truly loses efficacy through shorter mucosal contact time. That pharmacological risk, plus the unknown margin and slow enrollment since 2021, keeps the estimate below 90%.

Xanomeline showed reductions in hallucinations and delusions in the 1990s Alzheimer's trial, and KarXT is proven in acute schizophrenia, so the biological rationale is plausible. Against that, dementia-related psychosis trials have high placebo response and a mixed record: pimavanserin's efficacy was inconsistent and many antipsychotic trials in this population failed. KarXT's adjunctive schizophrenia trial (ARISE) also missed its endpoint, and this trial is still recruiting at its nominal completion date, suggesting delays and leaving its result unknown. With 406 patients the trial is adequately powered for a moderate effect, so I put the chance of success near a coin flip.

LY3537021 is a long-acting GIP receptor agonist being tested as an antiemetic. The idea rests mainly on animal data and Lilly's interest in reducing incretin-related nausea, so this is essentially a first efficacy test of a new mechanism in humans. It is added on top of triple antiemetic prophylaxis (5-HT3 antagonist, NK1 antagonist and dexamethasone), which already gives a high delayed-phase complete response rate (about 65–80%). With roughly 100 patients per arm, that ceiling leaves limited room and limited power to reach p<0.05 unless the effect is olanzapine-sized (about 15 percentage points or more).

Obefazimod, which upregulates miR-124, has positive Phase 2b and Phase 3 (ABTECT) induction results in ulcerative colitis, so the drug has real anti-inflammatory activity in IBD. However, many agents that work in UC have failed or underperformed in Crohn's disease, and CD has high and noisy placebo responses on CDAI. The primary endpoint, change from baseline in CDAI at week 12, is continuous, there are three doses with about 53 patients per arm, and one dose succeeding counts, all of which help power. Balancing the mechanism's UC validation against the CD translation risk, the chance of success is roughly a coin flip.

Relutrigine, a preferential persistent sodium current inhibitor, showed large placebo-adjusted motor seizure reductions in the EMBOLD trial in SCN2A/SCN8A DEE, and Praxis has reported strong signals there, which supports a real anticonvulsant effect. This trial, however, enrolls a broad, heterogeneous DEE population, which likely dilutes the effect. Sodium-channel mechanisms may also be neutral or harmful in some subtypes, such as SCN1A Dravet syndrome. With about 80 patients per arm, a 16-week treatment period and a placebo-controlled seizure-frequency endpoint, power is reasonable for a moderate effect, so I put success modestly above the Phase 3 epilepsy base rate.

Navenibart is a long-acting anti-plasma kallikrein monoclonal antibody, a mechanism already validated by lanadelumab, which cut attacks by about 87% versus placebo in HELP. In the Phase 1b/2 ALPHA-STAR study, navenibart reduced attacks by roughly 90% or more from baseline. ALPHA-ORBIT has three active arms against placebo on attack rate, a hard, objective endpoint where placebo effects are modest, and even 157 patients gives ample power for an effect of this size. Topline is expected around early 2027, so the result is not yet public, and the remaining risk is mainly unexpected failure of the every-6-month arm or trial-conduct problems.

BMS-986446 (PRX005) is an anti-MTBR tau antibody, and this Phase 2 proof-of-concept trial uses slowing of tau PET accumulation at week 76 as its primary endpoint, a biomarker target that is easier to hit than a clinical one. N-terminal tau antibodies (gosuranemab, tilavonemab, semorinemab) showed no tau PET benefit. More encouragingly, UCB's mid-region antibody bepranemab showed slowing of tau PET accumulation despite missing its clinical primary, and MTBR-directed antibodies are mechanistically favored. With about 310 patients, two dose arms and a noisy longitudinal tau PET endpoint, success is plausible but far from assured, so I estimate somewhat below even odds.

Stapokibart, an anti-IL-4Rα antibody, already met its rTNSS primary endpoint in an adult Phase 3 seasonal allergic rhinitis trial in China and has been approved there, so this adolescent add-on study is essentially an extension of a proven drug. The main risks are the small sample (~68 per arm) against a modest adult effect size on rTNSS, and high, variable placebo response tied to the autumn pollen season. Sponsors usually power such pediatric extensions on the adult effect, but noise in seasonal symptom scores makes failure plausible. I estimate roughly a 70% chance of success.

This appears to be SOL-R, a non-inferiority trial of OTX-TKI (Axpaxli) redosed about every 24 weeks versus aflibercept 2 mg every 8 weeks, with a likely margin of about 4.5 letters on BCVA change and a large sample. Non-inferiority trials of durable anti-VEGF approaches against on-label aflibercept have usually succeeded. Phase 1/2 data for OTX-TKI showed BCVA roughly maintained compared with aflibercept, and a similar TKI implant (EYP-1901) met non-inferiority in phase 2. The main risks are less potent VEGF suppression from a TKI depot causing gradual vision loss before redosing, and the dilution caused by rescue rules, so the forecast sits moderately above the base rate.

This is EVER-132-002, the Asian Phase 3 trial of sacituzumab govitecan versus physician's-choice chemotherapy in HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer. I recall it was reported (around ESMO 2024) as meeting its primary endpoint, IRC-assessed PFS (HR about 0.67), with an overall survival benefit as well. That is consistent with TROPiCS-02, where the same drug improved PFS in the same setting. The registry's primary completion date likely reflects a final analysis, so I place high confidence in success with some allowance for imperfect recall.

The first-listed primary outcome is incidence and severity of adverse events in a small Phase 1/2a MAD and crossover study, so there is no formal efficacy comparison. Sponsors typically report such trials as having met the endpoint when the drug is 'safe and well tolerated.' BBI-001 is an oral agent meant to reduce dietary iron absorption and is given only briefly here, so a disqualifying safety signal is fairly unlikely. Some probability is held back for tolerability problems, trial discontinuation, or results that are ambiguous or never reported, given primary completion is planned for February 2027.

MEDI0618 is an anti-PACAP monoclonal antibody, a mechanism with partial validation: Lundbeck's anti-PACAP Lu AG09222 beat placebo on monthly migraine days in the phase 2 HOPE trial (about -2 days), whereas Amgen's PAC1 receptor antibody failed. The primary comparison (Dose A vs placebo in about 64 per arm of CGRP-naive patients who failed at least two preventives) has reasonable power if the effect is about 1.5-2 monthly migraine days. That power falls off quickly for smaller effects given episodic migraine's high placebo response. Balancing the mechanism's support against the modest sample and phase 2 uncertainty, I put the chance of success slightly above even.

SHJ002 is a first-in-class topical antisense oligonucleotide against a microRNA, tested here in a small (n=140) exploratory Phase II trial against an active atropine comparator rather than placebo. No margin is stated, so success means significant superiority over atropine on change in cycloplegic spherical equivalent, which is a high bar for a novel mechanism with no published efficacy data in myopia. Atropine, even at low dose, has a real effect, and this study is likely underpowered to show a difference against it. A positive head-to-head result is therefore unlikely.

Topical artesunate has shown encouraging histologic regression of HPV-associated HSIL in earlier work, including cervical HSIL studies and small anal HSIL phase 1 studies from the same sponsor. Even so, this is a tiny (n=48, 2:1) single-sponsor phase 2. Its primary endpoint includes partial response, which also captures spontaneous regression in the placebo arm, limiting power to detect a significant difference. The trial is still recruiting, and no results are public, so I estimate a modestly below-even chance of a statistically significant win.

The first-listed primary outcome is a safety count (participants with TEAEs), not an efficacy comparison, so whether this trial 'meets its primary endpoint' will likely depend on how the sponsor frames its topline efficacy readouts, such as ESS change at Week 4. Orexin-2 agonists have shown wake-promoting effects in NT2 and IH, with early ORX750 and ALKS 2680 data supporting some benefit even without orexin deficiency. However, effect sizes outside NT1 are smaller, and this is a 96-patient, 4-week dose-finding study. The trial is still recruiting, with primary completion around end of November 2026, so no result is public, and the ambiguous safety endpoint keeps the estimate close to a coin flip with a slight lean positive.

Brenipatide (LY3537031) is a Lilly incretin-class agent being tested in addictions. The human evidence for GLP-1 agonists on smoking abstinence is mixed: an exenatide pilot was positive, a dulaglutide trial was negative on abstinence, and semaglutide data are small. Even proven drugs such as varenicline produce only modest absolute gains in relapse-prevention trials, and about 111 patients per arm can only detect a large effect on continuous abstinence over 24 weeks. Lilly's investment suggests some conviction, but a first test of this mechanism in a hard behavioral endpoint warrants a probability below 50%.

This is a double-blind extension in which both arms receive itepekimab, and the only primary endpoint is descriptive safety (AE incidence). There is no prespecified efficacy comparison against a control, so 'success' mostly means completing the study without an unexpected safety signal; itepekimab's safety profile has been benign across asthma, COPD and CRSwNP trials. Uncertainty remains because enrollment was small (59, possibly signalling a curtailed program) and it is ambiguous how a safety-only endpoint will be scored.

AK105 is penpulimab, and this is the APOLLO first-line HCC trial of penpulimab plus anlotinib versus sorafenib. PD-1/PD-L1 plus anti-angiogenic combinations have repeatedly beaten sorafenib on overall survival, as in IMbrave150, ORIENT-32 and CARES-310, which gives a high base rate. I recall APOLLO being reported around 2024 with a significant OS benefit (median roughly 16.5 vs 13.2 months, HR about 0.69), followed by NMPA approval of the combination in China. That recollection is not certain, so the probability is high but short of certainty.

Cenerimod's phase 2b CARE study missed its primary endpoint for the 4 mg dose after multiplicity adjustment, and the efficacy signals came mainly from post hoc subgroups such as high interferon signature and mucocutaneous/musculoskeletal disease. This phase 3 enriches for those features, but that rationale is post hoc. SLE phase 3 programs fail often, and SRI-4 at 12 months on top of background therapy usually carries a high placebo response. No other S1P modulator has proven efficacy in SLE. With about 420 patients the trial is reasonably powered, so I place success modestly below a coin flip.

Tinengotinib is a multi-kinase inhibitor that also hits FGFR resistance mutations. Phase 2 data in FGFR-inhibitor-refractory FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma showed meaningful responses and a median PFS of roughly 6–7 months, against an expected 2–4 months for FOLFOX/FOLFIRI in later lines. The efficacy primary, Part B PFS by blinded independent review, favors success, and open-label bias is limited by the independent review. Risks include a small sample, a phase 2 signal that may not hold up in a randomized trial, and a small sponsor, so I place the probability modestly above the oncology phase 3 base rate.

Ecnoglutide (XW003) gave about 15% mean weight loss at 48 weeks in the Chinese phase 3 SLIMMER trial, while semaglutide 2.4 mg gave about 12–13% in Chinese/East Asian populations (STEP 7), so any true advantage is probably modest, around 1–3 percentage points. With roughly 80 participants per arm and an SD near 7%, a difference of that size is only borderline detectable, and the small open-label 'switching' phase 2 may not even be powered for formal superiority. Sponsor confidence in running a head-to-head and possible higher dosing push the estimate up slightly, but a statistically significant superiority result is roughly a coin flip or a bit less.

QY201 appears to be an oral JAK-pathway inhibitor. That class has consistently beaten placebo on percent change in F-VASI at week 24 in phase 2 vitiligo trials, including ritlecitinib, upadacitinib and povorcitinib. With about 50 patients per arm, three dose arms and a continuous, sensitive endpoint, at least one dose reaching significance is likely. The main risks are uncertainty about the drug's potency at these doses, a single-site trial run by a small sponsor, and the low F-VASI entry threshold, which could add noise.

E2814 (etalanetug) is an anti-MTBR tau antibody, and the primary endpoint, change in CSF MTBR-tau-243, is close to a direct target-engagement readout for its epitope. Eisai's Phase 1b/2 and DIAN-TU data showed robust, dose-dependent reductions in CSF MTBR-tau-243, so a positive dose-response signal against placebo plus lecanemab at 6 months is highly plausible even with about 21 participants per arm. The main risks are assay or analysis quirks, an attenuated incremental effect on top of lecanemab, and how the dose-response test is defined. Primary completion is December 2026, and I am not aware of any public results.

Iza-bren (BL-B01D1), an EGFR×HER3 bispecific ADC with a topoisomerase I payload, showed high response rates (about 50–60%) and encouraging survival in second-line SCLC in early-phase Chinese studies. Baili has already reported positive Chinese phase 3 readouts for this drug in other tumors. Topotecan is a weak comparator, and tarlatamab beat chemotherapy on OS in DeLLphi-304, so a meaningful OS advantage is plausible in this large 722-patient trial. OS in relapsed SCLC is still a hard endpoint (lurbinectedin's ATLANTIS failed against topotecan), and I don't recall a public topline for this trial, so I stay below 80%.

This is Clarity AD, the Phase 3 trial of lecanemab in early Alzheimer's disease. Topline results were announced in September 2022 and published in NEJM (van Dyck et al., 2023). The core study met its primary endpoint, with a 27% slowing of CDR-SB decline at 18 months (difference -0.45, p<0.001), and these data supported full FDA approval. The registered primary completion date reflects the ongoing extension phase, but the first-listed core-study primary endpoint was clearly met.

Lacripep, a lacritin-derived peptide, missed its primary endpoints in an earlier Phase 2 dry-eye trial in Sjögren's patients, so efficacy evidence for the mechanism is thin. This is a small (n≈54, about 27 per arm) vehicle-controlled Phase 2 trial in Stage 1 NK. Its primary endpoint is change in central corneal fluorescein staining on a coarse 0–3 NEI scale, where vehicle response and regression to the mean can be substantial even after a run-in. Small sponsor, limited power and an unvalidated mechanism in this indication point to below-average odds of a statistically significant win.

Guselkumab is proven in adult UC: QUASAR showed robust induction and maintenance efficacy, and the mechanism carries over well to pediatric extrapolation studies. This pediatric trial has no placebo arm; both maintenance arms are guselkumab, so the Week 56 remission primary is likely descriptive or compared with a historical or adult placebo benchmark. A sponsor-defined success, such as remission clearly above adult placebo rates of roughly 20%, seems likely. There is still uncertainty from the small sample, the open-ended way 'success' may be judged, and the possibility of no formal hypothesis test.

This is APPEAR-C3G, Novartis's pivotal Phase 3 trial of iptacopan in C3G. The adult cohort, which is the first-listed primary endpoint, reported in 2024 a statistically significant 35.1% placebo-adjusted reduction in 24-hour UPCR at 6 months (p≈0.0014). That result supported FDA approval of Fabhalta for C3G in 2025. The record remains open only for the added adolescent cohort, so the residual risk is mainly in how the outcome gets adjudicated.

TRD205 is a novel oral non-opioid analgesic from Tide Pharmaceutical, and the move to Phase IIb suggests the earlier Phase IIa in this setting was encouraging. Hip arthroplasty is a harder acute pain model than bunionectomy or abdominoplasty, because baseline multimodal analgesia and rescue opioids compress drug-placebo differences in resting pain. With about 40 patients per arm, a single site, and three doses (any one beating placebo counts), the trial has a reasonable but not high chance of reaching significance on resting-pain NRS AUC0-48h. I start near the Phase 2 base rate and adjust modestly upward for the multiple doses and the presumed positive prior signal.

AZD0780 is an oral small-molecule PCSK9 inhibitor that cut LDL-C by about 50% versus placebo on top of statins in the phase IIb PURSUIT trial. Oral PCSK9 inhibitors such as enlicitide have also met LDL-C endpoints in phase III, including in HeFH (CORALreef HeFH). With roughly 470 patients randomised 2:1 and an expected placebo-adjusted LDL-C reduction of 40–50% at 12 weeks, the trial is overpowered, and HeFH patients respond well to PCSK9 inhibition because they are heterozygous. Topline results are not yet public, as primary completion is planned for January 2027.

In placebo-controlled Phase 3 trials on top of statins (BROADWAY, BROOKLYN), obicetrapib 10 mg lowered LDL-C by about 30-35%. Bempedoic acid's placebo-adjusted effect on top of statins is about 17-18% (CLEAR Harmony), so obicetrapib should lead by roughly 12-18 percentage points. With about 213 patients per arm and a typical SD of 20-25%, power to show superiority in this short 12-week biomarker trial is very high. The main risks are operational (a single UK site, a still-recruiting trial run by the licensee Menarini) or an unexpectedly weak obicetrapib effect, but the record gives no sign of either.

This is a tiny (n=24), single-site, sequential dose-escalation Phase IIa trial in China whose first-listed primary outcome is safety (AE incidence), not an efficacy comparison. With only about 6 patients per arm, any formal superiority test against placebo would almost certainly be underpowered. Success will therefore likely be judged as acceptable safety and tolerability over 8 weeks, which early oral RA drugs often show, though such small Chinese biotech trials often go unreported. I know of no public results, so I set a moderate probability that reflects both the likely 'safe and well tolerated' framing and the ambiguity of scoring a safety-only endpoint.

The primary endpoint is descriptive safety and tolerability (incidence of AEs/SAEs at 12 months), not a powered efficacy comparison, so 'success' will mean the sponsor reporting an acceptable safety profile. To my knowledge, SparingVision has publicly described Step 1 dose escalation as well tolerated, with DSMB clearance to proceed to the randomized Step 2. Subretinal AAV therapies generally have manageable safety profiles, usually limited to surgery-related events and steroid-responsive inflammation. The main risks are unexpected inflammation or toxicity at higher doses, or this trial being judged on its exploratory efficacy measures, so I keep a modest discount.

The first-listed primary outcome is a descriptive safety measure (participants with at least one TEAE), with no prespecified superiority test, so 'success' will likely be judged on whether Takeda calls the topline positive on tolerability and efficacy. Orexin-2 agonists have shown robust wakefulness effects in NT1. In NT2 the effects are more modest but still significant, for example alixorexton in Vibrance-2, and TAK-360 was designed for orexin-intact populations. Against this, the trial is small (n=88), still recruiting, and orexin agonists tend to produce more adverse events than placebo (insomnia, urinary frequency), which makes a strict 'favorable comparison' reading ambiguous.

In the Phase 2 T2D cohort, maridebart cafraglutide produced roughly 15-17% mean weight loss at 52 weeks versus about 1-2% on placebo. This trial randomizes about 1,100 participants to three doses against placebo over 72 weeks, so it is heavily powered for a large, well-established incretin-class effect. Tolerability-driven discontinuation could shrink the treatment-policy estimand, but it is very unlikely to erase statistical significance. Primary completion is not until January 2027, so I do not believe results are public yet.

The first-listed primary outcome is Part 1 safety, and the efficacy endpoints are complete response and overall response rate, largely in single-arm cohorts. The randomized Part 3 comparison against glofitamab alone is optional and would be underpowered to show a significant gain in complete response over an already active bispecific. PIM/FLT3 inhibition has a weak track record in lymphoma, and early MEN1703 monotherapy activity appears modest, so a clearly positive topline is uncertain. Some chance remains that the sponsor reports encouraging combination complete-response rates that would read as a success.

The primary outcomes are purely safety and tolerability measures (TEAEs, labs, vitals, ECG, C-SSRS), with no efficacy comparison, so 'success' here amounts to the sponsor reporting DNL593 as generally well tolerated. Denali's previously disclosed Part A single-ascending-dose data in healthy volunteers were described as generally well tolerated, and the transport-vehicle platform has a reasonably established safety profile. The main risks are platform-related adverse events (e.g., infusion reactions or anemia-type effects seen with TfR-targeting molecules), or deprioritization or ambiguous reporting by Denali. I have not seen the Part B topline results.

ATMOSPHERE is a pivotal test of whether one subretinal dose of ABBV-RGX-314, with supplemental anti-VEGF rescue allowed, is non-inferior to monthly ranibizumab on mean BCVA change at week 54 in previously treated nAMD patients. Phase 1/2a data at the higher doses showed roughly stable BCVA with large cuts in injection burden, and rescue injections plus a likely ~4–5 letter non-inferiority margin make success plausible. Risks remain: monthly ranibizumab is a strong control, the vitrectomy and subretinal procedure can cost vision, and dose-dependent variability and inflammation could erode mean BCVA. Primary completion is December 2026, so topline results are not yet public.

The primary outcomes are safety and tolerability counts with no prespecified efficacy comparison, so 'success' here means acceptable safety and positive sponsor framing. Centessa has publicly reported interim CRYSTAL-1 data (2025) showing ORX750 was generally well tolerated, with large, statistically significant MWT improvements versus placebo in NT1, NT2 and IH. That supports advancing to registrational studies. The residual risk is that final data show safety signals seen with other orexin agonists, such as visual disturbances, insomnia, urinary effects or hepatotoxicity as with TAK-994, or that a safety-only primary is scored ambiguously.

The first-listed primary endpoint is safety and tolerability (type and severity of AEs), not a statistical efficacy comparison, so success hinges on the drug being judged well tolerated. As I recall, Vaderis reported Part I topline data in 2024 saying VAD044 (an oral AKT inhibitor) was well tolerated and met its primary safety and tolerability endpoint, with clinically meaningful reductions in nosebleeds at 40 mg. Some uncertainty remains because a descriptive safety endpoint does not map cleanly onto a superiority comparison, and the long Part II extension is still ongoing.

As registered, the trial is a small open-label Phase 2 of infigratinib (n≈24, two doses) measuring change from baseline in annualized height velocity at 26 weeks against each child's own observational-study baseline, which is an easy bar for a drug with proven growth-promoting FGFR3-pathway activity. Infigratinib raised height velocity by about 2.5 cm/yr in PROPEL 2 for achondroplasia, and the related CNP-pathway drug vosoritide increased it by about 1.8 cm/yr in hypochondroplasia, so a clinically and statistically meaningful within-patient gain is likely even with about 12 children per arm. The main risks are a smaller effect in hypochondroplasia's milder, more heterogeneous genetics, regression-to-the-mean issues, and some ambiguity over how a single-arm 'success' is judged. I do not recall a public topline for this trial, so this is a forecast rather than a recalled result.

AMG 732 appears to be a subcutaneous IGF-1R–targeting antibody, a follow-on to teprotumumab; the exclusions for teprotumumab hypersensitivity and prior IGF-1R inhibitor use point to this mechanism. The mechanism is well validated in active TED, with proptosis reductions of roughly 2.5–3 mm versus placebo, and other subcutaneous IGF-1R agents have reported positive results. Part B is small (perhaps ~40–50 patients split across three doses plus placebo), and a phase 2 may be analyzed descriptively rather than with a formal test. Even so, the large expected effect size makes it likely that at least one dose shows a significant improvement over placebo.

IBI311 is Innovent's teprotumumab-like IGF-1R antibody, and it already met its primary endpoint in active TED in the RESTORE-1 phase 3. Teprotumumab itself beat placebo on proptosis response in chronic/inactive TED (about 62% vs 25%), and a Japanese inactive-TED trial also succeeded, so the mechanism is validated in this population. With 111 patients randomized 2:1, the trial has ample power for an effect of that size on an objective endpoint. The main risks are a smaller effect in long-standing disease (2–10 years) or a high placebo response, and I am not aware of any public topline result.

This is a tiny (n≈15) phase 1/2 placebo-controlled trial run by a small company testing an amniotic-derived biologic eye drop (d-MAPPS) in ocular GVHD, with a subjective symptom primary endpoint (UNC DEMS change). Placebo/sterile water drops tend to produce substantial symptom improvement in dry eye, and with roughly 7 patients per arm, statistical power to show a significant between-group difference is very low, even if the drug has some effect. Prior d-MAPPS data are open-label and uncontrolled. Success by formal statistical criteria is unlikely, though small sponsors sometimes report favorable trends.

HM15275 is Hanmi's GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist, a mechanism already validated by retatrutide's large weight-loss effects in phase 2, and early-phase data for HM15275 reportedly showed meaningful weight reduction. The primary endpoint is percent body-weight change versus placebo at 36 weeks, with about 53 participants per arm across four active doses, which gives ample power for the double-digit placebo-adjusted differences typical of incretin agonists. Failure would most likely require unexpected tolerability problems or high dropout, so success is very likely.

This is a tiny (n=15), descriptive phase II safety study whose primary outcome is adverse event reporting, with no prespecified efficacy comparison or non-inferiority margin, so a statistically significant win for Custodiol-N is very unlikely. The sponsor may well call it a success if safety looks comparable, and earlier Custodiol-N studies in adult heart and other transplants suggest a benign safety profile, but that kind of success doesn't clearly fit the definition used here. The trial is still recruiting, primary completion is planned for 2027-01, and enrollment may lag, so results could be delayed or never formally reported. My estimate reflects mostly the chance that a descriptive safety success is scored as meeting the endpoint.

This is a descriptive phase 2 pharmacokinetic study (Cmax, Tmax, AUC, Ctrough) of two subcutaneous nivolumab regimens. It has no prespecified efficacy comparison, so "success" would mean the sponsor reporting that the PK targets were achieved. Subcutaneous nivolumab (Opdivo Qvantig) already showed noninferior Cavg and Cmin exposure versus IV in CheckMate-67T, which makes adequate exposure with IV ipilimumab and chemotherapy highly likely. The main uncertainty is whether a descriptive PK trial resolves cleanly as "met," or whether exposure on one regimen falls short of the IV benchmark.

The primary outcome is safety (TEAEs, immunogenicity, safety visual assessments) at 6 months, not a prespecified efficacy comparison, so success would most plausibly be judged as acceptable tolerability. Earlier jCell (famzeretcel) trials, including the Phase 2b at doses up to 8.8M cells, showed a generally benign safety profile with no major signals, though the Phase 2b missed its efficacy primary. The main risks are ambiguity in how a safety-only primary is scored and the possibility of unexpected inflammatory or immunogenic events. Primary completion is planned for December 2026, and I am not aware of any public results.

House dust mite SCIT has an established mechanism, but phase 3 allergen immunotherapy trials using combined symptom-medication scores often fail to reach significance because of large placebo responses and perennial, variable exposure. This trial is small (about 50 per arm), runs only 12 months, and has recruited slowly since 2020, all of which reduce power. Inmunotek's MM09 allergoid has supportive earlier data, and having two dose arms gives two chances at success, which partly offsets these weaknesses. No results appear to be public.

The first-listed primary outcome is a safety measure, the proportion of patients with at least one adverse event at Week 14, not an efficacy comparison. Under a strict superiority reading, a 48-patient trial is very unlikely to show a significantly lower adverse event rate on HRS-7085 than on placebo. Some weight goes to the chance the outcome is scored as success if the sponsor reports acceptable safety, and early Hengrui/Suncadia oral IBD agents in China have usually been tolerable. Results are not yet public and may never be fully reported, so the forecast stays low but not extreme.

A corticosteroid against sham after cataract surgery, with rescue use counted as failure, is a format where nearly every prior product has won on both anterior chamber cell clearing and pain-free endpoints (Dexycu, Dextenza, loteprednol and difluprednate gels). Subconjunctival triamcinolone is a well-established, potent periocular steroid, and 250 patients randomized 2:1 gives ample power for the usual 25–35 point differences. The main risks are the co-primary requirement, possible slower anterior chamber clearing from a depot suspension, and execution quality at a small sponsor whose protocol is sloppy. Results are not yet public, as primary completion is planned for December 2026.

Short-term perimenstrual prevention with triptans (frovatriptan, naratriptan, zolmitriptan) has repeatedly beaten placebo. Rimegepant has proven but modest preventive efficacy (about 0.8 fewer monthly migraine days versus placebo with every-other-day dosing), and daily dosing across the 7-day perimenstrual window should give good CGRP coverage during the highest-risk days. Risks are the high placebo response in menstrual migraine, the small 5-day window with low baseline counts limiting the absolute effect size, and a four-arm design leaving roughly 180 per arm. The sponsor is a large, experienced company and this is an approved drug, so I place success moderately above the phase 3 base rate.

CMS-D002 from China Medical System's subsidiary is most likely an oral hormonal agent such as a GnRH antagonist or progesterone receptor modulator, though I cannot confirm the mechanism. Drugs in those classes (elagolix, relugolix, linzagolix, SPRMs) routinely achieve responder rates of about 70–90% on the MBL <80 mL with ≥50% reduction endpoint, against roughly 10–20% on placebo. With about 30 patients per arm, three doses, and only one dose needing to win, the trial has ample power if the drug is active. Remaining risk comes from the unconfirmed mechanism, possible underdosing, and single-site execution; results are not yet public.

The first-listed primary outcome is a descriptive safety count, so the closest thing to a testable efficacy endpoint is the comparison of patients with at least a 50% peripheral Treg reduction by Day 42 across arms. PI3Kδ inhibition has a plausible mechanism for strongly depleting Tregs, and roginolisib's earlier studies reported Treg reductions, so a large difference between roginolisib arms and dostarlimab plus docetaxel is biologically plausible. Against that, only about 15 patients per arm, an open-label Phase I/IIa design likely analysed descriptively, possible chemotherapy effects on Tregs in the control arm, and uncertainty over whether a formal significance test will be reported all lower the chance of a clear statistically significant win.

This tests an untested urate-lowering mechanism: a CMA2 nutraceutical (NAC, L-carnitine, nicotinamide, L-serine) has no established urate-lowering effect, and nicotinic compounds can, if anything, raise uric acid. ScandiBio's Turkish CMA trials have often reported positive results, and a 336-patient Phase 3 suggests the sponsor has some prior signal and powered for a modest effect of about 0.4–0.5 mg/dL. Still, a 4-week change in serum uric acid against placebo is an objective endpoint that resists placebo effects, and the biological rationale is weak. On balance I put the chance of a significant result somewhat below even.

This Phase 3a trial tests lot-to-lot consistency and non-inferiority of GSK's refined Oka-strain varicella vaccine (VNS) against Varivax, a well-established live-attenuated platform where lot consistency and immunogenicity non-inferiority usually succeed. There is some uncertainty: GSK appears to be running additional Phase 3 immunogenicity studies, and the secondary 'adaptive seroresponse threshold' outcome hints that seroresponse margins on the new gE assay may be tight. Enrollment of about 1,840 gives ample power for the usual margins, but meeting several co-primary comparisons adds risk. The trial is still recruiting and its results are not public.

This is a small (n=20) first-in-human dose-ranging study with no placebo. Its primary endpoint is adverse events, not a statistical efficacy comparison, so 'success' would likely mean the sponsor reports NOV05 as safe and well tolerated. Topical tacrolimus is well characterized, and Novaliq's water-free semifluorinated alkane vehicle has been tolerated in approved products, so a favorable safety readout is likely. The main uncertainty is that a descriptive safety endpoint may not map cleanly onto 'met primary endpoint', and an unexpected ocular tolerability signal remains possible, so I stop short of a very high probability.

In its small Phase 2b, Descartes-08 gave higher MG composite and MG-ADL responder rates than placebo (roughly 71% vs 25% on MGC in the efficacy population). That trial was small, with uncertain effect size, wide confidence intervals and heterogeneity. AURORA is larger (n=128), restricted to AChR+ patients, and uses MG-ADL responders at Month 4, where placebo responses in gMG trials are often 30–45%. A shrunken but real effect (e.g., 55–60% vs 35–40%) would give only moderate power, so I put the odds slightly better than a coin flip.

The primary outcomes are descriptive safety measures (solicited, unsolicited and serious adverse events) with no formal hypothesis test, so success effectively means an acceptable safety profile. Hia glycoconjugate vaccines are structurally close to Hib conjugates, which have decades of safety data, and a prior phase 1 presumably supported moving to phase 2. Small alum-adjuvanted conjugate vaccine trials in healthy adults rarely raise safety signals. The main risk is ambiguity in how a descriptive safety-only trial is scored, plus a small chance of an unexpected reactogenicity finding.

This is a very small (n≈27, 2:1) phase II placebo-controlled trial of topical artesunate, and its primary outcome is a strict endpoint: complete histologic response at 18 weeks. Earlier artesunate work in cervical HSIL suggested regression, but complete responses with topical therapy for vulvar HSIL are modest (imiquimod reached about 35%). With only about 9 placebo patients, even a 0% placebo rate needs roughly 8/18 responders for p<0.05, so the trial is underpowered. The primary outcome is also framed descriptively, which may mean no formal significant comparison is reported, further lowering the chance of a clear win.

This is a drug–vaccine interaction study, so a sponsor would count it a success if TPOXX does not meaningfully reduce JYNNEOS immunogenicity (antibody GMT non-inferiority) and adds no safety signal. Tecovirimat blocks VP37-mediated egress of enveloped virus, while MVA-based JYNNEOS is replication-deficient in human cells, and non-human primate data suggested little interference with MVA immunogenicity. So 'no interference' is mechanistically likely. The main uncertainty is how success is scored: the first-listed outcome is adverse-event counts, no non-inferiority margin is stated, and roughly 50 per arm limits precision, so I land moderately above even odds.

Dopamine/norepinephrine-enhancing drugs have a good track record in binge eating disorder: lisdexamfetamine succeeded in its phase 3 program and dasotraline was positive in at least one trial. A small investigator-initiated study of solriamfetol in BED reportedly suggested benefit, and two doses at 150 per arm give reasonable power. Against that, placebo response in BED is high, a count-of-episodes endpoint is noisy, and Axsome's solriamfetol program outside sleep disorders has been mixed (positive in ADHD, failed in MDD). Overall this lands slightly above a coin flip.

VDPHL01 is an extended-release oral minoxidil, a mechanism with well-established efficacy in androgenetic alopecia, and earlier Veradermics data in men reportedly showed robust hair-count gains over placebo. The primary endpoint is change in non-vellus target-area hair count at Month 6 versus placebo, in roughly 480 subjects. That design is well powered for the effect sizes minoxidil typically produces, and two active doses give two chances to win. The main risks are execution problems or a weaker showing on the co-primary patient-reported benefit measure, and primary completion is planned for 2026-12, so results are not yet public.

The primary endpoint is the incidence and severity of adverse events. That is descriptive safety with no prespecified superiority test, so 'success' effectively means the sponsor reports acceptable safety and tolerability, as is typical in Phase Ib/IIa topline announcements. Ecnoglutide is already validated as a subcutaneous GLP-1 agonist in Phase 3, and earlier oral formulation data from Sciwind suggested GI-dominated, manageable tolerability. The main risks are a dose-limiting GI or other safety signal at the higher oral doses, or ambiguity in how a safety-only endpoint gets scored. The trial is still recruiting with primary completion in 2027, so its results are not public.

HRS5580 appears to be an NK-1 receptor antagonist from Hengrui/Shengdi. Adding an NK-1 antagonist to a 5-HT3 antagonist in high-risk PONV patients generally cuts vomiting and improves 72-hour complete response, as Chinese fosaprepitant and aprepitant studies showed. Complete-response endpoints that count rescue use are often diluted, because rescue is driven by nausea, which NK-1 agents affect less, so expected differences of roughly 10–20 points with about 87 patients per arm give only moderate power. Since success needs only one dose to beat palonosetron alone and the mechanism is validated, a modestly favourable probability seems right.

This is a tiny (n=6), crossover, dose-escalation study in ultra-rare MVID. Its primary outcomes are safety and tolerability (AEs, physical exam, labs), summarized descriptively with no formal hypothesis test, so 'success' would most likely mean the sponsor declaring crofelemer safe and well tolerated. Crofelemer is minimally absorbed, has a long safety record, and Jaguar/Napo has already promoted positive investigator-initiated MVID data, so a favorable topline framing is likely. Uncertainty remains because a strict statistical reading cannot be satisfied, and with six patients any efficacy signal will be noisy; primary completion is December 2026, so results are not yet public.

TachoSil is an established fibrin sealant patch. In head-to-head hemostasis trials, fibrinogen/thrombin patches have repeatedly beaten oxidized regenerated cellulose at early time points; EVARREST, for example, roughly doubled success rates versus Surgicel in soft tissue bleeding. The open-label design with surgeon-assessed hemostasis also tends to favor the experimental arm. The main risks are that Surgicel performs relatively well in mild (VIBe grade 1–2) bleeding, which narrows the gap, and that roughly 58 patients per arm gives only modest power if the difference is under about 20 percentage points.

4-MUST is a new salt of trimebutine, an established spasmolytic, combined with hymecromone (4-methylumbelliferone), a choleretic used for biliary dyskinesia, so both components are already in clinical use in Russia. Valenta has a track record of Russian placebo-controlled trials of its own products that report positive results. Against that, the primary endpoint is a subjective VAS pain score with a large placebo response in functional biliary disorders, the per-arm size is modest (about 75), and the trial is still recruiting with no public results. Three dose arms give multiple chances to hit significance, so I put the probability moderately above the Phase 2 base rate.

This is a small Phase 2a umbrella study, with roughly 84 participants split across three investigational drugs and placebo, so each arm has only about 14–21 patients. None of the three mechanisms (CD40L blockade, TNF/OX40L nanobody, BTK inhibition) has proven efficacy in primary FSGS or MCD, so detecting a statistically significant UPCR reduction at 12 weeks would need a large effect. Selecting for steroid- or immunosuppression-responsive disease and having three shots at success raise the chance somewhat, and the recent anti-nephrin autoantibody findings in MCD and FSGS lend some biological rationale to the B-cell-related agents. Even so, the historical record for new mechanisms in FSGS is poor, and exploratory Phase 2a trials are often not powered for formal significance.

Oral nintedanib's efficacy in IPF is well established, and inhaled delivery to treatment-naive patients could plausibly match or exceed it, so a real FVC signal is biologically credible. However, the trial is small (~53 per arm) and runs only 12 weeks; with a typical SD of 150–200 mL, it would need roughly a 70 mL placebo-adjusted difference for p<0.05, versus an expected oral-nintedanib-like effect of about 30–60 mL. POC studies like this are often powered with relaxed alpha or analyzed in a Bayesian framework, so a 'positive' sponsor readout may not reach conventional two-sided significance. Two doses give two chances, but overall the odds sit below even.

Dato-DXd showed meaningful activity in EGFR-mutated NSCLC after osimertinib (TROPION-Lung05, ORR around 43%, leading to accelerated approval). Other ADCs have beaten platinum-pemetrexed on PFS in this post-TKI setting (sac-TMT in OptiTROP-Lung04; HER3-DXd modestly in HERTHENA-Lung02). Platinum-pemetrexed has a modest median PFS of about 5 months, and the trial has two shots on goal; the osimertinib combination arm is especially likely to show a PFS benefit. The main risks are that Dato-DXd alone may give PFS similar to chemotherapy and that toxicity in an open-label design could cut into the benefit, but one arm succeeding counts.

This is RC48-C016, a Chinese phase 3 of disitamab vedotin plus toripalimab versus gemcitabine-platinum in HER2-expressing first-line metastatic urothelial carcinoma. My recollection is that RemeGen announced in 2025 that the trial met both PFS and OS at interim analysis, with data presented at ESMO 2025 (PFS HR about 0.36, OS HR about 0.54). The analogous EV-302 result (ADC plus PD-1 versus chemotherapy) and strong phase 2 activity of this combination make success highly plausible even without that memory. Residual uncertainty reflects possible errors in my recall.

In earlier Danish trials, including a randomized phase 2 against standard care such as viscous lidocaine, the bupivacaine lozenge gave larger and longer oral pain relief in head and neck cancer patients during radiotherapy. The primary endpoint, pain reduction summed over 3 hours, favors a long-acting agent over short-acting lidocaine, and the open-label, patient-reported design adds further bias toward the novel product. The main risks are small-company execution, missing data on the last day of radiotherapy, and a modest sample of 150 if the true effect is smaller than in phase 2. The planned primary completion date looks unrealistic given the July 2026 start, and no results are public.

Jintrolong, a PEG-rhGH already approved in China, has shown height velocity comparable to daily GH in prior Chinese pediatric trials, including SGA populations, so the weekly arms will probably grow similarly to the Jintropin control. This small open-label Phase II (24 per arm) looks dose-finding and descriptive, with no stated non-inferiority margin or superiority hypothesis. Statistically significant superiority over daily GH is unlikely, while a sponsor-claimed 'comparable' or non-inferior result is plausible. Because it is unclear how success would be judged, I put the probability near the middle.

This is an essentially single-arm pivotal phase II design: stage 1 compares experimental arms only, and stage 2 is single-arm, so success most likely means the IC-ORR confidence bound clearing a prespecified historical threshold rather than beating a control. Earlier Chinese phase II data for utidelone, alone and with capecitabine or bevacizumab, in breast cancer brain metastases reported encouraging intracranial response rates of roughly 30–40%+, which supports a reasonable chance of clearing a modest bar. Against that, the US population is more heavily pretreated, the sponsor is a small company running a 12-site trial, the threshold and power are not disclosed, and enrollment or execution risk is real. On balance this sits slightly above even odds, and no results are public.

EX039 is a little-known oral compound from a small Taiwanese sponsor, tested as an add-on to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in a single-site, roughly 40-per-arm phase 2 with a 28-week ADAS-Cog primary endpoint. Phase 2 Alzheimer's symptomatic add-on trials have a very low success rate. Over 28 weeks placebo decline on ADAS-Cog is small, so this sample size is underpowered for plausible effects. The trial is still recruiting late into its planned timeline, results may not be reported cleanly, and a chance positive in one dose arm is the main route to success.

Novartis permanently halted recruitment in December 2022 because the HER2+ treatment landscape had changed. Only 19 patients were enrolled in total, most of them probably in the Part 1 safety run-in, so very few were randomized in Part 2. Part 2 participants are being unblinded, which means any PFS comparison will be descriptive and hugely underpowered, and a statistically significant PFS benefit is very unlikely. Part 1's DLT endpoint involves no comparison and cannot count as efficacy success, so the chance of meeting the primary endpoint is very low.

Tenapanor is already approved for IBS-C after two positive Phase 3 trials with clear gains in CSBM frequency. Other secretagogue-type drugs (linaclotide, plecanatide, lubiprostone) have reliably succeeded against placebo in chronic idiopathic constipation, including on this same stringent durable 9/12-week CSBM responder endpoint. With about 170 patients per arm, three doses, and placebo durable-response rates typically in the single digits to low teens, the trial looks well powered. The main risks are the stringent endpoint, a possibly modest effect in a non-IBS population, and the absence of a known Phase 2 CIC dataset.

The primary outcomes are purely safety and tolerability measures (TEAEs, vitals, labs, ECG) in a small 30-subject Phase Ib add-on study with no powered efficacy comparison, so success will most likely be judged as an acceptable safety profile. Phase Ia data already supported advancing to these doses. JL18008 appears to be a cytokine-type immunomodulator, and comparable agents such as IL-7 and IL-2 have generally been tolerable at studied doses in INRs. The main risks are dose-limiting toxicity at 70 μg/kg or ambiguity in how a safety-only endpoint is scored.

Systemic sclerosis has a poor track record in phase 3: tocilizumab (focuSSced), lenabasum (RESOLVE-1) and abatacept (ASSET) all missed their primary endpoints, and composite responder endpoints like CRISS can show high placebo responses, especially with background mycophenolate allowed. Anifrolumab is proven in SLE, and the type I IFN signature is elevated in a subset of SSc patients, but there is no randomized efficacy data in SSc, only small early-phase pharmacodynamic studies. The trial has a reasonable size (~314) and enriches for early, active, anticentromere-negative disease, but the effect of IFN blockade on skin and lung fibrosis is uncertain. Primary completion is January 2027, so no result is public.

The only primary outcome is safety and tolerability (CTCAE AE rate), so there is no prespecified efficacy comparison that could clearly succeed or fail. Such endpoints are usually reported as 'met' when the sponsor describes the drug as safe and well tolerated, but a statistically significant advantage over placebo on AE rate is implausible, which makes the outcome ambiguous. AND017 is an oral HIF-PH inhibitor, and the class (e.g., roxadustat) has shown erythropoietic activity and acceptable tolerability in thalassemia, so a favorable safety readout is likely if the trial is judged that way. Because the scoring convention is uncertain and the small single-country study is still recruiting, I stay only modestly above even.

This trial randomizes patients only between HLX43 doses and has no control arm, so 'success' depends on whether the reported ORR and PFS look clinically meaningful rather than on a formal superiority test. Early HLX43 phase 1 data showed antitumor activity across solid tumors, including some gynecologic responses. Topo-I ADCs often reach roughly 25-40% ORR in platinum-resistant ovarian and post-ICI cervical cancer, so an encouraging topline readout is plausible. Uncertainty remains high because there is no prespecified comparator or hypothesis, the PD-L1-targeted ADC approach is unproven, and the trial runs at a single center.

Large well-designed trials of intravenous MSCs in ischemic stroke (MASTERS, MASTERS-2, TREASURE, and the larger Chinese and Korean studies) have generally missed functional primary endpoints such as mRS, so the prior for a cell therapy in stroke is low. This trial is small (80 patients, single center) and is powered only for a large effect on Barthel Index or mRS, which are noisy endpoints in a heterogeneous moderate-to-severe stroke population. Small, company-sponsored, single-site studies sometimes report positive results on loosely defined endpoints, and the multiple timepoints give some room for that, but the trial was still recruiting and results may be delayed. Overall I put the chance of a clearly significant primary result at about 20%.

This is a Chinese non-inferiority immunogenicity trial of a MenACYW conjugate vaccine against a licensed CRM197 conjugate (CanSinoBIO Menhycia) in baseline-seronegative toddlers, a setting where conjugate vaccines typically produce very high seroconversion rates. Such trials usually meet their margins, and Sinovac has experience with meningococcal vaccines, so the base rate is high. The main risk is that non-inferiority must hold for all four serogroups on both seroconversion and GMT, and differences in carrier protein can produce a serogroup-specific shortfall, usually for Y or W135. Assuming a well-chosen dose, I put the probability of success near 88%.

The composite endpoint requires at least a 50% cut in calcium dose, which the control arm keeps at its full dose by design, so the control response rate should be near zero. Even a modest AMOR-1 response rate of about 25–30% in roughly 41 patients would likely reach significance. The main risk is that amorphous calcium carbonate's claimed doubling of bioavailability (from animal and small pilot human data) does not hold up. In that case many patients would fall below 8.0 mg/dL or need more active vitamin D, and the sponsor's analysis might not be a straightforward comparison against control.

Topical vasoconstriction with an α1 agonist (oxymetazoline) to prevent chemotherapy-induced alopecia is largely unproven in humans. Taxane and anthracycline regimens cause severe hair loss that even scalp cooling prevents only partially. The trial is small (about 20 per arm), uses a coarse CTCAE grade endpoint and has only two sites, so power to detect a modest effect is limited. Applied Biology often runs small trials that it reports as positive, which nudges the estimate up slightly, but the base rate for a new mechanism in this setting remains low.

SHR-A1811 (trastuzumab rezetecan) is a HER2-targeted topoisomerase-I ADC closely analogous to T-DXd, which beat T-DM1 by a large margin in second-line HER2+ MBC (DESTINY-Breast03). Pyrotinib plus capecitabine is a strong comparator (PHOEBE median PFS ~12.5 months), but early-phase SHR-A1811 data showed high ORR and long PFS in pretreated HER2+ disease. An open-label design with a BIRC-assessed PFS primary endpoint and ~381 patients gives ample power for a T-DXd-like effect. I believe Hengrui has publicly reported that this trial met its PFS endpoint, supporting a regulatory filing, though I hold that recollection with only moderate confidence.

This is an exploratory randomized phase 2 (about 60 per arm) adding PD-1 blockade to neoadjuvant CAPEOX in MMRp/MSS colon cancer, a setting where PD-1 monotherapy is largely inactive. Chemotherapy alone yields low major pathological response rates (FOxTROT-type data), so a large relative gain is conceivable, and some single-arm Chinese studies of PD-1 plus chemotherapy report higher regression. Still, the incremental benefit of PD-1 in MSS disease has generally been modest, and the trial is framed as looking for 'early signs of effectiveness' rather than powered for a formal significance test. Results have not been released, so I estimate a moderate-low probability of a statistically significant mPR difference.

HRS-5346 is Hengrui's oral small-molecule Lp(a) formation inhibitor, the same mechanism as muvalaplin, which reduced Lp(a) by roughly 70–85% in phase 2, and early HRS-5346 data reportedly showed robust dose-dependent reductions. This 60-patient trial has two dose arms and no placebo, so the primary endpoint is essentially a within-arm percent change from baseline, which will almost certainly be large and statistically significant at week 12. The main risks are ambiguity about how 'success' is judged without a control arm, or an unexpected safety or tolerability issue.

This is an open-label, single-arm Phase 1/2 dose-escalation and expansion study with no control arm, so 'success' means defining an MTD/recommended dose and showing meaningful ORR rather than winning a statistical comparison. Corbus has publicly reported interim data for CRB-701 showing a manageable MMAE-type safety profile and encouraging response rates in Nectin-4-expressing tumors such as HNSCC and cervical cancer. Nectin-4 is also a validated ADC target, given enfortumab vedotin's approval. The main uncertainties are how 'meeting the primary endpoint' will be judged for a non-comparative design and whether ORR holds up across the expansion cohorts. Final results are not yet public.

This trial closely replicates NADINA: two cycles of neoadjuvant anti-CTLA-4 plus anti-PD-1 with response-directed surgery, versus surgery plus adjuvant PD-1 therapy. In NADINA, a similar-sized trial (n=423), neoadjuvant ipilimumab plus nivolumab gave a large, highly significant EFS benefit (HR about 0.32), and SWOG S1801 supports the broader neoadjuvant-first principle. The main uncertainties are whether Biocad's nurulimab/prolgolimab combination matches ipi/nivo in potency, open-label conduct, and the timing of the EFS analysis. Primary completion is planned for 2027-01 and no results are public, but the size of the class effect makes success fairly likely.

This is a small open-label, two-dose exploratory Phase 2 with no control arm. Success would most plausibly mean a significant within-arm reduction in FT4 from baseline at week 16, which is a fairly lenient bar if any background antithyroid therapy or spontaneous improvement contributes. BTK inhibition acts indirectly on TRAb-producing B cells and plasma cells, and its effect on thyroid hormone levels within 16 weeks is unproven, unlike FcRn blockers, which lower IgG rapidly. Given the mechanistic uncertainty, the small sample, and the lack of a clear formal hypothesis test, I put this near a coin flip, slightly below.

GHK-Cu has an extensive preclinical and cosmetic literature, but rigorous controlled human wound-healing evidence is sparse and inconsistent, and topical agents rarely speed re-epithelialization of small acute wounds in healthy adults. The paired split-wound design with 60 participants gives decent power. However, assessments only on days 3, 7, 10, 14 and 21 make time-to-healing coarse, and a real difference of a day or two could be missed. A small, obscure sponsor and a sloppy registration slightly raise the chance of a favorable sponsor-reported result, but the base rate for a first test of this mechanism stays low.

Elismetrep is a first-in-class oral TRPM8 antagonist, licensed from Kallyope to TriGemX. Its Phase 2 acute migraine trial was reported positive on both 2-hour pain freedom and most-bothersome-symptom freedom, and this trial uses the same co-primary endpoints, two doses and a large sample (~600 per arm), so power is high for modest effects. Acute migraine Phase 3s that follow positive Phase 2 results with standard FDA endpoints have historically succeeded often (triptans, gepants, lasmiditan). The main risks are that the mechanism is new, a single Phase 2 may have overstated the effect, both co-primaries must win, and the MBS endpoint carries a high placebo response.

Disease-modifying drug trials in knee osteoarthritis almost always fail on structural endpoints. Diacerein's structural evidence is weak: it slowed joint-space narrowing in the hip (ECHODIAH), but knee data are inconsistent and modest. With about 64 patients per arm at a single site, detecting a between-group difference in two-year MRI cartilage volume loss, which is small and variable, is underpowered unless the effect is large. Small, sponsor-run single-country trials sometimes report positive results, which nudges the estimate slightly above a pure base rate.

The first-listed primary outcome (Part A TEAE count) is a safety measure, so the relevant efficacy comparison is Part B: percent body-weight change versus placebo at 36 weeks. NNC0662-0419 appears to be a potent incretin- or amylin-class agent, given the exclusions for prior GLP-1, GIP and amylin agonists and the requirement that participants be willing to lose more than 25% of body weight. Drugs in this class reliably beat placebo on weight loss, even in modestly sized phase 2 dose-ranging arms. The main uncertainties are how this multi-part, safety-led design gets scored, and the small chance of tolerability or development problems.

This is a descriptive Phase 3 safety and immunogenicity bridging study of Pfizer's already-approved RSVpreF (Abrysvo) in Indian adults, with no formal hypothesis test. RSVpreF has consistently produced robust neutralizing titer rises against both RSV A and B versus placebo, with acceptable reactogenicity, across prior trials. The main uncertainty is how a descriptive safety endpoint gets scored, since local reactions will be higher in the vaccine arm and that is not 'favoring' the vaccine in a superiority sense. Such trials are usually read as successful when they report results in line with the known profile, and primary completion is not until January 2027, so no result is public yet.

VENT-03 is a first-in-class oral cGAS inhibitor, tested here in a very small (n=24) four-week phase 2a with a mechanistic primary endpoint: percent change in skin interferon gene signature. Biomarker endpoints are easier to move than clinical scores, and IFN-pathway drugs such as anifrolumab and litifilimab clearly suppress the skin IFN signature. However, CLE interferon is driven largely by pDC TLR7/9 signaling, so it is unclear how much of it is cGAS-dependent, and the sample is underpowered for anything short of a large effect. The trial may also be analyzed descriptively, without formal significance testing, which further lowers the chance of a clear statistical win.

Complement factor B inhibition is mechanistically plausible in AAV, given the alternative pathway and C5a axis that avacopan validated. However, in ADVOCATE (n=331) avacopan improved week-52 sustained remission by only about 11 percentage points (65.7% vs 54.9%). This 84-patient phase 2 trial adds iptacopan on top of rituximab-based standard of care, and with about 42 per arm it is underpowered to show a modest sustained-remission difference at conventional significance. Unless the effect is much larger than avacopan's or the trial uses a lenient alpha, a statistically significant primary result looks unlikely, though positive trends are possible.

KDS2010 is a reversible MAO-B inhibitor being tested for obesity on the basis of astrocytic GABA hypothalamic biology and preliminary Phase 1 observations, but MAO-B inhibition has no proven weight-loss efficacy in humans (selegiline was not meaningfully effective). The trial is a small, staged Phase 2a with about 22 active versus 11 placebo patients per dose stage over 12 weeks, so it is powered to detect only large effects of roughly 3–4% placebo-adjusted weight loss. A dose-finding exploratory design and a first-in-mechanism test in obesity point to a low chance of a statistically significant primary result, though pooling the placebo groups or the 240 mg arm could yield a signal.

Actual enrollment is 89 against a planned 660, so only the Stage 1 dose-optimization portion appears to have run and the Stage 2 OS comparison likely will not happen, which may reflect a strategic or efficacy-driven decision. The first-listed primary endpoint is investigator-assessed ORR in Stage 1, with roughly 30 patients per arm, which is almost certainly descriptive. Even if formally compared, it is badly underpowered to show a significant gain over active standards like atezolizumab-bevacizumab or STRIDE. Phase 1 activity of anti-GARP/TGF-β livmoniplimab plus PD-1 was encouraging but not clearly superior, so a statistically significant win is unlikely.

Sonelokimab is an IL-17A/F nanobody, a mechanism already validated in TNF-inadequate-responder psoriatic arthritis: bimekizumab's BE COMPLETE showed ACR50 of about 43% vs 7% for placebo. Sonelokimab's own Phase 2 ARGO trial showed a clear ACR50 separation from placebo. With about 600 patients, a placebo control and an objective-ish ACR50 endpoint, power is ample even allowing for some placebo inflation like that seen in MoonLake's VELA hidradenitis program. Primary completion is expected January 2027, so I do not believe results are public yet.

The first-listed primary outcome is safety (incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events), not efficacy, so there is no formal superiority test against placebo. Such trials are usually reported as having 'met' the endpoint when the drug is described as safe and well tolerated. ENV-294 is an oral, first-in-class anti-inflammatory that has already been through Phase 1, which lowers the risk of a disqualifying safety signal over 12 weeks in about 50 patients. Remaining uncertainty comes from how a safety-primary trial gets scored and from the chance of tolerability problems or an underwhelming readout; recruitment was still ongoing and no results are public.

The primary endpoints are descriptive PopPK and PK/PD parameter estimates (CL/F, Vd/F, Ka, IC50 for pruritus inhibition), with no prespecified hypothesis test, so 'success' mostly means getting usable model estimates. That is likely, since nemolizumab PK is well characterized. The IC50 component depends on a real exposure-response signal for itch, which is plausible given nemolizumab's strong anti-pruritic effects in prurigo nodularis and atopic dermatitis. However, CPUO is heterogeneous, and with roughly 10 placebo patients any efficacy comparison is underpowered. Because it is unclear how a descriptive endpoint will be scored as a win, I land moderately above even odds.

This is a small (n=40), two-site Phase II trial from a small company testing a first-in-class topical aimed at mutant keratin aggregation in EBS, with mixed localized, intermediate and severe subtypes. The primary endpoint, change in blister surface area, is highly variable and prone to large placebo responses because flares resolve on their own. Prior topical EBS programs, such as diacerein in a Phase 2/3, have failed to separate from placebo. A small company's sponsor-defined analysis might still report a favorable p-value, but statistical success on the primary comparison looks unlikely, and no results are public yet.

This is a first-in-human phase 1/2 trial of RIG-101, an intranasal innate-immune (RIG-I pathway) agent, from a small biotech. The first-listed primaries are safety measures, so the scored efficacy outcome is likely the Part B lower respiratory symptom score AUC after rhinovirus RV-A16 challenge in mild-to-moderate asthmatics. Part B will be small, and challenge-model symptom endpoints are noisy. Antiviral and innate-immune approaches to virus-induced asthma worsening, such as inhaled interferon-beta, have mostly failed to show significant symptom benefit, so a significant LRSS reduction is uncertain, although lenient safety-based interpretations add some upside.

The first-listed primary endpoint is Phase 2 ORR comparing selinexor plus R-GDP with R-GDP alone. That comparison involves a small, open-label, likely underpowered randomization in transplant-ineligible relapsed/refractory DLBCL, where R-GDP already produces substantial response rates. Selinexor's single-agent activity in DLBCL is modest (SADAL ORR about 28%), and Karyopharm has deprioritized its DLBCL program in favor of myelofibrosis and endometrial cancer, which makes a robust Phase 3 PFS readout unlikely. Add-on strategies to salvage chemoimmunotherapy in this setting have historically failed, so a statistically significant win is improbable.

This is a small crossover bridging study by GE Healthcare comparing a reformulation (GE-287) of the approved amyloid PET tracer Vizamyl, where success means showing comparable SUVr and biodistribution rather than superiority. The active moiety is unchanged and the excipients were changed for tolerability and manufacturing, so regional SUVr values should be highly concordant, and sponsors in these studies typically declare equivalence or comparability. The main risks are an undefined equivalence margin with only 20 participants, and possible biodistribution differences from the excipient change (e.g., PS80), which could alter early organ SUV in the heart, liver or kidneys. Overall, success is likely.

This is a small (n=84), open-label, three-site Italian phase 1/2 trial run by a small sponsor, testing nightly peritoneal ultrafiltration against no intervention in diuretic-resistant congestive HFrEF; no result from it is public. The composite primary endpoint is dominated by soft, partly investigator-driven components (a ≥50% diuretic dose increase, or escalation to IV diuretics or ultrafiltration), and control-arm event rates should be high in this population, so a large effect is plausible. Observational peritoneal ultrafiltration data in refractory heart failure also look favorable. Against that, the small sample, recruitment and feasibility problems that are likely to delay the trial, the adaptive re-sizing, and the low base rate for phase 2 heart-failure trials keep my estimate below even.

The first-listed primary outcome is the incidence of treatment-emergent AEs and SAEs, comparing eletriptan plus standard of care with standard of care alone, in an open-label trial of 28 patients that is still recruiting. A statistically significant difference favoring the drug on AE incidence is very unlikely, because acute SCI patients have frequent AEs in both arms and the trial is tiny. Eletriptan's well-known safety profile, though, makes a sponsor topline of 'safe and well tolerated' quite likely, which might be scored as success. Given that ambiguity, plus possible delays from a small two-site Spanish trial, I place this near even odds.

LIBREXIA-AF is a large non-inferiority trial of milvexian 100 mg twice daily against apixaban for stroke and systemic embolism, a strong active comparator that sets a high bar. The closest precedent is OCEANIC-AF, where asundexian, another factor XIa inhibitor, was clearly inferior to apixaban and stopped early; that raises real doubt about whether this mechanism matches factor Xa inhibition for stroke prevention in AF. Offsetting this, milvexian is dosed for more complete factor XIa suppression, and the monitoring committee has let the trial continue through interim looks that would likely have caught an asundexian-sized efficacy gap. With LIBREXIA-ACS stopped for futility adding mechanism uncertainty, I put the chance of meeting the non-inferiority margin near a coin flip.

BAT6026 is Bio-Thera's anti-OX40 antibody. Its mechanism is validated in atopic dermatitis by rocatinlimab and amlitelimab, so an efficacy signal and acceptable tolerability are plausible. However, the registered primary outcomes are purely descriptive safety measures (AEs, vital signs, ECG, labs) in a 33-patient Phase Ib with 9:3 randomization per cohort, so no powered superiority comparison exists and 'success' depends on how the safety readout is framed. Such trials are usually reported as 'well tolerated', but with no formal statistical test and a small placebo group, any efficacy comparison could easily miss significance, so I stay moderately above even odds.

The primary endpoint is safety and tolerability, measured as AE counts, in a small open-label proof-of-concept trial with no powered efficacy comparison, so 'success' most plausibly means the sponsor reports the drug as safe and well tolerated. TNP-2092 (rifaquizinone) has prior phase 1 data and an earlier PJI study, and the 14-day local intra-articular dosing keeps systemic exposure low, so a favorable safety readout is likely. The main uncertainty is how a safety-only primary endpoint gets scored, along with the small chance of local tolerability signals or delays, since the trial is still recruiting with primary completion planned for January 2027. I am not aware of any public results.

This is a first-in-human Phase 1/2a trial of BMS-986470, an oral degrader of ZBTB7A/WIZ meant to induce fetal hemoglobin, and its first-listed primary endpoints are descriptive safety counts with no formal efficacy hypothesis test.
