The FAI score is a novel imaging endpoint with untested responsiveness to drug therapy over 24 weeks, and enrolling patients with high baseline FAI invites regression to the mean in both arms. Having two doses and 240 patients helps somewhat, but the weak prior mechanistic evidence and small-biotech phase 2 base rates argue for a below-even probability.

IL-1β blockade is validated in acute gout (canakinumab, anakinra), and dapansutrile's small open-label phase 2a showed meaningful pain reduction, so the NLRP3 mechanism is biologically plausible. Rescue medication is barred until after the Day 4 (72-hour) assessment, which should widen any drug–placebo gap, and 300 patients randomized 2:1 gives reasonable power for a roughly 10 mm VAS difference. Against that, placebo response in self-limiting gout flares is large, there are no prior randomized controlled data for this drug, and slow enrollment by a small sponsor adds uncertainty about dose, exposure and trial execution. I put the chance of success near a coin flip, slightly favoring success.

This is a small (32-patient), open-label, two-site Taiwanese trial comparing bevacizumab with or without NaviFUS blood-brain-barrier opening in recurrent GBM, with PFS-6 as the primary endpoint. With about 16 patients per arm and a bevacizumab control PFS-6 of roughly 40%, only a very large effect (well over 35 percentage points) would reach two-sided significance. Bevacizumab is a large antibody whose antiangiogenic action does not clearly depend on crossing the BBB, and the phase 1 NaviFUS data are encouraging but uncontrolled. The 'pivotal' label and sponsor-driven design may mean a lenient or one-sided analysis, but this is still a likely miss on a strict significance criterion.

Topical eye drops to reverse age-related cataract (lanosterol/oxysterol-type approaches) have never shown convincing efficacy in humans, so the base rate for this mechanism and indication is very low. Enrollment ended at only 8 subjects, about 4 per arm, against a planned 40, which leaves essentially no power to detect a significant BCDVA difference. This is an exploratory pilot with many descriptive outcomes, and statistical significance on the first-listed BCDVA change is highly unlikely.

Velodrome is most likely a non-inferiority comparison of the same PDS ranibizumab implant refilled every 36 weeks versus every 24 weeks, with BCVA change as the primary endpoint. My understanding is that supplemental intravitreal ranibizumab is allowed, which tends to protect visual outcomes and makes non-inferiority easier to show. The risk is real, though: pharmacokinetic modeling suggests ranibizumab levels fall substantially by week 36, and the 2022 implant recall and enrollment pause may have added heterogeneity. Weighing the high historical success of anti-VEGF non-inferiority trials against the meaningfully longer interval, I estimate about 70%.

This trial tests as-needed ICS/SABA rescue, a concept already validated. In AstraZeneca's MANDALA trial, as-needed budesonide/albuterol at 160/180 cut time to first severe exacerbation by about 27% versus albuterol alone (p<0.001), while the lower dose missed significance. Here the primary comparison is the higher fluticasone propionate dose (110 mcg per use) versus albuterol, in an event-driven design of about 2,800 exacerbation-prone patients, which should give good power for a similar effect. Remaining risks are that a dry-powder inhaler used in children as young as 4 could dilute the effect, the event-driven design could under-accrue events, and fluticasone propionate may have a less favourable dose-response than budesonide, so I sit somewhat below near-certainty.

This is a small (n=60) Phase 2 trial with day-21 all-cause mortality as the first primary outcome. Day-21 mortality in early antifungal therapy is low, roughly 5-15%, so the trial has essentially no power to show a statistically significant superiority difference against active LAmB or voriconazole. The design is descriptive, estimating safety and efficacy rather than testing a hypothesis, and no non-inferiority margin is stated. The sponsor may well report favorable numbers, but formal statistical success on mortality is very unlikely.

Gemcitabine monotherapy is a weak second-line comparator in cervical cancer, with median PFS of about 2–3 months, and TIL therapy (Iovance LN-145, early GT101 data) has shown objective response rates around 40% in this disease. Measuring PFS from first study treatment rather than randomization also helps the TIL arm, because it skips the manufacturing delay. Against that, the trial is a small (n=100) open-label phase II, many Chinese patients will have had prior PD-1/PD-L1 therapy that may blunt TIL efficacy, and it is still recruiting. There is also a real chance of manufacturing failures, dropout or incomplete reporting.

Tunlametinib, a MEK inhibitor already approved in China, plus vemurafenib showed encouraging early-phase activity in BRAF V600E colorectal cancer, reportedly with response rates and PFS above historical chemotherapy benchmarks. The control, doublet chemotherapy with or without bevacizumab or cetuximab, gives short PFS in BRAF-mutant disease (about 2–4 months, as BEACON showed). An open-label PFS endpoint further favors the experimental arm. Against that, BRAF+MEK without EGFR blockade has historically been weak in CRC, and the trial is modest in size (165) and still recruiting, so meaningful uncertainty remains.

This is a first-in-human Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study whose primary endpoint is descriptive safety and tolerability, with no formal efficacy comparison. Such trials are usually reported as having met the endpoint when the drug proves acceptably tolerated and escalation completes. The step-up priming regimen suggests a B-cell-depleting T-cell engager, which carries real risks of cytokine release syndrome and infection. Still, healthy-volunteer Part 1 finished and the study moved on to systemic sclerosis patients, which supports acceptable early safety, and I am not aware of any public results.

The closest precedent, BMS's RELATIVITY-098, tested adjuvant relatlimab plus nivolumab against nivolumab in resected melanoma and failed to improve relapse-free survival, which is a strong negative signal for adding a LAG-3 antibody in this setting. Fianlimab plus cemiplimab produced impressive phase 1 response rates in metastatic melanoma, but beating an active anti-PD-1 comparator in the adjuvant setting is a hard bar. The trial is large and allows two fianlimab dose arms, which modestly raises the chance that one arm succeeds. Overall, I estimate a below-base-rate probability of success.

This is a small, open-label, dose-finding Phase II with three HLX43 dose arms, no control arm and no prespecified hypothesis test, so 'success' would rest on whether IRRC-assessed ORR looks clinically meaningful. HLX43 has shown encouraging responses in NSCLC, particularly squamous, but previously treated microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer responds poorly to both PD-L1-directed and non-HER2-targeted topo-I ADC approaches, with ORRs often in the single digits to low teens. A modest ORR that the sponsor may not frame as positive seems the most likely outcome, and I am not aware of any published result from this trial.

This is an open-label, uncontrolled-style phase I/II dose-escalation study whose first-listed primary outcome is AE incidence, so there is no formal superiority test, and success will in practice mean an acceptable safety profile plus encouraging bleeding-rate reductions. SR604 appears to be a subcutaneous non-factor rebalancing agent, a mechanism already validated by anti-TFPI antibodies (concizumab, marstacimab) and SerpinPC. That makes reduced ABR in on-demand patients with frequent prior bleeds likely. Thrombotic events, a known class risk, or immunogenicity could still derail it, and ambiguity over how success is defined adds uncertainty.

Benralizumab consistently cut exacerbations by roughly 30-50% in adult eosinophilic asthma, and other type-2 biologics (dupilumab in VOYAGE, mepolizumab in MUPPITS-2) succeeded in children, which supports a real effect here. Against that, only 94 patients are enrolled in an event-driven time-to-first-exacerbation design, so the study has few events and modest power. Pediatric trials also tend to see large placebo responses, and the adolescent subgroups in SIROCCO/CALIMA showed weaker benralizumab effects. I put success somewhat above a coin flip, and I don't know of any public results.

This first-in-human Phase 1/2 trial of ABCL635, an NK3R-targeting antibody, has only descriptive safety primary endpoints (AEs, ECG, physical exam, labs), with no formal statistical comparison. A topline announcement would call it met if the drug proved safe and tolerable, which is the usual outcome for a biologic against a validated target (fezolinetant and elinzanetant), especially as a long-acting antibody may avoid the liver signals seen with small molecules. The main risks are unexpected safety or immunogenicity findings, or the sponsor framing a weak Part C efficacy result as a failure, so the estimate is moderately high. I do not recall this trial's own results being public.

Tulisokibart is an anti-TL1A antibody with positive Phase 2 data in ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, but TL1A blockade has no proven efficacy in psoriatic arthritis or any rheumatologic indication. There is some biologic rationale, since TL1A drives Th17/IL-17 and ILC3 pathways, and ACR20 at week 16 against placebo is a comparatively easy endpoint, with three doses each getting a shot at significance. Still, about 35 patients per arm and a 25–30% placebo ACR20 rate need a delta near 30 points to reach significance, which only well-established mechanisms reliably deliver. With no public result yet (primary completion is planned for February 2027), I sit near the base rate for a first test of a new mechanism in this disease.

This is a small (n=63) randomized phase 2 comparing GeoVax's synthetic MVA vaccine against an active, effective comparator, mRNA vaccine, in post-HCT/CAR-T patients. The composite responder endpoint (≥3-fold rise in neutralizing antibodies or IFN-γ) will likely be met by a high fraction of both arms, which makes a statistically significant superiority difference hard to show even with a one-sided test. GeoVax's public interim updates have described robust or comparable responses, especially T-cell responses, rather than clear superiority on the primary composite. Given the active control and small sample, success on the formal comparison looks unlikely, though a sponsor-favorable framing is possible.

This is an open-label Phase I/II dose-escalation and expansion study whose first-listed primary outcomes are DLTs and adverse events, with no formal efficacy comparison, so 'meeting the primary endpoint' mostly means identifying a tolerable dose with encouraging activity. Earlier data presented at ASH showed englumafusp alfa plus glofitamab giving high ORR and CR rates in heavily pretreated DLBCL with manageable CRS, and Roche went on to a large Part III expansion in second-line patients. Against that, there is uncertainty about Roche's continued commitment to the CD19-4-1BBL program, and it is unclear how a safety-primary, single-arm study would be judged. I put the probability modestly above even.

This is a Phase 1/2a first-in-human study of RN3161, an siRNA from Rona Therapeutics, and every primary outcome is a descriptive safety or tolerability measure (AEs, vitals, ECG, labs). There is no prespecified superiority test, so a sponsor would most likely call the primary endpoint met if the drug proves acceptably safe and tolerable. Most siRNA programs clear early safety readily. The main risks are an unexpected safety signal or an ambiguous judgment on whether a descriptive safety endpoint was met. Primary completion is planned for 2027, and I don't believe any results are public yet.

This is a Phase I/II dose-finding safety and immunogenicity study of SK Bioscience's mosaic RBD nanoparticle pan-sarbecovirus vaccine (built on the SKYCovione/GBP510 platform, with Gates/CEPI backing). Its first-listed primary outcome is a descriptive safety measure (immediate reactions), not a superiority comparison against Comirnaty. Such trials are usually reported as having "met" their primary endpoint when safety is acceptable, and this platform has a good safety and immunogenicity record. The main risks are an unfavorable safety signal or the outcome being judged ambiguous because no formal hypothesis test is prespecified, which limits confidence somewhat.

The primary endpoint is purely a safety and tolerability count (treatment-related AEs and lab abnormalities) in a 24-patient dose-ranging Phase II with no prespecified efficacy hypothesis test. A statistically significant advantage over placebo plus rituximab is essentially impossible on such an endpoint at this sample size. Resolution therefore hinges on interpretation: a sponsor would likely call the trial successful if HLX79 was 'safe and well tolerated', which is plausible for a sialidase fusion protein added to a well-characterized anti-CD20 backbone. Given that ambiguity and no public results (primary completion is 2027-01), a near-midpoint estimate is appropriate.

This is an open-label, non-inferiority-style Phase 3 comparing 8-week bemnifosbuvir/ruzasvir with 12-week sofosbuvir/velpatasvir on SVR at week 24. In Phase 2, BEM/RZR achieved about 98% SVR12 in the per-protocol population, and DAA non-inferiority trials against SOF/VEL with a margin of roughly 10% usually succeed. The main risks are the shorter duration in an ex-US population likely enriched for genotype 3 and cirrhotic patients, plus ITT losses to follow-up at sites in lower-resource countries, which could narrow the margin. I do not recall this trial's result being public.

HRS-7535 is Hengrui's oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist, and earlier phase 2 obesity and diabetes trials showed clear, dose-dependent weight loss over placebo. The primary endpoint here is percent change in body weight at 36 weeks against placebo, with about 225 patients, so even a modest effect in obese HFpEF patients should be highly significant. The main risks are operational: high discontinuation from GI intolerance, or enrollment and completion problems at what is listed as a single site that is still recruiting. I have not seen this trial's result reported.

ASKB589 is an anti-CLDN18.2 monoclonal antibody, a mechanism validated by zolbetuximab, which significantly improved PFS when added to chemotherapy in SPOTLIGHT and GLOW (HR ~0.69–0.75). ASKB589's own phase 2 data with CAPOX plus a PD-1 inhibitor showed high response rates. The added benefit on top of chemo-immunotherapy is unproven and may be smaller, and a possibly broader CLDN18.2 positivity cutoff could dilute the effect. Still, a large 780-patient trial with an IRC-assessed PFS endpoint gives reasonable power, so the odds of success are modestly better than even.

This is a Phase 3 trial of efdamrofusp alfa (a VEGF/complement bispecific) against aflibercept 2 mg Q8W in treatment-naive nAMD, with mean BCVA change averaged over weeks 44–52 as the primary endpoint, and it is almost certainly a non-inferiority design. Non-inferiority BCVA trials of potent anti-VEGF agents against aflibercept (faricimab, brolucizumab, aflibercept 8 mg) have nearly all met their margins. The Phase 2 STAR data for the 8 mg dose showed BCVA gains numerically comparable to or better than aflibercept. The main residual risks are a possible superiority hypothesis, extended-interval dosing underperforming, or execution issues, and I do not know of any topline result yet.

Sufenidone (SC1011) appears to be a pirfenidone-like antifibrotic, and that class has validated efficacy on annual FVC decline against placebo in IPF, which supports a reasonable prior. However, roughly 100 patients per arm is modest for this noisy endpoint: pirfenidone's CAPACITY 006 failed, and nintedanib's TOMORROW (about 85 per arm) narrowly missed on FVC decline rate. The small Chinese sponsor, single listed site, seamless phase 2/3 design and stale registration add execution risk, and no results are public, so I put the chance near even, slightly below.

Mezigdomide is a more potent CELMoD than pomalidomide, with preclinical activity in IMiD-resistant disease and high response rates for MeziVd in phase 1/2 lenalidomide-exposed cohorts. That makes a PFS advantage over PVd (median about 11 months in OPTIMISMM) plausible in this 810-patient trial. Against that, it is an active head-to-head comparison within the same mechanism, neutropenia may limit dose intensity, and phase 3 trials in myeloma fail fairly often even with strong early data. I am not aware of any topline readout, and the trial is still recruiting with primary completion planned for 2027.

The primary outcome is the incidence of adverse events in a small Phase 1b MAD study (n=18), with no formal efficacy hypothesis test, so success will most likely mean a topline report that EC5026 was safe and well tolerated. EC5026, an sEH inhibitor, has already completed Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers without major safety signals. The 2–4 mg doses and 28-day exposure are modest, which favors a benign safety readout. The main risks are an unexpected safety signal (for example endocrine or HPA-axis effects, given the exclusion criteria), enrollment delays at a single recruiting site, or ambiguity about how a safety-only endpoint is scored.

KarXT (xanomeline-trospium) is proven in acute schizophrenia, and xanomeline alone reduced hallucinations and delusions in Alzheimer's patients in 1990s trials, which gives real mechanistic support. Against that, Alzheimer's psychosis trials have high placebo response and a poor track record (pimavanserin's acute results were mixed), the adjunctive schizophrenia trial ARISE failed, and cholinergic tolerability may limit dosing in elderly patients. BMS reportedly enlarged and extended this trial, which may signal concern about variability. I do not know of any topline result, so a roughly even probability seems appropriate.

The only primary outcome is the incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events, with no prespecified efficacy comparison, so a superiority 'success' (significantly fewer adverse events than vehicle) is very unlikely. A sponsor topline, however, would probably call it met if the gel is well tolerated, which is plausible given lotilaner's clean safety record as Xdemvy in Demodex blepharitis. With primary completion planned for end of 2026 and no known public readout, the result depends mostly on how a safety-only endpoint is judged. I therefore settle near the middle.

This is a small (n=51), open-label phase I/II dose-exploration trial of umbilical cord MSCs given with CABG, with roughly 12 patients per arm. The first-listed primary outcome is phase I safety, and the phase II LVEF comparison against CABG alone is likely underpowered or only descriptive. Prior trials of MSCs given alongside CABG, such as PERFECT and the CSCC_ASCII-type studies, have mostly shown no significant LVEF benefit over surgery alone, and CABG by itself improves LVEF substantially, which raises the bar for showing added benefit. Chinese sponsors sometimes report favorable results, but a statistically significant between-arm LVEF difference in a study this size is unlikely.

No adjunct to therapeutic hypothermia for neonatal HIE has yet shown benefit in a well-powered randomized trial; erythropoietin (HEAL), xenon, and others failed, so the base rate for this indication is very low. RLS-0071 is a novel complement/neutrophil-modulating peptide with no prior efficacy data in neonates, and the trial is a seamless Phase 2/3 with dose escalation. Its primary endpoint, the Day 4–7 MRI Weeke score, is a continuous measure that is more sensitive than clinical outcomes, but the 173 participants are split across moderate/severe HIE and two doses, which limits power. The trial is still recruiting close to its planned primary completion, and no results are public.

The single-arm Phase 2 VIRO-15 trial reported striking ORR (~54%) and PFS (~11 months) in heavily pretreated PRROC, but single-arm results in selected patients often shrink in randomized testing. Here the control arm gets active bevacizumab plus chemotherapy, which can include a platinum doublet, so the comparator is strong. Oncolytic viruses have a poor Phase 3 track record, ovarian cancer Phase 3 success rates are low, and a 186-patient open-label trial from a small sponsor adds risk. Blinded independent central review of PFS and the plausible platinum-resensitization mechanism give some upside, but failure remains more likely than success.

This is a non-inferiority immunogenicity trial comparing CanSino's PCV13i, a 13-valent conjugate on CRM197/TT carriers, with Prevnar 13 in Thai infants, using IgG ≥0.35 µg/mL seroresponse 30 days after the booster as the primary measure. PCV13i has already shown non-inferiority to Prevnar 13 in Chinese pivotal trials, and post-booster seroresponse rates for most serotypes approach 100%, which makes typical -10% margins easy to meet. The main risk is that non-inferiority probably has to hold for every serotype, with serotype 3 or a carrier-specific serotype (TT-conjugated) as the likeliest problems, plus some regulatory or operational uncertainty. Primary completion is expected in 2027, so no results are public.

The first-listed primary outcome is a safety measure, the number of treatment-emergent adverse events. It has no prespecified efficacy comparison, and a 40-patient trial is very unlikely to show a significant difference favoring ebselen over placebo. The sponsor would probably describe the drug as 'safe and well tolerated', which could be scored as a success. But the trial is small, appears delayed (start date listed as 2026-12 while recruiting), and no results are public, so the probability stays low to moderate.

ZT006 appears to be an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist tablet. Oral small-molecule GLP-1 agonists such as orforglipron have consistently produced large, highly significant placebo-adjusted weight loss in Phase 2 trials at 26–36 weeks. Even with only about 30 participants per arm, a placebo-adjusted difference of 5% or more at week 28 in at least one of five active arms would very likely reach significance. The main risks are an unusually weak molecule or tolerability-driven dropout, and primary completion (December 2026) has not yet passed, so results are not public.

Upadacitinib plus TCS has shown large EASI-75 effects in adults and adolescents, including in Japanese patients (about 65-77% vs about 26% on placebo plus TCS in AD Up and Rising Up). Pediatric biologic trials with TCS, such as dupilumab, kept similarly large separations. With about 50 per arm and an expected absolute difference near 40 percentage points, power is very high, so the main risks are an unusually high placebo-plus-TCS response or an underperforming pediatric dose. I am not aware of a public topline result for this trial.

Brivekimig is a TNF/OX40L bispecific nanobody. Its anti-TNF component works through a mechanism already proven in HS (adalimumab), and Sanofi's Phase 2a HS study reportedly showed meaningful improvements over placebo, which prompted this dose-ranging Phase 2b. HiSCR75 is a stringent endpoint, but placebo rates are usually around 15–25%, and with about 52 patients per arm and three doses, a 20-point or larger difference in at least one arm is plausible. The main risks are the HS-typical high placebo response and the inclusion of biologic-experienced patients, who may respond less to a TNF-containing agent.

In the phase 2 placebo-controlled trial (Mayer et al., NEJM 2024), felzartamab produced morphologic AMR resolution at week 24 in about 82% of patients versus 20% on placebo, with consistent reductions in MVI, molecular scores and dd-cfDNA. TRANSCEND uses a similar week-24 biopsy endpoint against placebo, and 132 patients give high power even if the true effect is well below the phase 2 estimate. The main risks are regression from a very small phase 2, heterogeneity in a broader multinational population including chronic active AMR, and stricter central Banff 2022 reading. Primary completion is December 2026, so results are not yet public.

This is a descriptive, dose-finding Phase 2 immunogenicity study with no placebo or active comparator, so 'success' means robust anti-rF1V antibody responses, which Dynavax and DoD would likely report as positive. An earlier Phase 2 trial found that adding the CpG 1018 adjuvant to rF1V produced strong, accelerated antibody responses compared with alum-adjuvanted rF1V. Two Part 1 regimens have already been selected for Part 2, which suggests acceptable early immunogenicity and safety. The main risk is ambiguity in how a single-arm descriptive endpoint is judged, along with possible safety findings.

The record says an urgent safety measure, issued after an IDMC review, permanently stopped tazemetostat and placebo, halted enrollment and unblinded the study. Post-measure efficacy analyses are described as descriptive only, so a prespecified, statistically significant PFS win in the ITT-WT population is very unlikely to be declared. A safety-driven stop also suggests the benefit-risk balance did not favour the combination, likely because of the known secondary-malignancy risk of EZH2 inhibition. Some small residual chance remains that a pre-stop analysis showed a significant PFS benefit, but no such topline result is known.

This is one of a series of near-identical registrations from a single individual sponsor, the 'Pharmacogenomics ANDA SNP' studies. They have implausible designs (600 patients at one site, start-to-completion in about 10 weeks) and a descriptive primary outcome with no prespecified comparison or hypothesis test. These studies are not known to have run or reported any results, so a topline announcement of a statistically significant primary endpoint is very unlikely. Even if data emerged, the outcome is not a superiority or non-inferiority comparison that could be judged met.

The first-listed primary outcome is incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events in a small (n=48) placebo-controlled multiple-ascending-dose study of a biologic, SV001, in IPF, so no formal superiority test is planned. Sponsors of such safety-primary trials usually report the result as met when the drug is described as safe and well tolerated, which is the common outcome for early-phase biologics. The probability is held below the high range because a safety endpoint does not map neatly onto statistical success, there may be tolerability signals, and a small Chinese sponsor may report results late or incompletely. I am not aware of any public topline results.

The first primary efficacy endpoint is the phase 2 PSA50 comparison, with roughly 45–50 patients per arm against an active Lu-PSMA-617 control that already gives PSA50 near 46–50%. A statistically significant gain would need a very large added effect, roughly 25–30 percentage points. Anti-CTLA4 therapy has a poor record in mCRPC (ipilimumab failed in phase 3), and immunotherapy combined with Lu-PSMA has shown only modest, uncontrolled signals. Gotistobart's improved safety profile may help tolerability, but this small open-label phase 2 is unlikely to show significance on PSA50 or rPFS, and I don't recall any public results.

S-337395 is Shionogi's oral RSV L-polymerase inhibitor, and in a human challenge study it cut viral load AUC substantially. That supports a real antiviral effect, and the primary endpoint is virologic rather than clinical, which is easier to hit. However, outpatient adults treated up to 72 hours after symptom onset often have falling viral loads, which dilutes drug–placebo differences. For example, Enanta's zelicapavir showed only modest virologic effects in high-risk adults. The first-listed Day 2 timepoint may also show a smaller separation than later days, so with about 64 patients per arm and two doses, I estimate a moderately better-than-even chance of success.

HDAC inhibitors added to standard therapy have almost always failed in solid-tumor phase 3 trials, and the support here is only a small single-arm phase 1b showing durable responses with pazopanib. The sponsor, Xynomic, is small and financially strained, and the trial has recruited slowly since 2018. It is still recruiting with a projected 2026 completion, so it may be underpowered or never finish. The PFS endpoint against a pazopanib control gives some chance of a modest positive effect, but added toxicity and dose reductions could erode the benefit.

LP-300 (dimesna/Tavocept) already failed its earlier Phase 3 trials in NSCLC. The never-smoker hypothesis rests on a post-hoc subgroup signal, and this trial's only supporting data are small, uncontrolled lead-in response rates. With about 90 patients randomized 2:1, the trial is underpowered to show a statistically significant PFS or OS gain over carboplatin-pemetrexed in post-TKI patients, especially since chemotherapy is reasonably active in this setting. Slow enrollment, limited sponsor resources and an open-label phase 2 design make a formal statistically significant win unlikely, though not impossible.

TQC2731 is an anti-TSLP antibody, and the closest precedent is tezepelumab's phase 2a COURSE trial in COPD, which missed its primary exacerbation endpoint overall (about 17% reduction) and showed benefit mainly in patients with eosinophils of 150 or more. This trial has no apparent eosinophil enrichment, and with roughly 258 patients and a 24-week exacerbation window it is underpowered for a modest effect. A sponsor-favorable analysis or a lenient alpha could help, but the base rate for a phase 2 trial of a new biologic in COPD exacerbations is low.

EVOKE-03 tests whether adding sacituzumab govitecan to pembrolizumab beats pembrolizumab alone in first-line PD-L1 ≥50% NSCLC, with BICR PFS as the first-listed primary endpoint. In general, adding a cytotoxic payload to pembrolizumab in PD-L1-high disease tends to improve PFS, and EVOKE-02 showed a high response rate (~67–69%) in this subgroup. Against that, EVOKE-01 failed in second-line NSCLC, TROP-2 ADCs have shown only modest single-agent lung activity, and toxicity and dose reductions could blunt the benefit. With about 614 patients and an open-label design, a PFS win is more likely than not; OS would be harder, but PFS is the endpoint scored here.

This is a small (60 patients total, including dose escalation), open-label phase 1/2 trial of an LNP-formulated Akt-1 antisense oligonucleotide plus sorafenib. The predecessor, Archexin/RX-0201, showed only modest activity in earlier trials. Sorafenib's ORR after checkpoint-inhibitor failure is low (about 5–10%), so a randomized ORR comparison with roughly 15–20 patients per arm has little power to reach p<0.05 unless the effect is very large, and the study is likely not powered for formal significance at all. A new mechanism in second-line HCC, a weak antisense track record, and an underpowered comparison together make a statistically significant win unlikely.

The primary endpoint is descriptive safety (number of participants with AEs) in a small Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study, so there is no formal efficacy test. 'Success' here would essentially mean an acceptable safety and tolerability profile, which most such trials report. The main risk is the EEV-PMO platform: Entrada's ENTR-601-44 drew an FDA clinical hold and showed hypomagnesemia/renal signals, so a dose-limiting safety finding or program discontinuation is plausible. I am not aware of topline results for this trial being public yet.

This is a small (n=80), single-site, open-label pathogen-focused CRE trial against best available therapy, similar in design to TANGO II and CREDIBLE-CR, which are usually descriptive rather than powered for formal hypothesis testing. The first-listed primary endpoint covers only the cUTI subgroup, probably a fraction of the 80 patients, so a statistically significant difference is unlikely. Best available therapy in China often includes ceftazidime-avibactam, which works well against KPC-producing strains, further narrowing any plausible advantage. The drug may well look numerically favorable, but a formal significant win on this endpoint seems improbable.

KN026 (anbenitamab), a HER2 biparatopic antibody, has shown strong activity, including positive phase 3 data in HER2+ gastric cancer and high response rates with docetaxel in HER2+ breast cancer; HB1801 is likely CSPC's albumin-bound docetaxel. The record does not say whether the design is superiority or non-inferiority against an active TH-P ± carboplatin comparator, which already achieves roughly 55-65% tpCR in Chinese patients. With 520 patients, a superiority trial could detect only about a 12-point gain in tpCR, which would be ambitious, while a non-inferiority trial would likely succeed. Weighing those two scenarios gives a near-coin-flip estimate tilted slightly toward success.

The first-listed primary outcome is safety (SAEs/DLTs) and involves no formal comparison, so success likely hinges on the cytologic regression endpoint versus placebo. With only about 45 participants, 30-day follow-up, and high spontaneous regression of ASC-US/LSIL in placebo arms, a statistically significant difference is hard to reach. Prior EGCG (Polyphenon E) trials in cervical lesions were largely negative, and this is a small sponsor's first proof-of-concept study at a single site. Some chance of a nominally positive result or a safety-only 'success' claim keeps this above the floor.

NBI-1065890 appears to be Neurocrine's next-generation VMAT2 inhibitor, a mechanism already proven in tardive dyskinesia. Valbenazine's KINECT 2 and 3 and deutetrabenazine's ARM-TD and AIM-TD trials all met the same AIMS endpoint, scored by blinded central video raters. With about 50 patients per arm and plausible placebo-adjusted effects of 2 to 3 points (SD roughly 3 to 4), power is reasonable, and Neurocrine has deep experience running TD trials. The main risks are phase 2 dose and PK uncertainty for a new molecule and the modest sample size, so the forecast is moderately above base rate rather than near certain.

AP306 (EOS789) is a pan-phosphate transporter inhibitor, and Alebund's earlier Chinese Phase 2 in hemodialysis patients reported clinically meaningful serum phosphate reductions versus placebo, so mechanism and drug-level proof of concept exist. This Phase 2b compares six fixed-dose arms against placebo on change in serum phosphate over 8 weeks, a responsive surrogate where binders and tenapanor typically separate from placebo by roughly 1 mg/dL or more, especially after binder washout. With about 24 patients per arm, power for at least one dose to reach significance is reasonable. Remaining risks are small arms, GI tolerability causing dropouts, and a possibly modest effect at fixed doses.

LBL-024 is a PD-L1/4-1BB bispecific that has shown encouraging single-arm activity in extrapulmonary neuroendocrine carcinoma. Early combination data with etoposide-platinum in first-line NEC reportedly gave high response rates, and the sponsor has moved toward pivotal development. However, this is an open-label phase Ib/II whose first-listed efficacy endpoint (ORR) may be analysed only descriptively, and any formal comparison against an active atezolizumab-plus-EP control would be underpowered in a small randomized subset. The probability of a statistically significant ORR advantage being reported is therefore uncertain, near even.

This is a small open-label phase II in China that randomizes patients between two doses of a new class I/IIb HDAC inhibitor, with no control arm. Success therefore depends on ORR clearing a prespecified historical threshold, which tends to favour sponsor-declared success. Purinostat has reportedly shown encouraging early activity in R/R DLBCL and received Chinese breakthrough designation. However, HDAC inhibitors have historically produced only modest single-agent response rates in DLBCL, and the sample per arm is small, so the probability is set moderately above even.

The first-listed primary outcome is incidence and severity of adverse events, a descriptive safety measure with no prespecified superiority test, so a statistically significant result favoring the investigational arms is unlikely. Tobemstomig (PD-1/LAG-3 bispecific) plus tiragolumab is expected to cause at least as many adverse events as atezolizumab alone. Tiragolumab failed across several Phase 3 trials and Roche has deprioritized both drugs, so there is little reason to expect a favorable efficacy or safety signal either. The only meaningful upside is that a sponsor might describe an acceptable safety profile as having met the endpoint, so I put the probability at about 20%.

GQ1005 is a HER2-targeted ADC carrying a DXd-type topoisomerase-I payload, tested here in the setting where DESTINY-Breast03 showed trastuzumab deruxtecan beating T-DM1 with an HR of about 0.28. Several Chinese HER2-ADC analogues have since beaten T-DM1 on PFS in similar second-line trials. Even a much smaller effect (HR about 0.5) should be detectable with 228 patients. The main risks are unproven differences in GQ1005's conjugation, potency or toxicity, and possible underpowering if its effect is modest; no topline result is known.

Hemay005 (mufemilast) is an oral PDE4 inhibitor similar to apremilast, which met its Phase 2 UC remission endpoint (about 32% vs 12% placebo at week 12 in roughly 170 patients), so the mechanism has proof of concept. This trial is much smaller, with about 30 patients per arm. Significance would need something like a 30–35% vs 10% remission gap, which is plausible but well short of assured power. Base rates for Phase 2 UC and the unreplicated efficacy of this specific compound in UC argue for a below-even estimate, offset somewhat by two dose arms giving two chances.

This is a tiny phase II trial (17 enrolled, 2:1 randomization, roughly 11 artesunate vs 6 placebo) from a small sponsor, and it appears designed for descriptive estimation rather than a powered hypothesis test. Earlier open-label artesunate studies in cervical and anal HSIL reported regression rates of about 60%, but spontaneous regression of HSIL in HIV-negative patients can reach 20–30%. Reaching a two-sided p<0.05 with six controls would need a near-total contrast, such as 9/11 vs 0/6. Even if the drug works, a formally significant result on the primary endpoint is unlikely.

Basimglurant, an mGluR5 negative allosteric modulator, has no proven analgesic efficacy in humans, and Roche's earlier trials of it in depression and fragile X were disappointing, so this is essentially a first efficacy test of the mechanism in trigeminal neuralgia. The enriched randomized-withdrawal design helps by randomizing only open-label responders, but the closest precedent, vixotrigine's randomized-withdrawal phase 2 in TN, missed its time-to-loss-of-efficacy primary endpoint despite a favorable trend. With 166 enrolled, perhaps around 100 will be randomized, which leaves limited power for a time-to-event endpoint in a disease where the placebo response and withdrawal-period noise are substantial. I don't know of any topline result, and primary completion is planned for 2027.

Lutikizumab, an anti-IL-1α/β antibody, showed a clear signal in its Phase 2 study of anti-TNF-experienced HS patients (HiSCR50 roughly 59% vs 35% for placebo at week 16), and IL-17 agents have repeatedly succeeded in HS Phase 3. Each arm has about 640 participants, so the trial is heavily powered, though HiSCR75 is a stricter endpoint and placebo responses in HS can be high. Recent HS programs (e.g., sonelokimab's VELA-2) show that misses happen even after strong Phase 2 data. Primary completion is December 2026 and I don't believe results are public yet.

This is a small (n=24), single-site, exploratory 4-way crossover of single doses of pudafensine, a monoamine reuptake inhibitor with positive Phase 2 erectile dysfunction data, in a new indication, provoked vestibulodynia. A single dose of a reuptake inhibitor plausibly changes the vestibular pain threshold, and the crossover design with three doses improves power and offers several chances to win. Still, pain endpoints carry large placebo and variance effects, and first tests of a mechanism in a hard pain condition usually miss formal significance. Small sponsors often announce such studies as 'positive' on trends, but under a strict p<0.05 criterion success is less likely than not.

E2086 is Eisai's oral orexin-2 receptor agonist. Other drugs in this class (oveporexton/TAK-861, alixorexton/ALKS 2680, ORX750) have produced very large, highly significant MWT gains over placebo in NT1, and alixorexton also reached significance in NT2. Eisai's own early E2086 data in NT1 pointed to wakefulness benefits, and a small sample is enough given these effect sizes, especially in the NT1 cohort with a sequential three-dose design. The main risks are a weaker NT2 effect, ambiguity in how the cohorts are combined for the primary analysis, and tolerability limiting the doses, but success remains likely.

HEC585 (yinfenidone) is a pirfenidone-derived antifibrotic, and the mechanism has supportive but modest evidence in non-IPF progressive fibrosis (uILD, RELIEF). With about 37 patients per arm and only 24 weeks of follow-up, the expected FVC difference of roughly 50–80 mL against a between-patient SD near 200 mL leaves the trial clearly underpowered for p<0.05. The study is still recruiting at a single site close to its planned primary completion, which adds execution risk, though having two doses gives it two chances to succeed. No results are public, so I forecast moderately below even odds.

RemeGen's Chinese phase 3 (RC48-C016) of disitamab vedotin plus toripalimab against gemcitabine-platinum in HER2-expressing first-line urothelial cancer showed large PFS and OS benefits (HR roughly 0.36 for PFS). EV-302 also showed that an MMAE ADC plus pembrolizumab beats platinum chemotherapy, with a PFS HR of about 0.45. A HER2-selected population, a chemotherapy comparator and about 412 patients give ample power for BICR-assessed PFS. The main risks are a weaker effect at HER2 IHC 1+ in a global population and toxicity, but success is highly likely.

B007 appears to be a subcutaneous B-cell–targeting antibody given on days 1 and 15. That class has mixed results in gMG: BeatMG with rituximab failed, while RINOMAX and inebilizumab's MINT trial succeeded, though only modestly and with slow onset. The primary endpoint is an MG-ADL ≥2-point responder rate at about 16 weeks, where placebo responses are often 30–40%; with about 104 patients possibly split across two doses, power to detect a modest early B-cell-depletion effect is limited. Chinese industry-run phase II/III trials in MG often report positive results, which partly offsets this, so I put the chance of success near even.

This is ASCENT-04/KEYNOTE-D19. In April 2025 Gilead announced that the trial met its primary endpoint of BICR-assessed PFS. Data presented at ASCO 2025 showed median PFS of 11.2 vs 7.8 months (HR ~0.65, p<0.001) for sacituzumab govitecan plus pembrolizumab versus chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab in PD-L1+ first-line mTNBC.

Earlier field trials of Sanaria's radiation-attenuated PfSPZ Vaccine in malaria-exposed adults in Mali and Burkina Faso showed moderate efficacy (about 30–50% by time-to-event), which was statistically significant in at least some analyses. The replication-competent LARC2 parasite is expected to be more potent, and its single-gene predecessor GA2 protected about 90% of volunteers against controlled human malaria infection. Against that, field protection against diverse heterologous strains in semi-immune adults has consistently been much lower than in challenge studies. A high rainy-season attack rate gives roughly 60 participants per arm reasonable power for a moderate effect, and two vaccine arms give two chances, but the effect size remains uncertain, so I put the odds slightly above even.

This is a factorial fixed-dose-combination study from Boryung, likely pairing an already-approved antihypertensive (possibly fimasartan) with an approved antidiabetic. The first primary endpoint compares the full combination against the same regimen with a placebo in place of the antihypertensive component (A-1). An approved antihypertensive against placebo typically lowers sitting systolic pressure by 6 to 10 mmHg more over 12 weeks, and about 69 patients per arm gives ample power. The main risks are operational, such as slow enrollment at 3 sites and a large placebo response, so success is highly likely.

This Phase 1/2 dose-ranging study's first-listed primary outcomes are descriptive safety counts plus GMT immunogenicity measures, with no prespecified hypothesis test against placebo. Such trials are usually judged successful if the vaccine is tolerable and immunogenic. mRNA RSV vaccines (e.g., Moderna's mRESVIA) and hMPV mRNA candidates have consistently raised neutralizing titers in older adults, so immunogenicity versus placebo is very likely. The main risks are ambiguity in how a descriptive endpoint gets scored, reactogenicity concerns in older adults, and Sanofi's own changing mRNA portfolio priorities.

OCTA-C1-INH is a plasma-derived C1-INH concentrate given at 20 IU/kg, the same dose and endpoint design that let Berinert beat placebo in IMPACT-1 (median time to onset of relief about 0.5 h vs 1.5 h, p=0.0025). The mechanism is well established, and the time-to-relief endpoint has repeatedly separated from placebo in acute HAE trials of C1-INH, icatibant and ecallantide. The main risks are a high placebo response, variable multinational site quality, and a blinded subset possibly smaller than the 124 enrolled, since some participants are open-label. The trial is still recruiting, so no result is public.

This is a descriptive Phase 3a safety study: the primary outcomes are percentages of children with solicited and unsolicited adverse events, with no formal superiority or non-inferiority hypothesis, so 'success' in practice means GSK reports a safety profile comparable to Varivax. GSK's investigational varicella vaccine is a live-attenuated product with earlier pediatric trials behind it and co-administered routine vaccines, which makes an unexpected safety signal unlikely. The main risk is how a descriptive outcome gets scored rather than the vaccine itself, plus a small chance of a reactogenicity imbalance such as more fever or rash. I don't know of any public topline result for this trial.

IDH1 inhibition has been validated in previously treated IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma: ivosidenib in ClarIDHy clearly improved PFS. Its intention-to-treat OS benefit (HR ~0.79) was not significant, largely because of crossover, while crossover-adjusted OS suggested an HR near 0.5. This trial uses OS as primary with about 165 patients randomized 2:1 and no stated crossover, so a true HR of about 0.6 would give reasonable power. However, the small sample, OS as a demanding endpoint, uncertain potency of this new Chinese IDH1 inhibitor, and possible post-progression access to other therapies leave substantial risk, so I put the chance at about even.

Ascorbate as an endothelial free-radical scavenger has some support from small studies: intravenous and intracameral ascorbic acid reduced endothelial cell loss after phacoemulsification of hard nuclei. Robust evidence for topical 5% drops is lacking, though, and aqueous ascorbate is already physiologically high, which may limit any added benefit. With about 100 patients per arm, the most damaging brunescent cataracts excluded, and the high variability of specular microscopy cell counts, the trial is powered only for a moderate effect. Given a roughly 30–40% base rate for phase 2 ophthalmology trials and a small sponsor, a modest probability is appropriate.

Part II of this study appears to match OptiTROP-Lung03: sacituzumab tirumotecan (SKB264) versus docetaxel in EGFR-mutant NSCLC after failure of EGFR-TKI and platinum chemotherapy. As I recall, the reported ORR was about 45% versus 16%, with significantly longer PFS, and it supported Chinese approval in this setting. Even without that, TROP2 ADCs consistently give much higher response rates than docetaxel (roughly 10–15% ORR) in pretreated EGFR-mutant disease, so an ORR comparison is a low bar. The main residual uncertainties are whether my match of this registration to that trial is correct and how the multi-cohort primary endpoint is formally scored.

Norovirus vaccines have a poor efficacy record: Takeda's bivalent VLP showed weak or non-significant protection in adult field and challenge studies, and HilleVax's infant trial failed in 2024. mRNA-1403 produced robust HBGA-blocking antibody responses in Phase 1/2, the trial is large (about 38,000 participants) and event-driven, and the primary endpoint is restricted to vaccine-matched genotypes, all of which improve the odds. Against that are shifting circulating strains (the GII.17 surge), the clinical hold over a Guillain-Barré case, and an untested correlate of protection, so the outcome looks close to a coin flip.

CBT-001 is a topical nintedanib-type multikinase inhibitor, and its Phase 2 trial reportedly showed significant reductions in both conjunctival hyperemia and pterygium lesion vascularity/length versus vehicle. The first-listed primary endpoint, change in hyperemia at 3 months, is a short-term, pharmacologically plausible anti-angiogenic effect. With two doses and about 220 per arm, the trial is reasonably powered. Risks include a high vehicle response on a subjective grading scale, heterogeneity across multinational sites, and the generally modest Phase 3 success rates in ophthalmology; I am not aware of a public topline result for this trial.

Novocure's PANOVA-3 showed that adding tumor treating fields to gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel in locally advanced pancreatic cancer improved overall survival (HR ~0.82, p≈0.04), so the mechanism has precedent in this exact setting. That effect was modest and only just significant, though, and this Chinese copy-device trial is of similar size (512), unblinded, run at only five sites, and depends on device compliance that may differ. With a true HR near 0.82, power to reach p<0.05 on OS is roughly 50%, offset slightly by the tendency of sponsor-run Chinese device trials to report positively. I know of no public result for this trial.

Acute ischemic stroke neuroprotection and recovery trials have a very poor track record. DiaMedica's own Phase 2 ReMEDy1 missed its primary endpoint, with only post-hoc subgroup signals, and the dichotomized mRS 0–1 endpoint in a moderate-severity, non-thrombectomy population needs a sizable effect to reach significance. The trial has a futility interim at 200 patients, has had slow enrollment and a prior clinical hold for hypotension, and is still recruiting, so a success at the final analysis looks unlikely.

HRS9531 is Hengrui's GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, and its Chinese phase 3 obesity trials have shown large weight loss, comparable to tirzepatide. In SURMOUNT-OSA, tirzepatide cut AHI by about 25–29 events/h versus about 5 with placebo in both the PAP and non-PAP trials, with very small p-values. With 144 patients over 52 weeks and a placebo comparator, this trial is well powered for an effect of that size, so the main risks are dropout or an operational problem. The trial's primary completion is planned for December 2026, and I am not aware of any public topline result.

Tilpisertib fosmecarbil is a prodrug of Gilead's TPL2/MAP3K8 inhibitor, a new mechanism in UC with no validated proof of concept; the parent compound GS-4875 did not produce a public efficacy signal that would raise confidence. The trial enrolls only advanced-therapy-experienced patients, where placebo clinical response is about 25-30% and drug effects tend to be smaller. With roughly 44 patients per arm, a difference of about 20-25 points would be needed for significance, though having three doses gives several chances to succeed. The base rate for novel-mechanism Phase 2 trials in UC is modest, so I put the probability below even.

SHR-3167 appears to be HengRui's once-weekly basal insulin, and this small open-label phase II trial (n=102, 2 sites) compares two titration algorithms of the same drug, with no true control arm. The primary endpoint, the proportion of patients with any hypoglycemic event, looks descriptive rather than a powered superiority or non-inferiority test. Even if one algorithm produced fewer hypoglycemic events, a statistically significant difference at this sample size is unlikely. A sponsor-defined success is therefore improbable, and no results are public yet.

TX000045 is a long-acting relaxin-Fc agonist. Tectonic's Phase 1b reported acute reductions in PVR and PCWP and increases in cardiac output in PH-HFpEF patients, and in CADENCE sotatercept lowered PVR significantly in CpcPH, so PVR is a plausible and fairly responsive hemodynamic endpoint. Against that, the primary analysis is restricted to the CpcPH subgroup, likely about 100–130 patients across three arms, and right-heart-catheterization PVR is noisy. Durability of relaxin's effect over 24 weeks of chronic dosing is also unproven, and Phase 2 cardiovascular proof-of-concept trials frequently miss.

The primary outcomes are descriptive safety measures (AEs, labs, ECGs, physical exams) in a small open-label Phase 2a with no formal hypothesis test, so 'success' will most likely be judged by whether the sponsor reports TRX-100 as safe and well tolerated. Tivoxavir marboxil is a cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor in the same class as approved baloxavir, and its Phase 1 data reportedly showed good tolerability, so a clean safety readout is likely. Traws Pharma is a small, financially constrained sponsor that tends to frame results positively. The remaining risk is an unexpected safety signal, a stalled or incomplete study, or ambiguity in how a descriptive endpoint gets graded.

CIELO is the first randomized placebo-controlled test of IL-6 receptor blockade in NMDAR and LGI1 encephalitis, supported only by small open-label tocilizumab series. The primary endpoint, a 1-point or greater mRS improvement without rescue therapy, likely has a high placebo response, because many patients improve with first-line immunotherapy and the natural course of these diseases. The NMDAR cohort is also small (roughly 60–80 patients), which leaves limited power. Roche's protocol amendments to the cohort design add some uncertainty, and a new mechanism in a rare neurological disease suggests a below-base-rate chance of success.

Vicagrel is a close structural analog of clopidogrel that needs less CYP2C19-dependent activation, and earlier PK/PD work showed comparable or better platelet inhibition. With 1,000 patients and a 6-month MACE endpoint, the trial cannot be powered for superiority, so it is almost certainly a non-inferiority registration study for Chinese approval. Near-copy non-inferiority trials with low event rates usually meet their margin. Remaining risks are execution problems (a single listed site, still recruiting near the planned completion date), an unknown margin, and possible ambiguity in how success is defined.

The primary endpoints are descriptive safety counts (reactogenicity, AEs, SAEs) with no formal hypothesis test, so 'success' amounts to an acceptable safety and tolerability profile that supports further development. Mid-study, Sanofi added a 480-participant extension at the low dose, which suggests the initial dose-ranging data were reassuring. mRNA H5 vaccines from other sponsors have generally been tolerable, with expected reactogenicity, though H5 immunogenicity can be modest. I am not aware of a public topline result, and how a purely descriptive safety endpoint will be scored is uncertain, so I keep the forecast well short of certainty.

JMKX003142 appears to be an aquaretic, likely a vasopressin V2 antagonist: the record excludes patients who cannot sense thirst and those likely to need diuretics. That mechanism was validated for slowing total kidney volume growth by tolvaptan, whose year-1 TKV effects were large relative to variability. With about 67 patients per arm in a rapidly progressive population, a 52-week percentage change in TKV against placebo should be well powered if the drug reaches adequate V2 blockade. The main risks are uncertainty about the mechanism and dose, a small single-site Chinese phase 2, and primary completion not due until 2027, so no results are public.

AND017 is an oral HIF-PHI, and essentially every HIF-PHI phase 3 non-inferiority trial against ESA in dialysis patients (roxadustat, daprodustat, vadadustat, enarodustat, desidustat) met its hemoglobin efficacy margin. The record is framed as maintenance of mean Hb over weeks 23–27 versus ESA in ESA-converted dialysis patients, which implies a non-inferiority design with a dose-titratable drug, an easy setting to win. The open-label design, 300 patients in China and earlier phase 2 data showing Hb effects support a high probability, tempered slightly by the small sponsor and limited published data.

HSK55718 is an undisclosed Haisco injectable analgesic, and the morphine active comparator suggests an opioid-like or opioid-alternative mechanism. Chinese postoperative pain trials of potent IV analgesics against placebo on SPID usually succeed, and here any of three doses (about 40 patients per arm) beating placebo counts. The main risks are a novel non-opioid mechanism with limited efficacy in visceral abdominal pain, and rescue medication shrinking the separation from placebo. I am not aware of any public results.

The first-listed primary outcome is descriptive Part 1 safety, so the meaningful test is the Part 2 placebo-controlled comparison of percent change in motor seizure frequency. ABS-1230 is a first-in-class selective KCNT1 inhibitor in a severe developmental epileptic encephalopathy. Quinidine, an earlier and less selective KCNT1-targeting approach, failed in a controlled setting, though a precision mechanism in a genetically defined population could produce large effects. The randomized portion is very small (likely about 30–45 patients over 12 weeks), seizure counts in this population are highly variable, and novel-mechanism phase 2 epilepsy trials fail more often than they succeed, so I place this somewhat below even odds.

This small open-label Phase 2a trial (n=36) has only safety primary endpoints, counts of AEs and SAEs, with no prespecified efficacy comparison, so a statistically significant result favoring RABI-767 is very unlikely. Whether it counts as success therefore depends mostly on whether the sponsor reports the drug as 'safe and well tolerated, meeting the primary endpoint.' Small sponsors often frame safety-primary results that way, but an invasive EUS-guided peripancreatic injection in predicted severe pancreatitis could add adverse events relative to standard care alone. The trial is still recruiting, so delays and limited disclosure are also plausible.

EscharEx (a bromelain-based enzymatic debrider) has repeatedly beaten gel vehicle on complete debridement in earlier phase 2 VLU trials, including ChronEx, so the first-listed endpoint plays to the drug's established mechanism. The adaptive design with a DMC and interim sample-size reassessment further lowers the risk of an underpowered result. The main risks are a strong vehicle response from autolytic debridement under hydrogel, variability in visual assessment across 60 sites, and a possible gatekeeping link to the harder wound-closure co-primary, which would shape how success is reported. I have not seen this trial's topline result made public.

CT-P51 is Celltrion's pembrolizumab biosimilar, and this small Georgia-only trial (n=225) has a descriptive safety primary endpoint (TEAE incidence) rather than a formal superiority or equivalence efficacy test. Celltrion's biosimilars have reliably shown comparable safety and efficacy to their reference products. A descriptive safety comparison is very likely to be reported as 'comparable safety,' which a sponsor would announce as meeting the objective. The main uncertainty is how a descriptive endpoint gets scored, plus a small risk of an unexpected imbalance or immunogenicity signal; no results are public yet (primary completion 2027-02).

This appears to be the FOENIX-CCA4 confirmatory and dose-optimization trial. Its primary endpoint is ICR-assessed ORR, most likely judged as each arm's response rate clearing a prespecified threshold rather than a head-to-head superiority test. Futibatinib 20 mg gave a 42% ORR in FOENIX-CCA2 in FGFR inhibitor-naive, previously treated FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma, so with about 60 patients per arm the 20 mg arm should comfortably exceed a plausible null rate of 15–20%. The main risks are ambiguity over how success is defined, lower response rates with broader real-world enrollment, and slow recruitment; the result does not appear to be public yet.

This is a long-term extension whose primary endpoint is the descriptive proportion of participants with TEAEs, with no prespecified superiority comparison, so 'success' most plausibly means a safety readout the sponsor reports as consistent with the known profile. The parent Phase 3 STOP-HS1 and STOP-HS2 trials reportedly met their primary endpoints, and povorcitinib's safety profile in HS and vitiligo looked consistent with the JAK1 class, with no major new signals. Incyte is pursuing regulatory filings and has every incentive to describe the LTE as supportive. The main risks are ambiguity in how a non-comparative endpoint gets scored and any emerging JAK-class safety signal over longer exposure.

The first-listed primary outcome is a safety count (SAEs or severe TEAEs) plus PK, not an efficacy comparison, so 'success' here mostly means the drug proved acceptably safe. Microgram-level vaginal lasofoxifene, an approved-elsewhere oral SERM with known vaginal benefits, is very likely to be safe over 14 days. The risk is that a safety-primary trial is scored on a placebo comparison, which would show no significant difference, or that this small sponsor's single-site trial, already delayed since 2023, never reports. That ambiguity keeps the estimate near the middle.

Endothelin-A antagonism has reliably lowered proteinuria in IgA nephropathy: atrasentan (ALIGN) and sparsentan (PROTECT) both met 36-week UPCR endpoints with large effects, and SC0062's phase 2 (2-SUCCEED) showed significant dose-dependent proteinuria reduction versus placebo. This trial uses a placebo comparator, a surrogate endpoint that is well suited to the mechanism, and 360 patients, which gives ample power for an expected roughly 30-40% relative reduction. The main risks are operational (dropouts, edema-related discontinuations, or growing SGLT2i use shrinking the treatment effect), but these rarely erase an effect this robust. Primary completion is planned for December 2026, and I do not recall any topline result being public yet.

Combined oral contraceptives, including cyproterone acetate/ethinyl estradiol (Diane-35) and low-dose EE 20 µg regimens such as drospirenone/EE 24+4, have repeatedly beaten placebo on inflammatory lesion counts in acne trials of similar size and duration. This trial uses an established antiandrogenic progestogen at an established dose, with only the estrogen dose reduced, over six cycles against placebo, with about 531 patients randomized 2:1. That gives ample power for the modest but consistent effects COCs typically show. The main risks are the high placebo response in acne, possible slightly lower efficacy with the reduced EE dose, and execution issues at a single-country sponsor. Recruitment started in August 2026 and primary completion is planned for February 2027, so no result is public yet.

The composite 'operational tolerance-like' endpoint favors the MIC arms by design: criterion 4 requires steroid-free therapy with ≤720 mg EC-MPS, which the protocol mandates for MIC patients, while ELITE-Symphony controls typically stay on steroids and full-dose MPS, so very few controls should qualify. The TOL-1 pilot suggested MIC induces regulatory B cells and is safe, supporting the Breg and no-DSA criteria, so even a modest responder rate in the 42 MIC patients could beat the 21 controls. The main risks are rejection or DSA after aggressive immunosuppression minimization, failure to reach the Breg threshold, and slow recruitment or early stopping in a small investigator-driven ATMP trial. No results are public, as the trial was still recruiting at the last update.

This is a 15-patient (5 per arm), single-site phase 1/2 trial of UC-MSC with or without secretome in severe ARDS. The first-listed primary outcome is the lung injury score, and its first timepoint is "before therapy," so there is no clear prespecified comparison. Larger MSC trials in ARDS (START, REALIST, several COVID-ARDS RCTs) have mostly failed on their primary efficacy endpoints, and with 5 patients per arm only a very large effect could reach p<0.05. The sponsor is a small company and the multiplicity of outcomes could let it claim a positive result on something, but under a strict definition success is unlikely.

NS-229 is a selective JAK1 inhibitor being tested in a small (n≈45) phase 2 EGPA trial. The primary endpoint is remission (BVAS 0 plus prednisone ≤4 mg/day at week 28), and patients enter on background steroids, many already on anti-IL-5 therapy. Placebo remission rates on endpoints like this are typically very low (single digits in MIRRA), so a moderate drug effect could reach significance even with this sample size, and case series of JAK inhibitors in refractory EGPA have shown steroid-sparing benefit. Against that, this is a first randomized test of the mechanism in a rare, heterogeneous disease, with a stringent steroid threshold and a short taper window, so the outcome is roughly a coin flip, slightly below even.

VQW-765, an alpha7 nicotinic partial agonist, missed significance on SUDS in the overall population of its Phase 2 public-speaking trial. Vanda's case for efficacy rested on post-hoc signals in women and in patients with optimal plasma exposure, yet this Phase 3 enrolls both sexes without exposure enrichment. Single-dose public-speaking challenge trials in social anxiety are noisy and have mixed results; Vistagen's fasedienol, for example, failed PALISADE-1 and PALISADE-3 and succeeded only in PALISADE-2. Vanda also has a track record of trials driven by subgroup findings, so despite the adequate 500-patient sample I put success below the Phase 3 base rate.

In adults, the CAPTAIN trial showed FF/UMEC/VI improved trough FEV1 over FF/VI by about 90–110 mL. Tiotropium add-on trials in adolescents showed similar modest gains, though results were inconsistent. With only about 69 patients per arm, a frequentist test would be underpowered for an effect of about 100 mL, but the Bayesian dynamic-borrowing design pulls in adult data, which makes declaring success much easier unless the adolescent results diverge. Primary completion is not due until 2027 and no results are public, so I put the probability modestly above even.

The mechanism is supported by the afamelanotide plus NB-UVB pilot (Lim et al., JAMA Dermatology 2015), which showed faster and greater repigmentation, especially in darker skin types like most Chinese patients, so MT-II, a potent MC1R agonist, could plausibly add benefit. Against that, this is a single-site, 60-patient phase 2 from an obscure sponsor with a templated-looking record, and the primary endpoint is total VASI change at 24 weeks, a noisy measure where NB-UVB alone produces substantial background repigmentation. Generalized tanning from MT-II may partly unblind assessors but could also confound lesion scoring. Given phase 2 dermatology base rates and the record-quality concerns, I put success somewhat below even.

Levulan Kerastick plus BLU-U blue-light PDT is already FDA-approved for AK, including the upper extremities, after a vehicle-controlled phase 3 that showed significantly higher complete clearance than vehicle PDT. This trial tests a reformulated version of the same 20% ALA product against vehicle, with up to two PDT sessions allowed, and about 260 patients is enough power even for a modest absolute difference in complete clearance. The main risks are a lower complete clearance rate on the extremities and the reformulation performing worse than expected, but a vehicle-controlled test of a proven photosensitizer usually succeeds. The primary completion date is in 2027, so no results are public.

The first-listed primary endpoint is non-inferiority on 12-month target lesion failure for Angiolite, a thin-strut cobalt-chromium sirolimus-eluting stent, versus Xience. Contemporary thin-strut drug-eluting stents nearly always meet non-inferiority against Xience in all-comer trials, and Angiolite has already shown comparable outcomes to Xience in earlier randomized and registry studies. With about 1,150 patients per stent arm and expected TLF around 5–6%, a typical absolute margin of about 3% leaves reasonable power, though the margin is not stated and event rates could be higher than planned. No results are public yet; primary completion is planned for January 2027.

ARTEMIS is a non-inferiority trial of BCVA change versus aflibercept 2 mg q8w, and Ixo-vec patients can receive aflibercept rescue. Rescue-allowed anti-VEGF NI designs (e.g., the port delivery system's Archway, newer anti-VEGF agents) usually meet a standard ~4–5 letter margin. Phase 2 LUNA and OPTIC data showed stable BCVA with large injection-burden reductions, and Lilly's 2025 acquisition of Adverum suggests outside confidence. The main risks are gene-therapy inflammation or hypotony eroding vision in a subset, variable rescue adherence, and modest sample size, so this sits somewhat below the typical NI success rate.

Raphamin is a Materia Medica Holding 'release-active' (ultra-high-dilution antibody) product with no plausible pharmacological mechanism, so a true drug effect on time to recurrence over 6 months would be unlikely. Against that, this sponsor's Russian multicenter placebo-controlled trials have fairly often reported statistically significant primary results, though several have also failed or gone unreported. Time to first recurrence in 415 women is a moderately powered, subjective symptom-based endpoint, which leaves room for either outcome. Balancing the weak biological prior against the sponsor's track record gives a probability somewhat below even.

Oral SERD monotherapy against fulvestrant or standard endocrine therapy in unselected (not ESR1-mutation-enriched) pretreated ER+/HER2- breast cancer has a mixed record. EMERALD and SERENA-2 were positive, while acelERA, AMEERA-3 and EMBER-3 in its overall population did not meet the endpoint. This trial is large (640), uses IRC-assessed PFS, and enrols a Chinese population that may be less CDK4/6-pretreated. Those features help, but without ESR1 enrichment a significant all-comers PFS benefit over fulvestrant 500 is roughly a coin flip, and I am not aware of any public topline result.

Pirfenidone is an established antifibrotic, and small Chinese studies suggest benefit in radiation pneumonitis, so the mechanism is plausible. The sponsor makes the pirfenidone product being tested, and Chinese industry trials often report positive results. However, the phase II stage randomizes only about 30 patients per arm, and 24-week DLCO change is noisy in a population that often partly recovers on steroids alone, so power to show a significant difference is limited. Overall this sits near the phase II/III base rate, slightly below even odds.

In SOLSTICE, tobevibart+elebsiran produced substantial rates of HDV RNA below quantification and undetectable, and its mechanism (HBsAg neutralization plus siRNA) differs from bulevirtide's entry inhibition, so it should still work in patients not suppressed on bulevirtide. The control is continued bulevirtide in patients already selected as non-suppressed after at least 24 weeks, so the comparator's 24-week rate on the strict undetectable endpoint should be very low. Even a modest combination response of 20–30% would likely reach significance with about 150 participants. The main risks are lower undetectable rates at week 24 in this refractory, high-viral-load population and the strictness of the target-not-detected criterion.

The first-listed primary outcome is safety (CTCAE adverse events), not a powered efficacy comparison, and the trial has only 15 patients randomized 6:6:3 with no formal hypothesis test. A statistically significant BCVA or CST difference versus 3 placebo patients, in anti-VEGF-refractory nAMD treated with a systemic anti-PRL3 antibody (a new mechanism here), is very unlikely. The main route to a 'success' is the small sponsor describing a clean safety profile, possibly alongside favorable descriptive efficacy, as positive topline results, so the probability is held somewhat above the very low chance of a significant efficacy result.

M108 (FG-M108) is an Fc-enhanced anti-CLDN18.2 antibody, a mechanism already validated in first-line HER2-negative gastric cancer: zolbetuximab met PFS in both SPOTLIGHT and GLOW, and GLOW used this same CAPOX backbone (HR ~0.69). The trial is placebo-controlled, has a PFS primary endpoint and enrolls 486 patients, which should give adequate power for an effect of that size. Restricting to PD-L1 CPS<5 avoids the immunotherapy comparator problem. Risks remain: the CLDN18.2 positivity cutoff may be lower and dilute the benefit, and earlier M108 data are limited to small single-arm studies from a smaller sponsor, so I put this somewhat above the base rate for validated-mechanism follow-ons.

Inclisiran has consistently cut LDL-C by about 50% versus placebo across the ORION trials. In ACS patients started on high-intensity statins, the VICTORION-INCEPTION and AMUNDSEN-type data also showed large placebo-adjusted reductions. With 305 patients and percent change in LDL-C at Day 150 as the primary endpoint, the trial has overwhelming power even though statin up-titration in both arms will lower LDL in the placebo group too. The main risks are operational or analytic quirks, not the drug's effect, and I am not aware of a published result.

TQB2102 is a biparatopic HER2 ADC with a topoisomerase-I payload, tested against single-agent chemotherapy on IRC-assessed PFS in chemo-naive, endocrine-pretreated HR+/HER2-low metastatic breast cancer. This is close to the DESTINY-Breast06 design, where T-DXd clearly beat chemotherapy on PFS (HR ~0.62). Chinese HER2 ADCs such as SHR-A1811 have also succeeded in similar HER2-low settings. Risks are that this is a less proven ADC, the open-label design, and a single-country trial, but with 542 patients and a mechanism-class effect this large, success is likely.

In TRIDENT-1, repotrectinib produced a 79% response rate and a median PFS of about 35.7 months in TKI-naïve ROS1+ NSCLC. Crizotinib's historical PFS in this setting is roughly 16–19 months, and it penetrates the CNS poorly, so intracranial progression is common on the control arm. A randomized comparison of about 190 patients should be powered to detect a plausible hazard ratio near 0.5, and next-generation ROS1/ALK TKIs have consistently beaten crizotinib on PFS in head-to-head trials. The main risks are an immature event count at the analysis and crizotinib doing better than expected, but success looks likely; I don't recall any public topline result.

AK112 (ivonescimab, a PD-1/VEGF bispecific) is being tested against a weak comparator, placebo plus nab-paclitaxel, in first-line TNBC. Both mechanisms have improved PFS over taxane alone in this setting: atezolizumab in IMpassion130 (ITT PFS HR ~0.80) and bevacizumab in E2100. Phase 2 ivonescimab-plus-chemo data in TNBC showed high response rates, and Akeso has a strong record of positive IRRC-assessed PFS trials in China (HARMONi-2, HARMONi-A, HARMONi-6). The main risks are an unselected PD-L1 population and modest size (416), but a PFS win looks likely, and I am not aware of a public readout.

This is a PK equivalence trial of a pembrolizumab biosimilar in resected NSCLC, a design modeled on Amgen's and Samsung Bioepis's PK-similarity studies, and well-developed biosimilar mAbs usually meet the 80–125% GMR bounds for AUC. Qilu has a solid biosimilar track record, and adjuvant patients without tumor burden give relatively homogeneous PK. Risks are the small sample (about 73 per arm) with two co-primary endpoints, including a cycle 7 steady-state AUC prone to dropout and variability, plus possible ADA or manufacturing differences. I estimate a high but not certain chance of success.

Anti-TL1A is now a validated mechanism in UC: tulisokibart, duvakitug and afimkibart all beat placebo on week 12–14 clinical remission in phase 2, typically by 15–25 percentage points over placebo rates of roughly 1–12%. With about 40 patients per arm across four BCD-261 dose arms and placebo, any one arm reaching significance would count, so power is reasonable if this Biocad antibody has potency comparable to the class. Remaining risks are uncertain potency and dosing of a new subcutaneous molecule, a possibly higher placebo response in Russian single-country sites, and small arm sizes. Primary completion is planned for 2027-01, and I am not aware of any public results.

This is a Hengrui phase III comparing its novel neuromuscular blocker HRS-9190 with rocuronium, with the primary endpoint being the rate of excellent or good Cooper intubation conditions. The trial is almost certainly a non-inferiority design, though the record does not state the margin. Both arms should reach near-ceiling rates (about 95% or more), and Chinese phase III non-inferiority trials of neuromuscular blockers with this endpoint very commonly succeed, especially after a sponsor has picked its dose in phase II. Residual risk comes from an unknown margin, possible slower onset at the chosen bolus dose, and execution at only two sites.

This is a small (n=60), open-label phase 2 pilot from a tiny sponsor (Skingenix, registered in 2011 and still recruiting in 2026), comparing an uncharacterized topical agent against active silver sulfadiazine on time to healing. Pilot studies of this size are rarely powered to show a statistically significant superiority difference, and the long, troubled history suggests recruitment and operational difficulties. Silver sulfadiazine is known to slow re-epithelialization somewhat, which gives a modest chance of a favorable signal, but formal significance on the primary endpoint is unlikely.

Liver-directed therapies often improve hepatic-specific PFS over systemic therapy alone, and the open-label, investigator-assessed hPFS endpoint favors the experimental arm. Against that, melphalan/HDS has only modest, uncontrolled activity in heavily pretreated colorectal liver metastases. The trial is small (90 patients, 2:1), and Arm A delays systemic FTD-TPI plus bevacizumab by roughly 12 weeks. The study only began in August 2025, is still recruiting, and may never be fully enrolled or adequately powered, which further lowers the chance of a clean positive readout.

Endothelin antagonists have clear evidence of kidney benefit: SONAR (atrasentan) reduced hard renal outcomes, PROTECT (sparsentan) improved eGFR slope, and the ZENITH-CKD phase 2b showed meaningful extra albuminuria lowering from zibotentan on top of dapagliflozin. The risk is that a 24-month change-in-eGFR primary absorbs the acute hemodynamic eGFR dip these drugs cause, and fluid retention may force discontinuations. Sparsentan's total-slope results were borderline in PROTECT, and DUPLEX missed its eGFR endpoint. The large, rapidly progressing high-proteinuria population (n≈1835) gives reasonable power, so I put success modestly above even odds.

610 (SSGJ-610) is an anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody, a mechanism well validated in severe eosinophilic asthma: mepolizumab and reslizumab consistently cut exacerbation rates by about 50% versus placebo, including in Chinese populations. A 480-patient, 52-week placebo-controlled trial with annualized severe exacerbation rate as the primary endpoint is well powered for an effect of that size. The main risks are a low placebo-arm exacerbation rate in a Chinese cohort and possibly loose eosinophil enrichment criteria. Primary completion is not expected until 2027, so no result is public.

KSI-101 is a bispecific IL-6/VEGF-trap fusion. The small open-label Phase 1b APEX study reported large BCVA gains and CST reductions in MESI, and sham-controlled trials of active agents in uveitic macular edema (e.g., PEACHTREE, HURON) have generally succeeded. Uncertainty comes from Roche's anti-IL-6 vamikibart, which gave mixed Phase 3 results (my recollection is that one of two trials missed), and from this trial's restriction to milder edema (CST 320–400 µm), which may limit the room for BCVA improvement over sham. With roughly 100 patients per arm, two doses, and a continuous BCVA primary endpoint, power should be reasonable, so I place the probability modestly above the Phase 3 base rate.

The only primary outcome is adverse-event incidence, a descriptive safety measure with no stated statistical comparison, so whether this trial 'meets its primary endpoint' depends on how the sponsor frames a topline result. LT3001 (odatroltide) has looked safe in earlier phase 2 work, including Lumosa's US trial, which reported acceptable symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage rates, so a 'safe and well tolerated' announcement is plausible. A strict reading that requires a significant favorable difference in AEs versus placebo would almost certainly fail, and efficacy signals in an unthrombolysed population treated up to 24 hours after onset are uncertain. Balancing these readings gives a near-coin-flip estimate leaning slightly positive.
